42: Doth make an earthquake of nobility.
43: O, what a noble combat hast thou fought
44: Between compulsion and a brave respect!
45: Let me wipe off this honorable dew
46: That silverly doth progress on thy cheeks.
47: My heart hath melted at a lady’s tears,
49: But this effusion of such manly drops,
50: This shower, blown up by tempest of the soul,
51: Startles mine eyes and makes me more amazed
52: Than had I seen the vaulty top of heaven
53: Figured quite o’er with burning meteors.
54: Lift up thy brow, renownèd Salisbury,
55: And with a great heart heave away this storm.
56: Commend these waters to those baby eyes
57: That never saw the giant world enraged,
58: Nor met with fortune other than at feasts
59: Full warm of blood, of mirth, of gossiping.
60: Come, come; for thou shalt thrust thy hand as deep
61: Into the purse of rich prosperity
62: As Louis himself.—So, nobles, shall you all,
63: That knit your sinews to the strength of mine.
64: And even there, methinks, an angel spake.
65: Look where the holy legate comes apace
66: To give us warrant from the hand of God,
67: And on our actions set the name of right
70: The next is this: King John hath reconciled
71: Himself to Rome; his spirit is come in
72: That so stood out against the holy Church,
73: The great metropolis and See of Rome.
74: Therefore thy threat’ning colors now wind up,
75: And tame the savage spirit of wild war
76: That, like a lion fostered up at hand,
77: It may lie gently at the foot of peace
78: And be no further harmful than in show.
79: Your Grace shall pardon me; I will not back.
80: I am too high-born to be propertied,
81: To be a secondary at control,
83: To any sovereign state throughout the world.
84: Your breath first kindled the dead coal of wars
85: Between this chastised kingdom and myself
86: And brought in matter that should feed this fire;
87: And now ’tis far too huge to be blown out
88: With that same weak wind which enkindled it.
89: You taught me how to know the face of right,
90: Acquainted me with interest to this land,
91: Yea, thrust this enterprise into my heart.
92: And come you now to tell me John hath made
93: His peace with Rome? What is that peace to me?
94: I, by the honor of my marriage bed,
95: After young Arthur claim this land for mine.
96: And now it is half conquered, must I back
97: Because that John hath made his peace with Rome?
98: Am I Rome’s slave? What penny hath Rome borne?
99: What men provided? What munition sent
100: To underprop this action? Is ’t not I
101: That undergo this charge? Who else but I,
102: And such as to my claim are liable,
103: Sweat in this business and maintain this war?
104: Have I not heard these islanders shout out
105: Vive le Roi as I have banked their towns?
106: Have I not here the best cards for the game
107: To win this easy match played for a crown?
108: And shall I now give o’er the yielded set?
109: No, no, on my soul, it never shall be said.
110: You look but on the outside of this work.
111: Outside or inside, I will not return
112: Till my attempt so much be glorified
113: As to my ample hope was promisèd
114: Before I drew this gallant head of war
115: And culled these fiery spirits from the world
116: To outlook conquest and to win renown
117: Even in the jaws of danger and of death.
118: What lusty trumpet thus doth summon us?
119: According to the fair play of the world,
120: Let me have audience. I am sent to speak,
121: My holy lord of Milan, from the King.
122: I come to learn how you have dealt for him,
123: And, as you answer, I do know the scope
124: And warrant limited unto my tongue.
126: And will not temporize with my entreaties.
127: He flatly says he’ll not lay down his arms.
128: By all the blood that ever fury breathed,
129: The youth says well! Now hear our English king,
130: For thus his royalty doth speak in me:
131: He is prepared—and reason too he should.
133: This harnessed masque and unadvisèd revel,
134: This unheard sauciness and boyish troops,
135: The King doth smile at, and is well prepared
136: To whip this dwarfish war, these pigmy arms,
137: From out the circle of his territories.
138: That hand which had the strength, even at your door,
139: To cudgel you and make you take the hatch,
140: To dive like buckets in concealèd wells,
141: To crouch in litter of your stable planks,
142: To lie like pawns locked up in chests and trunks,
143: To hug with swine, to seek sweet safety out
144: In vaults and prisons, and to thrill and shake
145: Even at the crying of your nation’s crow,
146: Thinking this voice an armèd Englishman—
147: Shall that victorious hand be feebled here
148: That in your chambers gave you chastisement?
149: No! Know the gallant monarch is in arms,
150: And like an eagle o’er his aerie towers
151: To souse annoyance that comes near his nest.—
152: And you degenerate, you ingrate revolts,
153: You bloody Neroes, ripping up the womb
154: Of your dear mother England, blush for shame!
155: For your own ladies and pale-visaged maids
156: Like Amazons come tripping after drums,
157: Their thimbles into armèd gauntlets change,
158: Their needles to lances, and their gentle hearts
160: There end thy brave and turn thy face in peace.
161: We grant thou canst outscold us. Fare thee well.
162: We hold our time too precious to be spent
167: Strike up the drums, and let the tongue of war
168: Plead for our interest and our being here.
169: Indeed, your drums being beaten will cry out,
170: And so shall you, being beaten. Do but start
171: An echo with the clamor of thy drum,
172: And even at hand a drum is ready braced
173: That shall reverberate all as loud as thine.
174: Sound but another, and another shall,
175: As loud as thine, rattle the welkin’s ear
176: And mock the deep-mouthed thunder. For at hand,
177: Not trusting to this halting legate here,
178: Whom he hath used rather for sport than need,
179: Is warlike John, and in his forehead sits
180: A bare-ribbed Death, whose office is this day
181: To feast upon whole thousands of the French.
182: Strike up our drums to find this danger out.
183: And thou shalt find it, dauphin, do not doubt.

1: How goes the day with us? O, tell me, Hubert.
2: Badly, I fear. How fares your Majesty?
3: This fever that hath troubled me so long
4: Lies heavy on me. O, my heart is sick.
5: My lord, your valiant kinsman, Faulconbridge,
6: Desires your Majesty to leave the field
7: And send him word by me which way you go.
8: Tell him toward Swinstead, to the abbey there.
9: Be of good comfort, for the great supply
10: That was expected by the Dauphin here
11: Are wracked three nights ago on Goodwin Sands.
12: This news was brought to Richard but even now.
13: The French fight coldly and retire themselves.
14: Ay me, this tyrant fever burns me up
15: And will not let me welcome this good news.
16: Set on toward Swinstead. To my litter straight.
17: Weakness possesseth me, and I am faint.

1: I did not think the King so stored with friends.
2: Up once again. Put spirit in the French.
3: If they miscarry, we miscarry too.
5: In spite of spite, alone upholds the day.

11: Fly, noble English; you are bought and sold.
12: Unthread the rude eye of rebellion

17: By cutting off your heads. Thus hath he sworn,
18: And I with him, and many more with me,
19: Upon the altar at Saint Edmundsbury,

22: May this be possible? May this be true?

24: Retaining but a quantity of life,
25: Which bleeds away even as a form of wax
26: Resolveth from his figure ’gainst the fire?
27: What in the world should make me now deceive,

29: Why should I then be false, since it is true

31: I say again, if Louis do win the day,
32: He is forsworn if e’er those eyes of yours
33: Behold another daybreak in the East.

35: Already smokes about the burning crest
36: Of the old, feeble, and day-wearied sun,

38: Paying the fine of rated treachery
39: Even with a treacherous fine of all your lives,
40: If Louis by your assistance win the day.
41: Commend me to one Hubert with your king;
42: The love of him, and this respect besides,
43: For that my grandsire was an Englishman,
44: Awakes my conscience to confess all this.
45: In lieu whereof, I pray you bear me hence
46: From forth the noise and rumor of the field,
47: Where I may think the remnant of my thoughts
48: In peace, and part this body and my soul
50: We do believe thee, and beshrew my soul
51: But I do love the favor and the form
52: Of this most fair occasion, by the which
53: We will untread the steps of damnèd flight,
54: And like a bated and retirèd flood,
55: Leaving our rankness and irregular course,
56: Stoop low within those bounds we have o’erlooked
57: And calmly run on in obedience
58: Even to our ocean, to our great King John.
59: My arm shall give thee help to bear thee hence,
60: For I do see the cruel pangs of death
61: Right in thine eye.—Away, my friends! New flight,
62: And happy newness, that intends old right.

1: The sun of heaven, methought, was loath to set,
2: But stayed and made the western welkin blush,
3: When English measured backward their own ground
5: In faint retire. O, bravely came we off,
6: When with a volley of our needless shot,
7: After such bloody toil, we bid good night
8: And wound our tott’ring colors clearly up,
9: Last in the field and almost lords of it.
10: Where is my prince, the Dauphin?
12: The Count Melun is slain. The English lords,
13: By his persuasion, are again fall’n off,
14: And your supply, which you have wished so long,
15: Are cast away and sunk on Goodwin Sands.
16: Ah, foul, shrewd news. Beshrew thy very heart!
17: I did not think to be so sad tonight
18: As this hath made me. Who was he that said
19: King John did fly an hour or two before
20: The stumbling night did part our weary powers?
21: Whoever spoke it, it is true, my lord.
22: Well, keep good quarter and good care tonight.
23: The day shall not be up so soon as I
24: To try the fair adventure of tomorrow.

1: Who’s there? Speak ho! Speak quickly, or I shoot.
6: Why may not I demand of thine affairs
7: As well as thou of mine? Hubert, I think?

44: Passing these flats, are taken by the tide.

46: Myself, well mounted, hardly have escaped.
47: Away before. Conduct me to the King.
48: I doubt he will be dead or ere I come.

13: Than when you left him. Even now he sung.

35: Upon a parchment, and against this fire
39: And none of you will bid the winter come

41: Nor let my kingdom’s rivers take their course
42: Through my burned bosom, nor entreat the North

47: O, that there were some virtue in my tears

51: Is, as a fiend, confined to tyrannize

54: And spleen of speed to see your Majesty.

82: To push destruction and perpetual shame

85: The Dauphin rages at our very heels.

88: Who half an hour since came from the Dauphin,

94: Nay, ’tis in a manner done already,

1: Old John of Gaunt, time-honored Lancaster,
2: Hast thou, according to thy oath and band,
3: Brought hither Henry Hereford, thy bold son,
4: Here to make good the boist’rous late appeal,
5: Which then our leisure would not let us hear,
6: Against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?
8: Tell me, moreover, hast thou sounded him
9: If he appeal the Duke on ancient malice
10: Or worthily, as a good subject should,
11: On some known ground of treachery in him?
12: As near as I could sift him on that argument,
13: On some apparent danger seen in him
14: Aimed at your Highness, no inveterate malice.
15: Then call them to our presence.
17: And frowning brow to brow, ourselves will hear
18: The accuser and the accusèd freely speak.
19: High stomached are they both and full of ire,
20: In rage deaf as the sea, hasty as fire.
21: Many years of happy days befall
22: My gracious sovereign, my most loving liege.
23: Each day still better other’s happiness
24: Until the heavens, envying earth’s good hap,
25: Add an immortal title to your crown.
26: We thank you both. Yet one but flatters us,
27: As well appeareth by the cause you come:
28: Namely, to appeal each other of high treason.
29: Cousin of Hereford, what dost thou object
30: Against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?
31: First—heaven be the record to my speech!—
32: In the devotion of a subject’s love,
33: Tend’ring the precious safety of my prince
34: And free from other misbegotten hate,
35: Come I appellant to this princely presence.—
36: Now, Thomas Mowbray, do I turn to thee;
37: And mark my greeting well, for what I speak
38: My body shall make good upon this earth
39: Or my divine soul answer it in heaven.
40: Thou art a traitor and a miscreant,
41: Too good to be so and too bad to live,
42: Since the more fair and crystal is the sky,
43: The uglier seem the clouds that in it fly.
44: Once more, the more to aggravate the note,
45: With a foul traitor’s name stuff I thy throat,
46: And wish, so please my sovereign, ere I move,
47: What my tongue speaks my right-drawn sword may prove.
49: Let not my cold words here accuse my zeal.
50: ’Tis not the trial of a woman’s war,
51: The bitter clamor of two eager tongues,
52: Can arbitrate this cause betwixt us twain.
53: The blood is hot that must be cooled for this.
54: Yet can I not of such tame patience boast
55: As to be hushed and naught at all to say.
56: First, the fair reverence of your Highness curbs me
57: From giving reins and spurs to my free speech,
58: Which else would post until it had returned
59: These terms of treason doubled down his throat.
60: Setting aside his high blood’s royalty,
61: And let him be no kinsman to my liege,
62: I do defy him, and I spit at him,
63: Call him a slanderous coward and a villain,
64: Which to maintain I would allow him odds
65: And meet him, were I tied to run afoot
66: Even to the frozen ridges of the Alps
68: Wherever Englishman durst set his foot.
69: Meantime let this defend my loyalty:
70: By all my hopes, most falsely doth he lie.
71: Pale trembling coward, there I throw my gage,
72: Disclaiming here the kindred of the King,
73: And lay aside my high blood’s royalty,
74: Which fear, not reverence, makes thee to except.
75: If guilty dread have left thee so much strength
76: As to take up mine honor’s pawn, then stoop.
77: By that and all the rites of knighthood else
78: Will I make good against thee, arm to arm,
79: What I have spoke or thou canst worse devise.
80: I take it up, and by that sword I swear
81: Which gently laid my knighthood on my shoulder,
82: I’ll answer thee in any fair degree
83: Or chivalrous design of knightly trial;
84: And when I mount, alive may I not light
85: If I be traitor or unjustly fight.
86: What doth our cousin lay to Mowbray’s charge?
87: It must be great that can inherit us
88: So much as of a thought of ill in him.
89: Look what I speak, my life shall prove it true:
90: That Mowbray hath received eight thousand nobles
91: In name of lendings for your Highness’ soldiers,
92: The which he hath detained for lewd employments,
93: Like a false traitor and injurious villain.
94: Besides I say, and will in battle prove,
95: Or here or elsewhere to the furthest verge
96: That ever was surveyed by English eye,
97: That all the treasons for these eighteen years
98: Complotted and contrivèd in this land
99: Fetch from false Mowbray their first head and spring.
101: Further I say, and further will maintain
102: Upon his bad life to make all this good,
103: That he did plot the Duke of Gloucester’s death,
105: And consequently, like a traitor coward,
106: Sluiced out his innocent soul through streams of blood,
108: Which blood, like sacrificing Abel’s, cries
109: Even from the tongueless caverns of the earth
110: To me for justice and rough chastisement.
111: And, by the glorious worth of my descent,
112: This arm shall do it, or this life be spent.
113: How high a pitch his resolution soars!—
114: Thomas of Norfolk, what sayst thou to this?
115: O, let my sovereign turn away his face
116: And bid his ears a little while be deaf,
117: Till I have told this slander of his blood
118: How God and good men hate so foul a liar.
119: Mowbray, impartial are our eyes and ears.
120: Were he my brother, nay, my kingdom’s heir,

125: The unstooping firmness of my upright soul.

202: We were not born to sue, but to command,
203: Which, since we cannot do, to make you friends,
204: Be ready, as your lives shall answer it,
205: At Coventry upon Saint Lambert’s day.
206: There shall your swords and lances arbitrate
207: The swelling difference of your settled hate.
208: Since we cannot atone you, we shall see
211: Be ready to direct these home alarms.

1: Alas, the part I had in Woodstock’s blood
2: Doth more solicit me than your exclaims
3: To stir against the butchers of his life.
4: But since correction lieth in those hands
5: Which made the fault that we cannot correct,
6: Put we our quarrel to the will of heaven,
7: Who, when they see the hours ripe on Earth,
8: Will rain hot vengeance on offenders’ heads.
9: Finds brotherhood in thee no sharper spur?
10: Hath love in thy old blood no living fire?
11: Edward’s seven sons, whereof thyself art one,
12: Were as seven vials of his sacred blood
13: Or seven fair branches springing from one root.
14: Some of those seven are dried by nature’s course,
15: Some of those branches by the Destinies cut.
16: But Thomas, my dear lord, my life, my Gloucester,
17: One vial full of Edward’s sacred blood,
18: One flourishing branch of his most royal root,
19: Is cracked and all the precious liquor spilt,
20: Is hacked down, and his summer leaves all faded,
21: By envy’s hand and murder’s bloody ax.
22: Ah, Gaunt, his blood was thine! That bed, that womb,
24: That metal, that self mold that fashioned thee
25: Made him a man; and though thou livest and breathest,
27: Yet art thou slain in him. Thou dost consent
28: In some large measure to thy father’s death
29: In that thou seest thy wretched brother die,
30: Who was the model of thy father’s life.
31: Call it not patience, Gaunt. It is despair.
32: In suff’ring thus thy brother to be slaughtered,
33: Thou showest the naked pathway to thy life,
34: Teaching stern murder how to butcher thee.
35: That which in mean men we entitle patience
36: Is pale, cold cowardice in noble breasts.
37: What shall I say? To safeguard thine own life,
38: The best way is to venge my Gloucester’s death.
39: God’s is the quarrel; for God’s substitute,
40: His deputy anointed in His sight,
41: Hath caused his death, the which if wrongfully
42: Let heaven revenge, for I may never lift
43: An angry arm against His minister.
44: Where, then, alas, may I complain myself?
45: To God, the widow’s champion and defense.
46: Why then I will. Farewell, old Gaunt.
47: Thou goest to Coventry, there to behold
48: Our cousin Hereford and fell Mowbray fight.
49: O, sit my husband’s wrongs on Hereford’s spear,
50: That it may enter butcher Mowbray’s breast!
51: Or if misfortune miss the first career,
52: Be Mowbray’s sins so heavy in his bosom
53: That they may break his foaming courser’s back
54: And throw the rider headlong in the lists,
55: A caitiff recreant to my cousin Hereford!
56: Farewell, old Gaunt. Thy sometime brother’s wife
57: With her companion, grief, must end her life.
58: Sister, farewell. I must to Coventry.
59: As much good stay with thee as go with me.
60: Yet one word more. Grief boundeth where it falls,
61: Not with the empty hollowness, but weight.
62: I take my leave before I have begun,
63: For sorrow ends not when it seemeth done.
64: Commend me to thy brother, Edmund York.
65: Lo, this is all. Nay, yet depart not so!
66: Though this be all, do not so quickly go;
67: I shall remember more. Bid him—ah, what?—
68: With all good speed at Plashy visit me.
69: Alack, and what shall good old York there see
70: But empty lodgings and unfurnished walls,
72: And what hear there for welcome but my groans?
73: Therefore commend me; let him not come there
74: To seek out sorrow that dwells everywhere.
75: Desolate, desolate, will I hence and die.
76: The last leave of thee takes my weeping eye.

1: My Lord Aumerle, is Harry Hereford armed?
2: Yea, at all points, and longs to enter in.
3: The Duke of Norfolk, sprightfully and bold,
4: Stays but the summons of the appellant’s trumpet.
5: Why then, the champions are prepared and stay
6: For nothing but his Majesty’s approach.
8: The cause of his arrival here in arms,
9: Ask him his name, and orderly proceed
10: To swear him in the justice of his cause.
11: In God’s name and the King’s, say who thou art
12: And why thou comest thus knightly clad in arms,
13: Against what man thou com’st, and what thy quarrel.
14: Speak truly on thy knighthood and thy oath,
15: As so defend thee heaven and thy valor.
16: My name is Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk,
17: Who hither come engagèd by my oath—
18: Which God defend a knight should violate!—
19: Both to defend my loyalty and truth
20: To God, my king, and my succeeding issue,
21: Against the Duke of Hereford that appeals me,
22: And by the grace of God and this mine arm
23: To prove him, in defending of myself,
24: A traitor to my God, my king, and me;
25: And as I truly fight, defend me heaven.
26: Marshal, ask yonder knight in arms
27: Both who he is and why he cometh hither
28: Thus plated in habiliments of war,
29: And formally, according to our law,
30: Depose him in the justice of his cause.
31: What is thy name? And wherefore com’st thou hither,
32: Before King Richard in his royal lists?
33: Against whom comest thou? And what’s thy quarrel?
34: Speak like a true knight, so defend thee heaven.
35: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby
36: Am I, who ready here do stand in arms
37: To prove, by God’s grace and my body’s valor,
38: In lists, on Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk,
39: That he is a traitor foul and dangerous
40: To God of heaven, King Richard, and to me.
41: And as I truly fight, defend me heaven.
42: On pain of death, no person be so bold
43: Or daring-hardy as to touch the lists,
44: Except the Marshal and such officers
45: Appointed to direct these fair designs.
46: Lord Marshal, let me kiss my sovereign’s hand
47: And bow my knee before his Majesty;
48: For Mowbray and myself are like two men
49: That vow a long and weary pilgrimage.
50: Then let us take a ceremonious leave
51: And loving farewell of our several friends.
52: The appellant in all duty greets your Highness
53: And craves to kiss your hand and take his leave.
54: We will descend and fold him in our arms.
55: Cousin of Hereford, as thy cause is right,
56: So be thy fortune in this royal fight.
57: Farewell, my blood—which, if today thou shed,
58: Lament we may but not revenge thee dead.
59: O, let no noble eye profane a tear
60: For me if I be gored with Mowbray’s spear.
61: As confident as is the falcon’s flight
62: Against a bird do I with Mowbray fight.
63: My loving lord, I take my leave of you.—
64: Of you, my noble cousin, Lord Aumerle;
65: Not sick, although I have to do with death,
66: But lusty, young, and cheerly drawing breath.—
67: Lo, as at English feasts, so I regreet
68: The daintiest last, to make the end most sweet.
69: O, thou the earthly author of my blood,
70: Whose youthful spirit in me regenerate
71: Doth with a twofold vigor lift me up
72: To reach at victory above my head,
73: Add proof unto mine armor with thy prayers,
74: And with thy blessings steel my lance’s point
75: That it may enter Mowbray’s waxen coat
76: And furbish new the name of John o’ Gaunt,
77: Even in the lusty havior of his son.
78: God in thy good cause make thee prosperous.
79: Be swift like lightning in the execution,
80: And let thy blows, doubly redoubled,
81: Fall like amazing thunder on the casque
83: Rouse up thy youthful blood, be valiant, and live.
84: Mine innocence and Saint George to thrive!
85: However God or fortune cast my lot,
86: There lives or dies, true to King Richard’s throne,
87: A loyal, just, and upright gentleman.
88: Never did captive with a freer heart
89: Cast off his chains of bondage and embrace
91: More than my dancing soul doth celebrate
92: This feast of battle with mine adversary.
93: Most mighty liege and my companion peers,
94: Take from my mouth the wish of happy years.
95: As gentle and as jocund as to jest
96: Go I to fight. Truth hath a quiet breast.
97: Farewell, my lord. Securely I espy
98: Virtue with valor couchèd in thine eye.—
99: Order the trial, marshal, and begin.
100: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby,
101: Receive thy lance; and God defend the right.
102: Strong as a tower in hope, I cry Amen!
103: Go bear this lance to Thomas, Duke of Norfolk.
104: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby
105: Stands here for God, his sovereign, and himself,
106: On pain to be found false and recreant,
107: To prove the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray,
108: A traitor to his God, his king, and him,
109: And dares him to set forward to the fight.
110: Here standeth Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk,
111: On pain to be found false and recreant,
112: Both to defend himself and to approve
113: Henry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby
114: To God, his sovereign, and to him disloyal,
115: Courageously and with a free desire
116: Attending but the signal to begin.
117: Sound, trumpets, and set forward, combatants.
118: Stay! The King hath thrown his warder down.
119: Let them lay by their helmets and their spears,
120: And both return back to their chairs again.
121: Withdraw with us, and let the trumpets sound
123: While we return these dukes what we decree.
125: And list what with our council we have done.
126: For that our kingdom’s earth should not be soiled
127: With that dear blood which it hath fosterèd;
128: And for our eyes do hate the dire aspect
129: Of civil wounds plowed up with neighbor’s sword;
130: And for we think the eagle-wingèd pride
132: With rival-hating envy, set on you
133: To wake our peace, which in our country’s cradle
134: Draws the sweet infant breath of gentle sleep,
135: Which, so roused up with boist’rous untuned drums,
137: With harsh resounding trumpets’ dreadful bray,
138: And grating shock of wrathful iron arms,
139: Might from our quiet confines fright fair peace
140: And make us wade even in our kindred’s blood:
141: Therefore we banish you our territories.
142: You, cousin Hereford, upon pain of life,
143: Till twice five summers have enriched our fields
144: Shall not regreet our fair dominions,
145: But tread the stranger paths of banishment.
146: Your will be done. This must my comfort be:
147: That sun that warms you here shall shine on me,
148: And those his golden beams to you here lent
149: Shall point on me and gild my banishment.
150: Norfolk, for thee remains a heavier doom,
151: Which I with some unwillingness pronounce:
152: The sly, slow hours shall not determinate
153: The dateless limit of thy dear exile.
154: The hopeless word of never to return
155: Breathe I against thee, upon pain of life.
156: A heavy sentence, my most sovereign liege,
157: And all unlooked-for from your Highness’ mouth.
158: A dearer merit, not so deep a maim
159: As to be cast forth in the common air,
160: Have I deservèd at your Highness’ hands.
161: The language I have learnt these forty years,
162: My native English, now I must forgo;
163: And now my tongue’s use is to me no more
164: Than an unstringèd viol or a harp,
165: Or like a cunning instrument cased up,
166: Or, being open, put into his hands
167: That knows no touch to tune the harmony.
168: Within my mouth you have enjailed my tongue,
169: Doubly portcullised with my teeth and lips,
171: Is made my jailor to attend on me.
172: I am too old to fawn upon a nurse,
173: Too far in years to be a pupil now.
174: What is thy sentence then but speechless death,
175: Which robs my tongue from breathing native breath?
177: It boots thee not to be compassionate.
178: After our sentence plaining comes too late.
179: Then thus I turn me from my country’s light,
180: To dwell in solemn shades of endless night.
181: Return again, and take an oath with thee.
182: Lay on our royal sword your banished hands.
184: Swear by the duty that you owe to God—
185: Our part therein we banish with yourselves—
186: To keep the oath that we administer:
187: You never shall, so help you truth and God,
188: Embrace each other’s love in banishment,
189: Nor never look upon each other’s face,
190: Nor never write, regreet, nor reconcile
191: This louring tempest of your homebred hate,
192: Nor never by advisèd purpose meet
193: To plot, contrive, or complot any ill
194: ’Gainst us, our state, our subjects, or our land.
196: And I, to keep all this.
197: Norfolk, so far as to mine enemy:
198: By this time, had the King permitted us,
199: One of our souls had wandered in the air,
200: Banished this frail sepulcher of our flesh,
201: As now our flesh is banished from this land.
202: Confess thy treasons ere thou fly the realm.
203: Since thou hast far to go, bear not along
204: The clogging burden of a guilty soul.
205: No, Bolingbroke; if ever I were traitor,
206: My name be blotted from the book of life,
207: And I from heaven banished as from hence.
208: But what thou art, God, thou, and I do know,
209: And all too soon, I fear, the King shall rue.—
210: Farewell, my liege. Now no way can I stray;
211: Save back to England, all the world’s my way.
212: Uncle, even in the glasses of thine eyes
213: I see thy grievèd heart. Thy sad aspect
214: Hath from the number of his banished years
217: Return with welcome home from banishment.
218: How long a time lies in one little word!
219: Four lagging winters and four wanton springs
220: End in a word; such is the breath of kings.
221: I thank my liege that in regard of me
222: He shortens four years of my son’s exile.
223: But little vantage shall I reap thereby;
224: For, ere the six years that he hath to spend
225: Can change their moons and bring their times about,
227: My oil-dried lamp and time-bewasted light
228: Shall be extinct with age and endless night;
229: My inch of taper will be burnt and done,
230: And blindfold death not let me see my son.
231: Why, uncle, thou hast many years to live.
232: But not a minute, king, that thou canst give.
233: Shorten my days thou canst with sullen sorrow,
234: And pluck nights from me, but not lend a morrow.
235: Thou canst help time to furrow me with age,
236: But stop no wrinkle in his pilgrimage.
237: Thy word is current with him for my death,
238: But dead, thy kingdom cannot buy my breath.
239: Thy son is banished upon good advice,
240: Whereto thy tongue a party verdict gave.
241: Why at our justice seem’st thou then to lour?
242: Things sweet to taste prove in digestion sour.
243: You urged me as a judge, but I had rather
244: You would have bid me argue like a father.
245: O, had it been a stranger, not my child,
246: To smooth his fault I should have been more mild.
247: A partial slander sought I to avoid,
248: And in the sentence my own life destroyed.
249: Alas, I looked when some of you should say
250: I was too strict, to make mine own away.
251: But you gave leave to my unwilling tongue
252: Against my will to do myself this wrong.
253: Cousin, farewell.—And, uncle, bid him so.
254: Six years we banish him, and he shall go.
255: Cousin, farewell. What presence must not know,
256: From where you do remain let paper show.
257: My lord, no leave take I, for I will ride,
258: As far as land will let me, by your side.
259: O, to what purpose dost thou hoard thy words,
260: That thou returnest no greeting to thy friends?
261: I have too few to take my leave of you,
262: When the tongue’s office should be prodigal
263: To breathe the abundant dolor of the heart.
264: Thy grief is but thy absence for a time.
265: Joy absent, grief is present for that time.
266: What is six winters? They are quickly gone.
267: To men in joy; but grief makes one hour ten.
268: Call it a travel that thou tak’st for pleasure.
269: My heart will sigh when I miscall it so,
270: Which finds it an enforcèd pilgrimage.
271: The sullen passage of thy weary steps
272: Esteem as foil wherein thou art to set
273: The precious jewel of thy home return.
274: Nay, rather every tedious stride I make
275: Will but remember me what a deal of world
276: I wander from the jewels that I love.
277: Must I not serve a long apprenticehood
278: To foreign passages, and in the end,
279: Having my freedom, boast of nothing else
280: But that I was a journeyman to grief?
281: All places that the eye of heaven visits
282: Are to a wise man ports and happy havens.
283: Teach thy necessity to reason thus:
284: There is no virtue like necessity.
285: Think not the King did banish thee,
286: But thou the King. Woe doth the heavier sit
287: Where it perceives it is but faintly borne.
288: Go, say I sent thee forth to purchase honor,
289: And not the King exiled thee; or suppose
290: Devouring pestilence hangs in our air
291: And thou art flying to a fresher clime.
292: Look what thy soul holds dear, imagine it
293: To lie that way thou goest, not whence thou com’st.
295: The grass whereon thou tread’st the presence strewed,
297: The flowers fair ladies, and thy steps no more
298: Than a delightful measure or a dance;
299: For gnarling sorrow hath less power to bite
300: The man that mocks at it and sets it light.
301: O, who can hold a fire in his hand
302: By thinking on the frosty Caucasus?
303: Or cloy the hungry edge of appetite
304: By bare imagination of a feast?
305: Or wallow naked in December snow
306: By thinking on fantastic summer’s heat?
307: O no, the apprehension of the good
308: Gives but the greater feeling to the worse.
309: Fell sorrow’s tooth doth never rankle more
310: Than when he bites but lanceth not the sore.
311: Come, come, my son, I’ll bring thee on thy way.
312: Had I thy youth and cause, I would not stay.
313: Then, England’s ground, farewell; sweet soil, adieu,
314: My mother and my nurse that bears me yet.
315: Where’er I wander, boast of this I can,
316: Though banished, yet a trueborn Englishman.

2: How far brought you high Hereford on his way?

4: But to the next highway, and there I left him.
5: And say, what store of parting tears were shed?
6: Faith, none for me, except the northeast wind,
7: Which then blew bitterly against our faces,
8: Awaked the sleeping rheum and so by chance
9: Did grace our hollow parting with a tear.
10: What said our cousin when you parted with him?
12: And, for my heart disdainèd that my tongue
13: Should so profane the word, that taught me craft
14: To counterfeit oppression of such grief
15: That words seemed buried in my sorrow’s grave.
16: Marry, would the word farewell have lengthened hours
18: And added years to his short banishment,
19: He should have had a volume of farewells.
20: But since it would not, he had none of me.
21: He is our cousin, cousin, but ’tis doubt,
22: When time shall call him home from banishment,
23: Whether our kinsman come to see his friends.
24: Ourself and Bushy, Bagot here and Green,
25: Observed his courtship to the common people,
26: How he did seem to dive into their hearts
28: What reverence he did throw away on slaves,
29: Wooing poor craftsmen with the craft of smiles
30: And patient underbearing of his fortune,
31: As ’twere to banish their affects with him.
32: Off goes his bonnet to an oysterwench;
33: A brace of draymen bid God speed him well
34: And had the tribute of his supple knee,
35: With Thanks, my countrymen, my loving friends,
36: As were our England in reversion his
37: And he our subjects’ next degree in hope.
38: Well, he is gone, and with him go these thoughts.
39: Now for the rebels which stand out in Ireland,
40: Expedient manage must be made, my liege,
41: Ere further leisure yield them further means
42: For their advantage and your Highness’ loss.
43: We will ourself in person to this war.
44: And, for our coffers, with too great a court
45: And liberal largess, are grown somewhat light,
46: We are enforced to farm our royal realm,
47: The revenue whereof shall furnish us
48: For our affairs in hand. If that come short,
49: Our substitutes at home shall have blank charters,
50: Whereto, when they shall know what men are rich,
51: They shall subscribe them for large sums of gold
52: And send them after to supply our wants,
53: For we will make for Ireland presently.
55: Old John of Gaunt is grievous sick, my lord,
56: Suddenly taken, and hath sent posthaste
57: To entreat your Majesty to visit him.
60: Now put it, God, in the physician’s mind
61: To help him to his grave immediately!
62: The lining of his coffers shall make coats
63: To deck our soldiers for these Irish wars.
64: Come, gentlemen, let’s all go visit him.
65: Pray God we may make haste and come too late.

1: Will the King come, that I may breathe my last
2: In wholesome counsel to his unstaid youth?
3: Vex not yourself nor strive not with your breath,
4: For all in vain comes counsel to his ear.
5: O, but they say the tongues of dying men
7: Where words are scarce, they are seldom spent in vain,
9: For they breathe truth that breathe their words in pain.
11: He that no more must say is listened more
12: Than they whom youth and ease have taught to gloze.
14: More are men’s ends marked than their lives before.
15: The setting sun and music at the close,
16: As the last taste of sweets, is sweetest last,
17: Writ in remembrance more than things long past.
18: Though Richard my life’s counsel would not hear,
19: My death’s sad tale may yet undeaf his ear.
20: No, it is stopped with other flattering sounds,
21: As praises, of whose taste the wise are fond;
22: Lascivious meters, to whose venom sound
23: The open ear of youth doth always listen;
24: Report of fashions in proud Italy,
25: Whose manners still our tardy-apish nation
27: Where doth the world thrust forth a vanity—
28: So it be new, there’s no respect how vile—
29: That is not quickly buzzed into his ears?
30: Then all too late comes counsel to be heard
31: Where will doth mutiny with wit’s regard.
32: Direct not him whose way himself will choose.
33: ’Tis breath thou lack’st, and that breath wilt thou lose.
35: Methinks I am a prophet new inspired
36: And thus expiring do foretell of him:
37: His rash fierce blaze of riot cannot last,
38: For violent fires soon burn out themselves;
39: Small showers last long, but sudden storms are short;
41: He tires betimes that spurs too fast betimes;
42: With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder;
44: Consuming means, soon preys upon itself.
45: This royal throne of kings, this sceptered isle,
46: This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars,
48: This fortress built by Nature for herself
49: Against infection and the hand of war,
50: This happy breed of men, this little world,
51: This precious stone set in the silver sea,
52: Which serves it in the office of a wall
53: Or as a moat defensive to a house,
54: Against the envy of less happier lands,
55: This blessèd plot, this earth, this realm, this England,
57: This nurse, this teeming womb of royal kings,
58: Feared by their breed and famous by their birth,
59: Renownèd for their deeds as far from home
60: For Christian service and true chivalry
61: As is the sepulcher in stubborn Jewry
62: Of the world’s ransom, blessèd Mary’s son,
63: This land of such dear souls, this dear dear land,
64: Dear for her reputation through the world,
65: Is now leased out—I die pronouncing it—
66: Like to a tenement or pelting farm.
67: England, bound in with the triumphant sea,
68: Whose rocky shore beats back the envious siege
69: Of wat’ry Neptune, is now bound in with shame,
70: With inky blots and rotten parchment bonds.
71: That England that was wont to conquer others
72: Hath made a shameful conquest of itself.
73: Ah, would the scandal vanish with my life,
74: How happy then were my ensuing death!
75: The King is come. Deal mildly with his youth,
76: For young hot colts being reined do rage the more.
77: How fares our noble uncle Lancaster?
78: What comfort, man? How is ’t with agèd Gaunt?
79: O, how that name befits my composition!
80: Old Gaunt indeed and gaunt in being old.
81: Within me grief hath kept a tedious fast,
82: And who abstains from meat that is not gaunt?
83: For sleeping England long time have I watched;
84: Watching breeds leanness, leanness is all gaunt.
85: The pleasure that some fathers feed upon
86: Is my strict fast—I mean my children’s looks—
87: And, therein fasting, hast thou made me gaunt.
88: Gaunt am I for the grave, gaunt as a grave,
89: Whose hollow womb inherits naught but bones.
90: Can sick men play so nicely with their names?
91: No, misery makes sport to mock itself.
92: Since thou dost seek to kill my name in me,
93: I mock my name, great king, to flatter thee.
94: Should dying men flatter with those that live?
95: No, no, men living flatter those that die.
96: Thou, now a-dying, sayest thou flatterest me.
97: O, no, thou diest, though I the sicker be.
98: I am in health, I breathe, and see thee ill.
99: Now He that made me knows I see thee ill,
100: Ill in myself to see, and in thee, seeing ill.
101: Thy deathbed is no lesser than thy land,
102: Wherein thou liest in reputation sick;
103: And thou, too careless-patient as thou art,
104: Commit’st thy anointed body to the cure
105: Of those physicians that first wounded thee.
106: A thousand flatterers sit within thy crown,
107: Whose compass is no bigger than thy head,
108: And yet encagèd in so small a verge,
109: The waste is no whit lesser than thy land.
110: O, had thy grandsire with a prophet’s eye
111: Seen how his son’s son should destroy his sons,

113: Deposing thee before thou wert possessed,

115: Why, cousin, wert thou regent of the world,
116: It were a shame to let this land by lease;
117: But, for thy world enjoying but this land,
118: Is it not more than shame to shame it so?
119: Landlord of England art thou now, not king.
120: Thy state of law is bondslave to the law,
125: Make pale our cheek, chasing the royal blood
126: With fury from his native residence.
127: Now, by my seat’s right royal majesty,
128: Wert thou not brother to great Edward’s son,
129: This tongue that runs so roundly in thy head
130: Should run thy head from thy unreverent shoulders.
131: O, spare me not, my brother Edward’s son,
132: For that I was his father Edward’s son!
133: That blood already, like the pelican,
134: Hast thou tapped out and drunkenly caroused.
136: Whom fair befall in heaven ’mongst happy souls—
137: May be a precedent and witness good
138: That thou respect’st not spilling Edward’s blood.
139: Join with the present sickness that I have,
140: And thy unkindness be like crooked age
141: To crop at once a too-long withered flower.
142: Live in thy shame, but die not shame with thee!
143: These words hereafter thy tormentors be!—
144: Convey me to my bed, then to my grave.
145: Love they to live that love and honor have.
146: And let them die that age and sullens have,
147: For both hast thou, and both become the grave.
148: I do beseech your Majesty, impute his words
149: To wayward sickliness and age in him.
150: He loves you, on my life, and holds you dear
151: As Harry, Duke of Hereford, were he here.
152: Right, you say true: as Hereford’s love, so his;
153: As theirs, so mine; and all be as it is.
154: My liege, old Gaunt commends him to your Majesty.
157: His tongue is now a stringless instrument;
158: Words, life, and all, old Lancaster hath spent.
159: Be York the next that must be bankrupt so!
160: Though death be poor, it ends a mortal woe.
161: The ripest fruit first falls, and so doth he;
162: His time is spent, our pilgrimage must be.
163: So much for that. Now for our Irish wars:
164: We must supplant those rough rugheaded kern,
165: Which live like venom where no venom else
166: But only they have privilege to live.
167: And, for these great affairs do ask some charge,
168: Towards our assistance we do seize to us
169: The plate, coin, revenues, and movables
170: Whereof our uncle Gaunt did stand possessed.
171: How long shall I be patient? Ah, how long
172: Shall tender duty make me suffer wrong?
173: Not Gloucester’s death, nor Hereford’s banishment,
174: Nor Gaunt’s rebukes, nor England’s private wrongs,
175: Nor the prevention of poor Bolingbroke
176: About his marriage, nor my own disgrace,
177: Have ever made me sour my patient cheek
178: Or bend one wrinkle on my sovereign’s face.
179: I am the last of noble Edward’s sons,
180: Of whom thy father, Prince of Wales, was first.
181: In war was never lion raged more fierce,
182: In peace was never gentle lamb more mild,
183: Than was that young and princely gentleman.
184: His face thou hast, for even so looked he,
185: Accomplished with the number of thy hours;
186: But when he frowned, it was against the French
187: And not against his friends. His noble hand
188: Did win what he did spend, and spent not that
189: Which his triumphant father’s hand had won.
190: His hands were guilty of no kindred blood,
191: But bloody with the enemies of his kin.
192: O, Richard! York is too far gone with grief,
193: Or else he never would compare between.
196: Pardon me if you please. If not, I, pleased
197: Not to be pardoned, am content withal.
198: Seek you to seize and gripe into your hands
199: The royalties and rights of banished Hereford?
200: Is not Gaunt dead? And doth not Hereford live?
201: Was not Gaunt just? And is not Harry true?
202: Did not the one deserve to have an heir?
203: Is not his heir a well-deserving son?
204: Take Hereford’s rights away, and take from time
205: His charters and his customary rights;
206: Let not tomorrow then ensue today;
207: Be not thyself; for how art thou a king
208: But by fair sequence and succession?
209: Now afore God—God forbid I say true!—
210: If you do wrongfully seize Hereford’s rights,
211: Call in the letters patents that he hath
212: By his attorneys general to sue
213: His livery, and deny his offered homage,
214: You pluck a thousand dangers on your head,
215: You lose a thousand well-disposèd hearts,
216: And prick my tender patience to those thoughts
217: Which honor and allegiance cannot think.
218: Think what you will, we seize into our hands
219: His plate, his goods, his money, and his lands.
220: I’ll not be by the while. My liege, farewell.
221: What will ensue hereof there’s none can tell;
222: But by bad courses may be understood
223: That their events can never fall out good.
224: Go, Bushy, to the Earl of Wiltshire straight.
225: Bid him repair to us to Ely House
226: To see this business. Tomorrow next
227: We will for Ireland, and ’tis time, I trow.
228: And we create, in absence of ourself,
229: Our uncle York Lord Governor of England,
230: For he is just and always loved us well.—
231: Come on, our queen. Tomorrow must we part.
232: Be merry, for our time of stay is short.
233: Well, lords, the Duke of Lancaster is dead.
234: And living too, for now his son is duke.
235: Barely in title, not in revenues.
236: Richly in both, if justice had her right.
237: My heart is great, but it must break with silence
238: Ere ’t be disburdened with a liberal tongue.
239: Nay, speak thy mind, and let him ne’er speak more
240: That speaks thy words again to do thee harm!
241: Tends that thou wouldst speak to the Duke of Hereford?
243: If it be so, out with it boldly, man.
244: Quick is mine ear to hear of good towards him.
245: No good at all that I can do for him,
246: Unless you call it good to pity him,
247: Bereft and gelded of his patrimony.
248: Now, afore God, ’tis shame such wrongs are borne
249: In him, a royal prince, and many more
250: Of noble blood in this declining land.
251: The King is not himself, but basely led
252: By flatterers; and what they will inform
253: Merely in hate ’gainst any of us all,
254: That will the King severely prosecute
255: ’Gainst us, our lives, our children, and our heirs.
256: The commons hath he pilled with grievous taxes,
257: And quite lost their hearts. The nobles hath he fined
258: For ancient quarrels, and quite lost their hearts.
259: And daily new exactions are devised,
260: As blanks, benevolences, and I wot not what.
261: But what i’ God’s name doth become of this?
262: Wars hath not wasted it, for warred he hath not,
264: That which his noble ancestors achieved with blows.
265: More hath he spent in peace than they in wars.
266: The Earl of Wiltshire hath the realm in farm.
267: The King grown bankrupt like a broken man.
268: Reproach and dissolution hangeth over him.
269: He hath not money for these Irish wars,
271: But by the robbing of the banished duke.
272: His noble kinsman. Most degenerate king!
273: But, lords, we hear this fearful tempest sing,
274: Yet seek no shelter to avoid the storm;
275: We see the wind sit sore upon our sails,
276: And yet we strike not, but securely perish.
277: We see the very wrack that we must suffer,
278: And unavoided is the danger now
279: For suffering so the causes of our wrack.
280: Not so. Even through the hollow eyes of death
281: I spy life peering; but I dare not say
282: How near the tidings of our comfort is.
283: Nay, let us share thy thoughts, as thou dost ours.
285: We three are but thyself, and speaking so
286: Thy words are but as thoughts. Therefore be bold.
287: Then thus: I have from Le Port Blanc,
288: A bay in Brittany, received intelligence
289: That Harry Duke of Hereford, Rainold Lord Cobham,
291: That late broke from the Duke of Exeter,
292: His brother, archbishop late of Canterbury,
293: Sir Thomas Erpingham, Sir John Ramston,
294: Sir John Norbery, Sir Robert Waterton, and Francis Coint—
296: All these well furnished by the Duke of Brittany
297: With eight tall ships, three thousand men of war,
298: Are making hither with all due expedience
299: And shortly mean to touch our northern shore.
300: Perhaps they had ere this, but that they stay
301: The first departing of the King for Ireland.
302: If then we shall shake off our slavish yoke,
303: Imp out our drooping country’s broken wing,
304: Redeem from broking pawn the blemished crown,
305: Wipe off the dust that hides our scepter’s gilt,
306: And make high majesty look like itself,
307: Away with me in post to Ravenspurgh.
308: But if you faint, as fearing to do so,
309: Stay and be secret, and myself will go.
310: To horse, to horse! Urge doubts to them that fear.
311: Hold out my horse, and I will first be there.

1: Madam, your Majesty is too much sad.
2: You promised, when you parted with the King,
5: To please the King I did; to please myself
6: I cannot do it. Yet I know no cause
7: Why I should welcome such a guest as grief,
8: Save bidding farewell to so sweet a guest
9: As my sweet Richard. Yet again methinks
10: Some unborn sorrow ripe in Fortune’s womb
11: Is coming towards me, and my inward soul
12: With nothing trembles. At some thing it grieves
13: More than with parting from my lord the King.
14: Each substance of a grief hath twenty shadows
15: Which shows like grief itself but is not so;
16: For sorrow’s eyes, glazed with blinding tears,
17: Divides one thing entire to many objects,
18: Like perspectives, which rightly gazed upon
19: Show nothing but confusion, eyed awry
20: Distinguish form. So your sweet Majesty,
21: Looking awry upon your lord’s departure,
22: Find shapes of grief more than himself to wail,
23: Which, looked on as it is, is naught but shadows
24: Of what it is not. Then, thrice-gracious queen,
25: More than your lord’s departure weep not. More is not seen,
27: Or if it be, ’tis with false sorrow’s eye,
28: Which for things true weeps things imaginary.
29: It may be so, but yet my inward soul
30: Persuades me it is otherwise. Howe’er it be,
31: I cannot but be sad—so heavy sad
32: As thought, on thinking on no thought I think,
33: Makes me with heavy nothing faint and shrink.
34: ’Tis nothing but conceit, my gracious lady.
35: ’Tis nothing less. Conceit is still derived
36: From some forefather grief. Mine is not so,
37: For nothing hath begot my something grief—
38: Or something hath the nothing that I grieve.
39: ’Tis in reversion that I do possess,
40: But what it is that is not yet known what,
41: I cannot name. ’Tis nameless woe, I wot.
42: God save your Majesty!—And well met, gentlemen.
43: I hope the King is not yet shipped for Ireland.
44: Why hopest thou so? ’Tis better hope he is,
45: For his designs crave haste, his haste good hope.
46: Then wherefore dost thou hope he is not shipped?
47: That he, our hope, might have retired his power
48: And driven into despair an enemy’s hope,
49: Who strongly hath set footing in this land.
51: And with uplifted arms is safe arrived
54: Ah, madam, ’tis too true. And that is worse,
55: The Lord Northumberland, his son young Harry Percy,
57: The Lords of Ross, Beaumont, and Willoughby,
58: With all their powerful friends, are fled to him.
59: Why have you not proclaimed Northumberland
60: And all the rest revolted faction traitors?
61: We have; whereupon the Earl of Worcester
62: Hath broken his staff, resigned his stewardship,
63: And all the Household servants fled with him
65: So, Green, thou art the midwife to my woe,
66: And Bolingbroke my sorrow’s dismal heir.
67: Now hath my soul brought forth her prodigy,
68: And I, a gasping new-delivered mother,
69: Have woe to woe, sorrow to sorrow joined.
72: I will despair and be at enmity
73: With cozening hope. He is a flatterer,
74: A parasite, a keeper-back of death,
75: Who gently would dissolve the bands of life
76: Which false hope lingers in extremity.
77: Here comes the Duke of York.
78: With signs of war about his agèd neck.
79: O, full of careful business are his looks!—
80: Uncle, for God’s sake speak comfortable words.
81: Should I do so, I should belie my thoughts.
82: Comfort’s in heaven, and we are on the Earth,
83: Where nothing lives but crosses, cares, and grief.
84: Your husband, he is gone to save far off
85: Whilst others come to make him lose at home.
86: Here am I left to underprop his land,
87: Who, weak with age, cannot support myself.
88: Now comes the sick hour that his surfeit made;
89: Now shall he try his friends that flattered him.
90: My lord, your son was gone before I came.
91: He was? Why, so go all which way it will.
92: The nobles they are fled; the commons they are cold
94: And will, I fear, revolt on Hereford’s side.
95: Sirrah, get thee to Plashy, to my sister Gloucester;
96: Bid her send me presently a thousand pound.
98: My lord, I had forgot to tell your Lordship:
99: Today as I came by I callèd there—
100: But I shall grieve you to report the rest.
102: An hour before I came, the Duchess died.
103: God for His mercy, what a tide of woes
104: Comes rushing on this woeful land at once!
105: I know not what to do. I would to God,
106: So my untruth had not provoked him to it,
107: The King had cut off my head with my brother’s!
108: What, are there no posts dispatched for Ireland?
109: How shall we do for money for these wars?—
110: Come, sister—cousin I would say, pray pardon me.—
112: Go, fellow, get thee home. Provide some carts
113: And bring away the armor that is there.
114: Gentlemen, will you go muster men?
115: If I know how or which way to order these affairs
116: Thus disorderly thrust into my hands,
117: Never believe me. Both are my kinsmen.
118: T’ one is my sovereign, whom both my oath
119: And duty bids defend; t’ other again
120: Is my kinsman, whom the King hath wronged,
121: Whom conscience and my kindred bids to right.
124: I’ll dispose of you.—Gentlemen, go muster up your men
126: And meet me presently at Berkeley.
128: But time will not permit. All is uneven,
129: And everything is left at six and seven.
130: The wind sits fair for news to go for Ireland,
131: But none returns. For us to levy power
134: Besides, our nearness to the King in love
135: Is near the hate of those love not the King.
136: And that is the wavering commons, for their love
137: Lies in their purses, and whoso empties them
138: By so much fills their hearts with deadly hate.
139: Wherein the King stands generally condemned.
140: If judgment lie in them, then so do we,
141: Because we ever have been near the King.
142: Well, I will for refuge straight to Bristow Castle.
143: The Earl of Wiltshire is already there.
144: Thither will I with you, for little office
145: Will the hateful commons perform for us,
146: Except like curs to tear us all to pieces.—
147: Will you go along with us?
148: No, I will to Ireland to his Majesty.
149: Farewell. If heart’s presages be not vain,
150: We three here part that ne’er shall meet again.
151: That’s as York thrives to beat back Bolingbroke.
152: Alas, poor duke, the task he undertakes
153: Is numb’ring sands and drinking oceans dry.
154: Where one on his side fights, thousands will fly.
155: Farewell at once, for once, for all, and ever.

1: How far is it, my lord, to Berkeley now?
3: I am a stranger here in Gloucestershire.
4: These high wild hills and rough uneven ways
5: Draws out our miles and makes them wearisome.
6: And yet your fair discourse hath been as sugar,
7: Making the hard way sweet and delectable.
8: But I bethink me what a weary way
9: From Ravenspurgh to Cotshall will be found
10: In Ross and Willoughby, wanting your company,
11: Which, I protest, hath very much beguiled
12: The tediousness and process of my travel.
13: But theirs is sweetened with the hope to have
14: The present benefit which I possess,
15: And hope to joy is little less in joy
16: Than hope enjoyed. By this the weary lords
17: Shall make their way seem short as mine hath done
18: By sight of what I have, your noble company.
19: Of much less value is my company
20: Than your good words. But who comes here?
21: It is my son, young Harry Percy,
22: Sent from my brother Worcester whencesoever.—
24: I had thought, my lord, to have learned his health of you.
26: Why, is he not with the Queen?
27: No, my good lord, he hath forsook the court,
28: Broken his staff of office, and dispersed
30: What was his reason? He was not so resolved
32: Because your Lordship was proclaimèd traitor.
33: But he, my lord, is gone to Ravenspurgh
34: To offer service to the Duke of Hereford,
35: And sent me over by Berkeley to discover
36: What power the Duke of York had levied there,
37: Then with directions to repair to Ravenspurgh.
38: Have you forgot the Duke of Hereford, boy?
39: No, my good lord, for that is not forgot
40: Which ne’er I did remember. To my knowledge
41: I never in my life did look on him.
42: Then learn to know him now. This is the Duke.
43: My gracious lord, I tender you my service,
44: Such as it is, being tender, raw, and young,
45: Which elder days shall ripen and confirm
46: To more approvèd service and desert.
47: I thank thee, gentle Percy, and be sure
48: I count myself in nothing else so happy
49: As in a soul rememb’ring my good friends;
50: And as my fortune ripens with thy love,
51: It shall be still thy true love’s recompense.
52: My heart this covenant makes, my hand thus seals it.
53: How far is it to Berkeley, and what stir
54: Keeps good old York there with his men of war?
55: There stands the castle by yon tuft of trees,
56: Manned with three hundred men, as I have heard,
57: And in it are the Lords of York, Berkeley, and Seymour,
59: None else of name and noble estimate.
60: Here come the Lords of Ross and Willoughby,
61: Bloody with spurring, fiery red with haste.
62: Welcome, my lords. I wot your love pursues
63: A banished traitor. All my treasury
64: Is yet but unfelt thanks, which, more enriched,
65: Shall be your love and labor’s recompense.
66: Your presence makes us rich, most noble lord.
67: And far surmounts our labor to attain it.
68: Evermore thank’s the exchequer of the poor,
69: Which, till my infant fortune comes to years,
70: Stands for my bounty. But who comes here?
71: It is my Lord of Berkeley, as I guess.
72: My Lord of Hereford, my message is to you.
73: My lord, my answer is—to Lancaster;
74: And I am come to seek that name in England.
75: And I must find that title in your tongue
76: Before I make reply to aught you say.
77: Mistake me not, my lord, ’tis not my meaning
78: To rase one title of your honor out.
79: To you, my lord, I come, what lord you will,
80: From the most gracious regent of this land,
81: The Duke of York, to know what pricks you on
82: To take advantage of the absent time,
83: And fright our native peace with self-borne arms.
84: I shall not need transport my words by you.
85: Here comes his Grace in person.
87: Show me thy humble heart and not thy knee,
88: Whose duty is deceivable and false.
91: Grace me no grace, nor uncle me no uncle.
92: I am no traitor’s uncle, and that word grace
93: In an ungracious mouth is but profane.
94: Why have those banished and forbidden legs
95: Dared once to touch a dust of England’s ground?
96: But then, more why: why have they dared to march
97: So many miles upon her peaceful bosom,
98: Frighting her pale-faced villages with war
100: Com’st thou because the anointed king is hence?
101: Why, foolish boy, the King is left behind
102: And in my loyal bosom lies his power.
103: Were I but now lord of such hot youth
104: As when brave Gaunt thy father and myself
105: Rescued the Black Prince, that young Mars of men,
106: From forth the ranks of many thousand French,
107: O, then, how quickly should this arm of mine,
108: Now prisoner to the palsy, chastise thee
109: And minister correction to thy fault!
110: My gracious uncle, let me know my fault.
111: On what condition stands it and wherein?
112: Even in condition of the worst degree,
113: In gross rebellion and detested treason.
114: Thou art a banished man and here art come,
115: Before the expiration of thy time,
116: In braving arms against thy sovereign.
117: As I was banished, I was banished Hereford,
118: But as I come, I come for Lancaster.
119: And, noble uncle, I beseech your Grace
120: Look on my wrongs with an indifferent eye.
121: You are my father, for methinks in you
122: I see old Gaunt alive. O, then, my father,
123: Will you permit that I shall stand condemned
124: A wandering vagabond, my rights and royalties
125: Plucked from my arms perforce and given away
126: To upstart unthrifts? Wherefore was I born?
127: If that my cousin king be king in England,
128: It must be granted I am Duke of Lancaster.
129: You have a son, Aumerle, my noble cousin.
130: Had you first died and he been thus trod down,
131: He should have found his uncle Gaunt a father
132: To rouse his wrongs and chase them to the bay.
133: I am denied to sue my livery here,
134: And yet my letters patents give me leave.
135: My father’s goods are all distrained and sold,
136: And these, and all, are all amiss employed.
137: What would you have me do? I am a subject,
138: And I challenge law. Attorneys are denied me,
139: And therefore personally I lay my claim
140: To my inheritance of free descent.
141: The noble duke hath been too much abused.
142: It stands your Grace upon to do him right.
143: Base men by his endowments are made great.
144: My lords of England, let me tell you this:
145: I have had feeling of my cousin’s wrongs
146: And labored all I could to do him right.
147: But in this kind to come, in braving arms,
148: Be his own carver and cut out his way
149: To find out right with wrong, it may not be.
150: And you that do abet him in this kind
151: Cherish rebellion and are rebels all.
152: The noble duke hath sworn his coming is
153: But for his own, and for the right of that
154: We all have strongly sworn to give him aid.
155: And let him never see joy that breaks that oath.
156: Well, well. I see the issue of these arms.
157: I cannot mend it, I must needs confess,
158: Because my power is weak and all ill-left.
159: But if I could, by Him that gave me life,
160: I would attach you all and make you stoop
161: Unto the sovereign mercy of the King.
162: But since I cannot, be it known unto you
163: I do remain as neuter. So fare you well—
164: Unless you please to enter in the castle
165: And there repose you for this night.
166: An offer, uncle, that we will accept.
167: But we must win your Grace to go with us
168: To Bristow Castle, which they say is held
169: By Bushy, Bagot, and their complices,
171: Which I have sworn to weed and pluck away.
172: It may be I will go with you; but yet I’ll pause,
173: For I am loath to break our country’s laws.
174: Nor friends nor foes, to me welcome you are.
175: Things past redress are now with me past care.

1: My Lord of Salisbury, we have stayed ten days
2: And hardly kept our countrymen together,
3: And yet we hear no tidings from the King.
4: Therefore we will disperse ourselves. Farewell.
5: Stay yet another day, thou trusty Welshman.
6: The King reposeth all his confidence in thee.
7: ’Tis thought the King is dead. We will not stay.
8: The bay trees in our country are all withered,
9: And meteors fright the fixèd stars of heaven;
10: The pale-faced moon looks bloody on the Earth,
11: And lean-looked prophets whisper fearful change;
12: Rich men look sad, and ruffians dance and leap,
13: The one in fear to lose what they enjoy,
14: The other to enjoy by rage and war.
15: These signs forerun the death or fall of kings.
16: Farewell. Our countrymen are gone and fled,
17: As well assured Richard their king is dead.
18: Ah, Richard! With the eyes of heavy mind
19: I see thy glory like a shooting star
20: Fall to the base earth from the firmament.
21: Thy sun sets weeping in the lowly west,
22: Witnessing storms to come, woe, and unrest.
23: Thy friends are fled to wait upon thy foes,
24: And crossly to thy good all fortune goes.

2: Bushy and Green, I will not vex your souls,
3: Since presently your souls must part your bodies,
4: With too much urging your pernicious lives,
5: For ’twere no charity; yet to wash your blood
6: From off my hands, here in the view of men
7: I will unfold some causes of your deaths:
8: You have misled a prince, a royal king,
9: A happy gentleman in blood and lineaments
10: By you unhappied and disfigured clean.
11: You have in manner with your sinful hours
12: Made a divorce betwixt his queen and him,
13: Broke the possession of a royal bed,
14: And stained the beauty of a fair queen’s cheeks
15: With tears drawn from her eyes by your foul wrongs.
16: Myself, a prince by fortune of my birth,
17: Near to the King in blood, and near in love
18: Till you did make him misinterpret me,
19: Have stooped my neck under your injuries
20: And sighed my English breath in foreign clouds,
21: Eating the bitter bread of banishment,
22: Whilst you have fed upon my seigniories,
23: Disparked my parks and felled my forest woods,
24: From my own windows torn my household coat,
25: Rased out my imprese, leaving me no sign,
26: Save men’s opinions and my living blood,
27: To show the world I am a gentleman.
28: This and much more, much more than twice all this,
30: Condemns you to the death.—See them delivered over
32: To execution and the hand of death.
33: More welcome is the stroke of death to me
34: Than Bolingbroke to England. Lords, farewell.
35: My comfort is that heaven will take our souls
36: And plague injustice with the pains of hell.
37: My Lord Northumberland, see them dispatched.
38: Uncle, you say the Queen is at your house.
40: For God’s sake, fairly let her be entreated.
41: Tell her I send to her my kind commends.
42: Take special care my greetings be delivered.
43: A gentleman of mine I have dispatched
44: With letters of your love to her at large.
46: To fight with Glendower and his complices.
47: A while to work, and after holiday.

1: Barkloughly Castle call they this at hand?
2: Yea, my lord. How brooks your Grace the air
3: After your late tossing on the breaking seas?
4: Needs must I like it well. I weep for joy
5: To stand upon my kingdom once again.
6: Dear earth, I do salute thee with my hand,
7: Though rebels wound thee with their horses’ hoofs.
8: As a long-parted mother with her child
9: Plays fondly with her tears and smiles in meeting,
10: So, weeping, smiling, greet I thee, my earth,
11: And do thee favors with my royal hands.
12: Feed not thy sovereign’s foe, my gentle earth,
13: Nor with thy sweets comfort his ravenous sense,
14: But let thy spiders, that suck up thy venom,
15: And heavy-gaited toads lie in their way,
16: Doing annoyance to the treacherous feet
17: Which with usurping steps do trample thee.
18: Yield stinging nettles to mine enemies,
19: And when they from thy bosom pluck a flower,
20: Guard it, I pray thee, with a lurking adder,
21: Whose double tongue may with a mortal touch

107: As surely as I live, my lord.

112: Great Duke of Lancaster, I come to thee
113: From plume-plucked Richard, who with willing soul
115: Adopts thee heir, and his high scepter yields
116: To the possession of thy royal hand.

121: Worst in this royal presence may I speak,
122: Yet best beseeming me to speak the truth.

124: Were enough noble to be upright judge

126: Learn him forbearance from so foul a wrong.
127: What subject can give sentence on his king?

130: Although apparent guilt be seen in them;
131: And shall the figure of God’s majesty,

136: That in a Christian climate souls refined
137: Should show so heinous, black, obscene a deed!

139: Stirred up by God thus boldly for his king.
140: My Lord of Hereford here, whom you call king,

142: And if you crown him, let me prophesy
143: The blood of English shall manure the ground

147: Shall kin with kin and kind with kind confound.

154: Prevent it, resist it, let it not be so,

158: My Lord of Westminster, be it your charge

163: He may surrender. So we shall proceed
166: Lords, you that here are under our arrest,
167: Procure your sureties for your days of answer.
168: Little are we beholding to your love
169: And little looked for at your helping hands.
170: Alack, why am I sent for to a king
171: Before I have shook off the regal thoughts
172: Wherewith I reigned? I hardly yet have learned
173: To insinuate, flatter, bow, and bend my knee.
174: Give sorrow leave awhile to tutor me
175: To this submission. Yet I well remember
176: The favors of these men. Were they not mine?

178: So Judas did to Christ, but He in twelve

181: God save the King! Will no man say amen?
182: Am I both priest and clerk? Well, then, amen.
183: God save the King, although I be not he,
184: And yet amen, if heaven do think him me.
185: To do what service am I sent for hither?
186: To do that office of thine own goodwill
187: Which tired majesty did make thee offer:
188: The resignation of thy state and crown
190: Give me the crown.—Here, cousin, seize the crown.
192: On this side my hand, on that side thine.
193: Now is this golden crown like a deep well
194: That owes two buckets, filling one another,
195: The emptier ever dancing in the air,
196: The other down, unseen, and full of water.
197: That bucket down and full of tears am I,
198: Drinking my griefs, whilst you mount up on high.
199: I thought you had been willing to resign.
200: My crown I am, but still my griefs are mine.
201: You may my glories and my state depose
202: But not my griefs; still am I king of those.
203: Part of your cares you give me with your crown.
204: Your cares set up do not pluck my cares down.
205: My care is loss of care, by old care done;
206: Your care is gain of care, by new care won.
207: The cares I give I have, though given away.
208: They ’tend the crown, yet still with me they stay.
209: Are you contented to resign the crown?
210: Ay, no; no, ay; for I must nothing be.
211: Therefore no no, for I resign to thee.
212: Now, mark me how I will undo myself.
213: I give this heavy weight from off my head
214: And this unwieldy scepter from my hand,
215: The pride of kingly sway from out my heart.
216: With mine own tears I wash away my balm,
217: With mine own hands I give away my crown,
218: With mine own tongue deny my sacred state,
219: With mine own breath release all duteous oaths.
220: All pomp and majesty I do forswear.
221: My manors, rents, revenues I forgo;
222: My acts, decrees, and statutes I deny.
223: God pardon all oaths that are broke to me.
224: God keep all vows unbroke are made to thee.
225: Make me, that nothing have, with nothing grieved,

229: God save King Henry, unkinged Richard says,

232: No more, but that you read
233: These accusations and these grievous crimes
234: Committed by your person and your followers
235: Against the state and profit of this land;

238: Must I do so? And must I ravel out
240: If thy offenses were upon record,

242: To read a lecture of them? If thou wouldst,

244: Containing the deposing of a king
245: And cracking the strong warrant of an oath,

248: Nay, all of you that stand and look upon me
249: Whilst that my wretchedness doth bait myself,

251: Showing an outward pity, yet you Pilates
252: Have here delivered me to my sour cross,
253: And water cannot wash away your sin.
254: My lord, dispatch. Read o’er these articles.
255: Mine eyes are full of tears; I cannot see.
256: And yet salt water blinds them not so much
257: But they can see a sort of traitors here.
258: Nay, if I turn mine eyes upon myself,
259: I find myself a traitor with the rest,
260: For I have given here my soul’s consent
261: T’ undeck the pompous body of a king,
262: Made glory base and sovereignty a slave,
263: Proud majesty a subject, state a peasant.
265: No lord of thine, thou haught insulting man,
266: Nor no man’s lord. I have no name, no title,
267: No, not that name was given me at the font,
268: But ’tis usurped. Alack the heavy day,
269: That I have worn so many winters out
270: And know not now what name to call myself.
271: O, that I were a mockery king of snow
272: Standing before the sun of Bolingbroke,
273: To melt myself away in water drops.—
274: Good king, great king, and yet not greatly good,
275: An if my word be sterling yet in England,
276: Let it command a mirror hither straight,
277: That it may show me what a face I have
278: Since it is bankrupt of his majesty.
279: Go, some of you, and fetch a looking-glass.
280: Read o’er this paper while the glass doth come.
281: Fiend, thou torments me ere I come to hell!
282: Urge it no more, my Lord Northumberland.
283: The commons will not then be satisfied.
284: They shall be satisfied. I’ll read enough
285: When I do see the very book indeed
286: Where all my sins are writ, and that’s myself.
287: Give me that glass, and therein will I read.
288: No deeper wrinkles yet? Hath sorrow struck
289: So many blows upon this face of mine
290: And made no deeper wounds? O flatt’ring glass,
291: Like to my followers in prosperity,
292: Thou dost beguile me. Was this face the face
293: That every day under his household roof
294: Did keep ten thousand men? Was this the face
295: That like the sun did make beholders wink?
296: Is this the face which faced so many follies,
297: That was at last outfaced by Bolingbroke?
298: A brittle glory shineth in this face.
299: As brittle as the glory is the face,
300: For there it is, cracked in an hundred shivers.—
301: Mark, silent king, the moral of this sport:
302: How soon my sorrow hath destroyed my face.
303: The shadow of your sorrow hath destroyed
306: The shadow of my sorrow? Ha, let’s see.
307: ’Tis very true. My grief lies all within;
308: And these external manners of laments
309: Are merely shadows to the unseen grief
310: That swells with silence in the tortured soul.
311: There lies the substance. And I thank thee, king,
312: For thy great bounty, that not only giv’st
313: Me cause to wail but teachest me the way
314: How to lament the cause. I’ll beg one boon
315: And then be gone and trouble you no more.
318: Fair cousin? I am greater than a king,
319: For when I was a king, my flatterers
320: Were then but subjects. Being now a subject,
321: I have a king here to my flatterer.
322: Being so great, I have no need to beg.
326: Then give me leave to go.
328: Whither you will, so I were from your sights.
329: Go, some of you, convey him to the Tower.
330: O, good! Convey? Conveyers are you all,
331: That rise thus nimbly by a true king’s fall.
332: On Wednesday next, we solemnly set down
334: A woeful pageant have we here beheld.
335: The woe’s to come. The children yet unborn
336: Shall feel this day as sharp to them as thorn.
337: You holy clergymen, is there no plot
338: To rid the realm of this pernicious blot?
340: Before I freely speak my mind herein,
341: You shall not only take the sacrament
342: To bury mine intents, but also to effect
343: Whatever I shall happen to devise.
344: I see your brows are full of discontent,
345: Your hearts of sorrow, and your eyes of tears.
346: Come home with me to supper. I’ll lay
347: A plot shall show us all a merry day.

1: This way the King will come. This is the way

14: Why should hard-favored grief be lodged in thee
15: When triumph is become an alehouse guest?

18: To think our former state a happy dream,
19: From which awaked, the truth of what we are
20: Shows us but this: I am sworn brother, sweet,
21: To grim necessity, and he and I
22: Will keep a league till death. Hie thee to France
23: And cloister thee in some religious house.

25: Which our profane hours here have thrown down.

28: Deposed thine intellect? Hath he been in thy heart?

30: And wounds the earth, if nothing else, with rage
31: To be o’er-powered; and wilt thou, pupil-like,
32: Take the correction, mildly kiss the rod,
33: And fawn on rage with base humility,
34: Which art a lion and the king of beasts?

42: With good old folks, and let them tell thee tales
43: Of woeful ages long ago betid;

46: And send the hearers weeping to their beds.
47: Forwhy the senseless brands will sympathize
48: The heavy accent of thy moving tongue,
49: And in compassion weep the fire out,
50: And some will mourn in ashes, some coal-black,

52: My lord, the mind of Bolingbroke is changed.

55: With all swift speed you must away to France.
57: The mounting Bolingbroke ascends my throne,
58: The time shall not be many hours of age
59: More than it is ere foul sin, gathering head,
60: Shall break into corruption. Thou shalt think,
61: Though he divide the realm and give thee half,
62: It is too little, helping him to all.
63: He shall think that thou, which knowest the way
64: To plant unrightful kings, wilt know again,
65: Being ne’er so little urged another way,

68: That fear to hate, and hate turns one or both
69: To worthy danger and deservèd death.
70: My guilt be on my head, and there an end.

78: Part us, Northumberland, I towards the north,

84: Ay, hand from hand, my love, and heart from heart.
85: Banish us both, and send the King with me.
86: That were some love, but little policy.
87: Then whither he goes, thither let me go.
88: So two together weeping make one woe.
89: Weep thou for me in France, I for thee here;
90: Better far off than, near, be ne’er the near.
91: Go, count thy way with sighs, I mine with groans.
92: So longest way shall have the longest moans.
93: Twice for one step I’ll groan, the way being short,
94: And piece the way out with a heavy heart.
95: Come, come, in wooing sorrow let’s be brief,
96: Since, wedding it, there is such length in grief.
97: One kiss shall stop our mouths, and dumbly part.
98: Thus give I mine, and thus take I thy heart.
99: Give me mine own again. ’Twere no good part
100: To take on me to keep and kill thy heart.
101: So, now I have mine own again, begone,
102: That I may strive to kill it with a groan.
103: We make woe wanton with this fond delay.
104: Once more, adieu! The rest let sorrow say.

36: The badges of his grief and patience,
