86: Me they concern; regent I am of France.
87: Give me my steelèd coat, I’ll fight for France.
88: Away with these disgraceful wailing robes.
89: Wounds will I lend the French instead of eyes
91: Lords, view these letters, full of bad mischance.
92: France is revolted from the English quite,
93: Except some petty towns of no import.
94: The Dauphin Charles is crownèd king in Rheims;
95: The Bastard of Orleance with him is joined;
96: Reignier, Duke of Anjou, doth take his part;
97: The Duke of Alanson flieth to his side.
98: The Dauphin crownèd king? All fly to him?
99: O, whither shall we fly from this reproach?
100: We will not fly but to our enemies’ throats.—
101: Bedford, if thou be slack, I’ll fight it out.
102: Gloucester, why doubt’st thou of my forwardness?
103: An army have I mustered in my thoughts,
105: My gracious lords, to add to your laments,
106: Wherewith you now bedew King Henry’s hearse,
107: I must inform you of a dismal fight
108: Betwixt the stout Lord Talbot and the French.
109: What? Wherein Talbot overcame, is ’t so?
110: O no, wherein Lord Talbot was o’erthrown.
111: The circumstance I’ll tell you more at large.
112: The tenth of August last, this dreadful lord,
113: Retiring from the siege of Orleance,
114: Having full scarce six thousand in his troop,
115: By three and twenty thousand of the French
116: Was round encompassèd and set upon.
117: No leisure had he to enrank his men.
118: He wanted pikes to set before his archers,
119: Instead whereof, sharp stakes plucked out of hedges
120: They pitchèd in the ground confusedly
121: To keep the horsemen off from breaking in.
122: More than three hours the fight continuèd,
123: Where valiant Talbot, above human thought,
124: Enacted wonders with his sword and lance.
125: Hundreds he sent to hell, and none durst stand him;
126: Here, there, and everywhere, enraged, he slew.
127: The French exclaimed the devil was in arms;
128: All the whole army stood agazed on him.
129: His soldiers, spying his undaunted spirit,
130: À Talbot! À Talbot! cried out amain
131: And rushed into the bowels of the battle.
132: Here had the conquest fully been sealed up
133: If Sir John Fastolf had not played the coward.
134: He, being in the vaward, placed behind
135: With purpose to relieve and follow them,
136: Cowardly fled, not having struck one stroke.
137: Hence grew the general wrack and massacre.
138: Enclosèd were they with their enemies.
139: A base Walloon, to win the Dauphin’s grace,
140: Thrust Talbot with a spear into the back,
141: Whom all France, with their chief assembled strength,
143: Durst not presume to look once in the face.
144: Is Talbot slain then? I will slay myself
145: For living idly here, in pomp and ease,
146: Whilst such a worthy leader, wanting aid,
147: Unto his dastard foemen is betrayed.
148: O, no, he lives, but is took prisoner,
149: And Lord Scales with him, and Lord Hungerford;
150: Most of the rest slaughtered or took likewise.
151: His ransom there is none but I shall pay.
152: I’ll hale the Dauphin headlong from his throne;
153: His crown shall be the ransom of my friend.
154: Four of their lords I’ll change for one of ours.
155: Farewell, my masters; to my task will I.
156: Bonfires in France forthwith I am to make,
157: To keep our great Saint George’s feast withal.
158: Ten thousand soldiers with me I will take,
159: Whose bloody deeds shall make all Europe quake.
160: So you had need; ’fore Orleance besieged,
161: The English army is grown weak and faint;
162: The Earl of Salisbury craveth supply
163: And hardly keeps his men from mutiny,
164: Since they so few watch such a multitude.
165: Remember, lords, your oaths to Henry sworn:
166: Either to quell the Dauphin utterly
167: Or bring him in obedience to your yoke.
168: I do remember it, and here take my leave
170: I’ll to the Tower with all the haste I can
171: To view th’ artillery and munition,
172: And then I will proclaim young Henry king.
173: To Eltham will I, where the young king is,
175: And for his safety there I’ll best devise.
176: Each hath his place and function to attend.
177: I am left out; for me nothing remains.
178: But long I will not be Jack-out-of-office.
179: The King from Eltham I intend to steal,
180: And sit at chiefest stern of public weal.

1: Mars his true moving, even as in the heavens
2: So in the Earth, to this day is not known.
3: Late did he shine upon the English side;
4: Now we are victors; upon us he smiles.
5: What towns of any moment but we have?
6: At pleasure here we lie, near Orleance.
7: Otherwhiles, the famished English, like pale ghosts,
8: Faintly besiege us one hour in a month.
9: They want their porridge and their fat bull beeves.
10: Either they must be dieted like mules
11: And have their provender tied to their mouths,
12: Or piteous they will look, like drownèd mice.
13: Let’s raise the siege. Why live we idly here?
14: Talbot is taken, whom we wont to fear.
16: And he may well in fretting spend his gall;
17: Nor men nor money hath he to make war.
18: Sound, sound alarum! We will rush on them.
19: Now for the honor of the forlorn French!
20: Him I forgive my death that killeth me
21: When he sees me go back one foot, or fly.
22: Whoever saw the like? What men have I!
23: Dogs, cowards, dastards! I would ne’er have fled
24: But that they left me ’midst my enemies.
26: He fighteth as one weary of his life.
27: The other lords, like lions wanting food,
28: Do rush upon us as their hungry prey.
29: Froissart, a countryman of ours, records
30: England all Olivers and Rolands bred
31: During the time Edward the Third did reign.
32: More truly now may this be verified,
33: For none but Samsons and Goliases
34: It sendeth forth to skirmish. One to ten!
35: Lean rawboned rascals! Who would e’er suppose
36: They had such courage and audacity?
37: Let’s leave this town, for they are hare-brained slaves,
38: And hunger will enforce them to be more eager.
39: Of old I know them; rather with their teeth
40: The walls they’ll tear down than forsake the siege.
41: I think by some odd gimmers or device
42: Their arms are set, like clocks, still to strike on;
43: Else ne’er could they hold out so as they do.
44: By my consent, we’ll even let them alone.
46: Where’s the Prince Dauphin? I have news for him.
47: Bastard of Orleance, thrice welcome to us.
48: Methinks your looks are sad, your cheer appalled.
49: Hath the late overthrow wrought this offence?
50: Be not dismayed, for succor is at hand.
51: A holy maid hither with me I bring,
52: Which, by a vision sent to her from heaven,
53: Ordainèd is to raise this tedious siege
54: And drive the English forth the bounds of France.
55: The spirit of deep prophecy she hath,
56: Exceeding the nine Sibyls of old Rome.
57: What’s past and what’s to come she can descry.
58: Speak, shall I call her in? Believe my words,
59: For they are certain and unfallible.
61: But first, to try her skill,
62: Reignier, stand thou as Dauphin in my place;
63: Question her proudly; let thy looks be stern.
64: By this means shall we sound what skill she hath.
65: Fair maid, is ’t thou wilt do these wondrous feats?
66: Reignier, is ’t thou that thinkest to beguile me?
67: Where is the Dauphin?—Come, come from behind.
68: I know thee well, though never seen before.
69: Be not amazed; there’s nothing hid from me.
70: In private will I talk with thee apart.—
71: Stand back, you lords, and give us leave a while.
72: She takes upon her bravely at first dash.
73: Dauphin, I am by birth a shepherd’s daughter,
74: My wit untrained in any kind of art.
75: Heaven and Our Lady gracious hath it pleased
76: To shine on my contemptible estate.
77: Lo, whilst I waited on my tender lambs,
78: And to sun’s parching heat displayed my cheeks,
79: God’s Mother deignèd to appear to me,
80: And in a vision full of majesty
81: Willed me to leave my base vocation
82: And free my country from calamity.
83: Her aid she promised and assured success.
84: In complete glory she revealed herself;
85: And whereas I was black and swart before,
86: With those clear rays which she infused on me
87: That beauty am I blest with, which you may see.
88: Ask me what question thou canst possible,
90: My courage try by combat, if thou dar’st,
91: And thou shalt find that I exceed my sex.
92: Resolve on this: thou shalt be fortunate
93: If thou receive me for thy warlike mate.
94: Thou hast astonished me with thy high terms.
95: Only this proof I’ll of thy valor make:
96: In single combat thou shalt buckle with me,
97: And if thou vanquishest, thy words are true;
99: I am prepared. Here is my keen-edged sword,
100: Decked with fine flower-de-luces on each side—
101: The which at Touraine, in Saint Katherine’s churchyard,
103: Out of a great deal of old iron I chose forth.
104: Then come, a’ God’s name! I fear no woman.
105: And while I live, I’ll ne’er fly from a man.
106: Stay, stay thy hands! Thou art an Amazon,
107: And fightest with the sword of Deborah.
108: Christ’s mother helps me; else I were too weak.
109: Whoe’er helps thee, ’tis thou that must help me.
110: Impatiently I burn with thy desire.
111: My heart and hands thou hast at once subdued.
112: Excellent Pucelle, if thy name be so,
113: Let me thy servant and not sovereign be.
114: ’Tis the French Dauphin sueth to thee thus.
115: I must not yield to any rights of love,
116: For my profession’s sacred from above.
117: When I have chasèd all thy foes from hence,
118: Then will I think upon a recompense.
119: Meantime look gracious on thy prostrate thrall.
120: My lord, methinks, is very long in talk.
121: Doubtless he shrives this woman to her smock,
122: Else ne’er could he so long protract his speech.
123: Shall we disturb him, since he keeps no mean?
124: He may mean more than we poor men do know.
125: These women are shrewd tempters with their tongues.
127: My lord, where are you? What devise you on?
128: Shall we give o’er Orleance, or no?
129: Why, no, I say. Distrustful recreants,
130: Fight till the last gasp. I’ll be your guard.
131: What she says I’ll confirm: we’ll fight it out.
132: Assigned am I to be the English scourge.
133: This night the siege assuredly I’ll raise.
134: Expect Saint Martin’s summer, halcyons’ days,
135: Since I have enterèd into these wars.
136: Glory is like a circle in the water,
137: Which never ceaseth to enlarge itself
138: Till by broad spreading it disperse to naught.
139: With Henry’s death, the English circle ends;
140: Dispersèd are the glories it included.
141: Now am I like that proud insulting ship
142: Which Caesar and his fortune bare at once.
143: Was Mahomet inspirèd with a dove?
144: Thou with an eagle art inspirèd then.
145: Helen, the mother of great Constantine,
146: Nor yet Saint Philip’s daughters were like thee.
147: Bright star of Venus, fall’n down on the Earth,
148: How may I reverently worship thee enough?
149: Leave off delays, and let us raise the siege.
150: Woman, do what thou canst to save our honors.
151: Drive them from Orleance and be immortalized.
152: Presently we’ll try. Come, let’s away about it.
153: No prophet will I trust if she prove false.

1: I am come to survey the Tower this day.
2: Since Henry’s death I fear there is conveyance.
3: Where be these warders that they wait not here?—
4: Open the gates! ’Tis Gloucester that calls.
5: Who’s there that knocks so imperiously?
6: It is the noble Duke of Gloucester.
7: Whoe’er he be, you may not be let in.
8: Villains, answer you so the Lord Protector?
9: The Lord protect him, so we answer him.
10: We do no otherwise than we are willed.
11: Who willed you? Or whose will stands but mine?
12: There’s none Protector of the realm but I.—
13: Break up the gates! I’ll be your warrantize.
14: Shall I be flouted thus by dunghill grooms?
15: What noise is this? What traitors have we here?
16: Lieutenant, is it you whose voice I hear?
17: Open the gates. Here’s Gloucester that would enter.
18: Have patience, noble duke, I may not open.
20: From him I have express commandment
21: That thou nor none of thine shall be let in.
24: Whom Henry, our late sovereign, ne’er could brook?
25: Thou art no friend to God or to the King.
26: Open the gates, or I’ll shut thee out shortly.
27: Open the gates unto the Lord Protector,
28: Or we’ll burst them open if that you come not quickly.
29: How now, ambitious Humphrey, what means this?
30: Peeled priest, dost thou command me to be shut out?
31: I do, thou most usurping proditor—
32: And not Protector—of the King or realm.
34: Thou that contrived’st to murder our dead lord,
35: Thou that giv’st whores indulgences to sin!
36: I’ll canvass thee in thy broad cardinal’s hat
37: If thou proceed in this thy insolence.
38: Nay, stand thou back. I will not budge a foot.
39: This be Damascus; be thou cursèd Cain
40: To slay thy brother Abel, if thou wilt.
41: I will not slay thee, but I’ll drive thee back.
42: Thy scarlet robes, as a child’s bearing-cloth,
43: I’ll use to carry thee out of this place.
44: Do what thou dar’st, I beard thee to thy face.
45: What, am I dared and bearded to my face?—
46: Draw, men, for all this privilegèd place.
49: I mean to tug it and to cuff you soundly.
50: Under my feet I’ll stamp thy cardinal’s hat;
51: In spite of pope or dignities of Church,
52: Here by the cheeks I’ll drag thee up and down.
53: Gloucester, thou wilt answer this before the Pope.
54: Winchester goose, I cry a rope, a rope!—
55: Now beat them hence; why do you let them stay?—
56: Thee I’ll chase hence, thou wolf in sheep’s array.—
57: Out, tawny coats, out, scarlet hypocrite!
58: Fie, lords, that you, being supreme magistrates,
59: Thus contumeliously should break the peace!
60: Peace, Mayor? Thou know’st little of my wrongs.
61: Here’s Beaufort, that regards nor God nor king,
62: Hath here distrained the Tower to his use.
63: Here’s Gloucester, a foe to citizens,
64: One that still motions war and never peace,
65: O’ercharging your free purses with large fines;
67: Because he is Protector of the realm,
68: And would have armor here out of the Tower
69: To crown himself king and suppress the Prince.
70: I will not answer thee with words, but blows.
71: Naught rests for me in this tumultuous strife
73: Come, officer, as loud as e’er thou canst, cry.
74: All manner of men, assembled here in
75: arms this day against God’s peace and the King’s, we
76: charge and command you, in his Highness’ name, to
77: repair to your several dwelling places, and not to
78: wear, handle, or use any sword, weapon, or dagger
80: Cardinal, I’ll be no breaker of the law,
81: But we shall meet and break our minds at large.
82: Gloucester, we’ll meet to thy cost, be sure.
83: Thy heartblood I will have for this day’s work.
84: I’ll call for clubs if you will not away.
85: This cardinal’s more haughty than the devil!
86: Mayor, farewell. Thou dost but what thou mayst.
88: For I intend to have it ere long.
89: See the coast cleared, and then we will depart.
90: Good God, these nobles should such stomachs bear!
92: I myself fight not once in forty year.

1: Sirrah, thou know’st how Orleance is besieged
2: And how the English have the suburbs won.
3: Father, I know, and oft have shot at them;
4: Howe’er, unfortunate, I missed my aim.
5: But now thou shalt not. Be thou ruled by me.
6: Chief master-gunner am I of this town;
7: Something I must do to procure me grace.
8: The Prince’s espials have informèd me
9: How the English, in the suburbs close entrenched,
10: Went through a secret grate of iron bars
11: In yonder tower, to overpeer the city,
12: And thence discover how with most advantage
13: They may vex us with shot or with assault.
15: A piece of ordnance ’gainst it I have placed,
16: And even these three days have I watched
17: If I could see them. Now do thou watch,
18: For I can stay no longer.
19: If thou spy’st any, run and bring me word;
20: And thou shalt find me at the Governor’s.
21: Father, I warrant you, take you no care;
22: I’ll never trouble you if I may spy them.
23: Talbot, my life, my joy, again returned!
24: How wert thou handled, being prisoner?
25: Or by what means gott’st thou to be released?
26: Discourse, I prithee, on this turret’s top.
27: The Duke of Bedford had a prisoner
28: Called the brave Lord Ponton de Santrailles;
29: For him was I exchanged and ransomèd.
30: But with a baser man-of-arms by far
31: Once in contempt they would have bartered me,
32: Which I disdaining, scorned, and cravèd death
33: Rather than I would be so vile-esteemed.
34: In fine, redeemed I was as I desired.
35: But O, the treacherous Fastolf wounds my heart,
36: Whom with my bare fists I would execute
37: If I now had him brought into my power.
38: Yet tell’st thou not how thou wert entertained.
39: With scoffs and scorns and contumelious taunts.
40: In open marketplace produced they me
41: To be a public spectacle to all.
42: Here, said they, is the terror of the French,
43: The scarecrow that affrights our children so.
44: Then broke I from the officers that led me,
45: And with my nails digged stones out of the ground
46: To hurl at the beholders of my shame.
47: My grisly countenance made others fly;
48: None durst come near for fear of sudden death.
49: In iron walls they deemed me not secure:
50: So great fear of my name ’mongst them were spread
51: That they supposed I could rend bars of steel
52: And spurn in pieces posts of adamant.
53: Wherefore a guard of chosen shot I had
54: That walked about me every minute-while;
55: And if I did but stir out of my bed,
56: Ready they were to shoot me to the heart.
57: I grieve to hear what torments you endured,
58: But we will be revenged sufficiently.
59: Now it is supper time in Orleance.
60: Here, through this grate, I count each one
61: And view the Frenchmen how they fortify.
62: Let us look in; the sight will much delight thee.
63: Sir Thomas Gargrave and Sir William Glansdale,
64: Let me have your express opinions
65: Where is best place to make our batt’ry next?
66: I think at the north gate, for there stands lords.
67: And I, here, at the bulwark of the bridge.
68: For aught I see, this city must be famished
70: O Lord, have mercy on us, wretched sinners!
71: O Lord, have mercy on me, woeful man!
72: What chance is this that suddenly hath crossed us?—
73: Speak, Salisbury—at least if thou canst, speak!
74: How far’st thou, mirror of all martial men?
75: One of thy eyes and thy cheek’s side struck off!—
77: That hath contrived this woeful tragedy!
79: Henry the Fifth he first trained to the wars.
80: Whilst any trump did sound or drum struck up,
81: His sword did ne’er leave striking in the field.—
82: Yet liv’st thou, Salisbury? Though thy speech doth fail,
83: One eye thou hast to look to heaven for grace.
84: The sun with one eye vieweth all the world.
85: Heaven, be thou gracious to none alive
86: If Salisbury wants mercy at thy hands!—
87: Sir Thomas Gargrave, hast thou any life?
88: Speak unto Talbot. Nay, look up to him.—
89: Bear hence his body; I will help to bury it.
90: Salisbury, cheer thy spirit with this comfort,
92: He beckons with his hand and smiles on me
93: As who should say When I am dead and gone,
94: Remember to avenge me on the French.
95: Plantagenet, I will; and, like thee, Nero,
96: Play on the lute, beholding the towns burn.
97: Wretched shall France be only in my name.
98: What stir is this? What tumult’s in the heavens?
99: Whence cometh this alarum and the noise?
100: My lord, my lord, the French have gathered head.
101: The Dauphin, with one Joan la Pucelle joined,
102: A holy prophetess new risen up,
103: Is come with a great power to raise the siege.
104: Hear, hear, how dying Salisbury doth groan;
105: It irks his heart he cannot be revenged.
106: Frenchmen, I’ll be a Salisbury to you.
107: Pucelle or puzel, dauphin or dogfish,
108: Your hearts I’ll stamp out with my horse’s heels
109: And make a quagmire of your mingled brains.
110: Convey we Salisbury into his tent,
111: And then try what these dastard Frenchmen dare.

1: Where is my strength, my valor, and my force?
2: Our English troops retire; I cannot stay them.
3: A woman clad in armor chaseth them.
4: Here, here she comes!—I’ll have a bout with thee.
5: Devil or devil’s dam, I’ll conjure thee.
6: Blood will I draw on thee—thou art a witch—
7: And straightway give thy soul to him thou serv’st.
8: Come, come; ’tis only I that must disgrace thee.
9: Heavens, can you suffer hell so to prevail?
10: My breast I’ll burst with straining of my courage,
11: And from my shoulders crack my arms asunder,
12: But I will chastise this high-minded strumpet.
13: Talbot, farewell. Thy hour is not yet come.
14: I must go victual Orleance forthwith.
15: O’ertake me if thou canst. I scorn thy strength.
16: Go, go, cheer up thy hunger-starvèd men.
17: Help Salisbury to make his testament.
18: This day is ours, as many more shall be.
19: My thoughts are whirlèd like a potter’s wheel.
20: I know not where I am nor what I do.
21: A witch by fear—not force, like Hannibal—
22: Drives back our troops, and conquers as she lists.
23: So bees with smoke and doves with noisome stench
24: Are from their hives and houses driven away.
25: They called us, for our fierceness, English dogs;
26: Now like to whelps we crying run away.
27: Hark, countrymen, either renew the fight,
28: Or tear the lions out of England’s coat.
29: Renounce your soil; give sheep in lions’ stead.
30: Sheep run not half so treacherous from the wolf,
31: Or horse or oxen from the leopard,
32: As you fly from your oft-subduèd slaves.
33: It will not be! Retire into your trenches.
34: You all consented unto Salisbury’s death,
35: For none would strike a stroke in his revenge.
37: In spite of us or aught that we could do.
38: O, would I were to die with Salisbury!
39: The shame hereof will make me hide my head.

1: Advance our waving colors on the walls.
2: Rescued is Orleance from the English.
3: Thus Joan la Pucelle hath performed her word.
5: How shall I honor thee for this success?
6: Thy promises are like Adonis’ garden
7: That one day bloomed and fruitful were the next.
8: France, triumph in thy glorious prophetess.
9: Recovered is the town of Orleance.
10: More blessèd hap did ne’er befall our state.
11: Why ring not bells aloud throughout the town?
12: Dauphin, command the citizens make bonfires
13: And feast and banquet in the open streets
14: To celebrate the joy that God hath given us.
15: All France will be replete with mirth and joy
16: When they shall hear how we have played the men.
17: ’Tis Joan, not we, by whom the day is won;
18: For which I will divide my crown with her,
19: And all the priests and friars in my realm
20: Shall in procession sing her endless praise.
21: A statelier pyramis to her I’ll rear
22: Than Rhodophe’s of Memphis ever was.
23: In memory of her, when she is dead,
24: Her ashes, in an urn more precious
25: Than the rich-jeweled coffer of Darius,
26: Transported shall be at high festivals
27: Before the kings and queens of France.
28: No longer on Saint Dennis will we cry,
29: But Joan la Pucelle shall be France’s saint.
30: Come in, and let us banquet royally
31: After this golden day of victory.

1: Sirs, take your places and be vigilant.
2: If any noise or soldier you perceive
3: Near to the walls, by some apparent sign
4: Let us have knowledge at the court of guard.
7: When others sleep upon their quiet beds,
8: Constrained to watch in darkness, rain, and cold.
10: By whose approach the regions of Artois,
11: Walloon, and Picardy are friends to us,
12: This happy night the Frenchmen are secure,
13: Having all day caroused and banqueted.
15: As fitting best to quittance their deceit
16: Contrived by art and baleful sorcery.
17: Coward of France, how much he wrongs his fame,
18: Despairing of his own arm’s fortitude,
19: To join with witches and the help of hell!
21: But what’s that Pucelle whom they term so pure?
23: A maid? And be so martial?
24: Pray God she prove not masculine ere long,
25: If underneath the standard of the French
26: She carry armor as she hath begun.
27: Well, let them practice and converse with spirits.
28: God is our fortress, in whose conquering name
29: Let us resolve to scale their flinty bulwarks.
30: Ascend, brave Talbot. We will follow thee.
31: Not all together. Better far, I guess,
32: That we do make our entrance several ways,
33: That if it chance the one of us do fail,
34: The other yet may rise against their force.
37: And here will Talbot mount, or make his grave.
38: Now, Salisbury, for thee and for the right
39: Of English Henry, shall this night appear
40: How much in duty I am bound to both.
41: Arm, arm! The enemy doth make assault.
42: How now, my lords? What, all unready so?
43: Unready? Ay, and glad we scaped so well.
44: ’Twas time, I trow, to wake and leave our beds,
45: Hearing alarums at our chamber doors.
46: Of all exploits since first I followed arms
47: Ne’er heard I of a warlike enterprise
48: More venturous or desperate than this.
49: I think this Talbot be a fiend of hell.
50: If not of hell, the heavens sure favor him.

21: Who now is girdled with a waist of iron
22: And hemmed about with grim destruction.
23: To Bordeaux, warlike duke! To Bordeaux, York!
24: Else farewell Talbot, France, and England’s honor.
25: O God, that Somerset, who in proud heart
26: Doth stop my cornets, were in Talbot’s place!
27: So should we save a valiant gentleman
28: By forfeiting a traitor and a coward.
29: Mad ire and wrathful fury makes me weep
30: That thus we die while remiss traitors sleep.
31: O, send some succor to the distressed lord!
32: He dies, we lose; I break my warlike word;
33: We mourn, France smiles; we lose, they daily get,
34: All long of this vile traitor Somerset.
35: Then God take mercy on brave Talbot’s soul,
36: And on his son, young John, who two hours since
37: I met in travel toward his warlike father.
38: This seven years did not Talbot see his son,
39: And now they meet where both their lives are done.
40: Alas, what joy shall noble Talbot have
41: To bid his young son welcome to his grave?
42: Away! Vexation almost stops my breath,
43: That sundered friends greet in the hour of death.
44: Lucy, farewell. No more my fortune can
45: But curse the cause I cannot aid the man.
46: Maine, Blois, Poictiers, and Tours are won away,
47: Long all of Somerset and his delay.
48: Thus while the vulture of sedition
49: Feeds in the bosom of such great commanders,
50: Sleeping neglection doth betray to loss
51: The conquest of our scarce-cold conqueror,
53: Henry the Fifth. Whiles they each other cross,
54: Lives, honors, lands, and all hurry to loss.

1: It is too late; I cannot send them now.
2: This expedition was by York and Talbot
3: Too rashly plotted. All our general force
4: Might with a sally of the very town
5: Be buckled with. The overdaring Talbot
6: Hath sullied all his gloss of former honor
7: By this unheedful, desperate, wild adventure.
8: York set him on to fight and die in shame
9: That, Talbot dead, great York might bear the name.
10: Here is Sir William Lucy, who with me
11: Set from our o’er-matched forces forth for aid.
12: How now, Sir William, whither were you sent?
13: Whither, my lord? From bought and sold Lord Talbot,
14: Who, ringed about with bold adversity,
15: Cries out for noble York and Somerset
16: To beat assailing Death from his weak regions;
17: And whiles the honorable captain there
18: Drops bloody sweat from his war-wearied limbs
19: And, in advantage ling’ring, looks for rescue,
20: You, his false hopes, the trust of England’s honor,
21: Keep off aloof with worthless emulation.
22: Let not your private discord keep away
23: The levied succors that should lend him aid,
25: Yield up his life unto a world of odds.
28: And Talbot perisheth by your default.
29: York set him on; York should have sent him aid.
30: And York as fast upon your Grace exclaims,
31: Swearing that you withhold his levied host
33: York lies. He might have sent and had the horse.
34: I owe him little duty and less love,
35: And take foul scorn to fawn on him by sending.
36: The fraud of England, not the force of France,
37: Hath now entrapped the noble-minded Talbot.
38: Never to England shall he bear his life,
39: But dies betrayed to fortune by your strife.
40: Come, go. I will dispatch the horsemen straight.
41: Within six hours they will be at his aid.
42: Too late comes rescue; he is ta’en or slain,
43: For fly he could not if he would have fled;
44: And fly would Talbot never, though he might.
45: If he be dead, brave Talbot, then adieu.
46: His fame lives in the world, his shame in you.

1: O young John Talbot, I did send for thee
2: To tutor thee in stratagems of war,
3: That Talbot’s name might be in thee revived
4: When sapless age and weak unable limbs
5: Should bring thy father to his drooping chair.
7: Now thou art come unto a feast of Death,
9: Therefore, dear boy, mount on my swiftest horse,
10: And I’ll direct thee how thou shalt escape
11: By sudden flight. Come, dally not, be gone.
12: Is my name Talbot? And am I your son?
13: And shall I fly? O, if you love my mother,
15: To make a bastard and a slave of me!
16: The world will say He is not Talbot’s blood,
17: That basely fled when noble Talbot stood.
18: Fly, to revenge my death if I be slain.
19: He that flies so will ne’er return again.
20: If we both stay, we both are sure to die.
21: Then let me stay and, father, do you fly.
22: Your loss is great; so your regard should be.
23: My worth unknown, no loss is known in me.
24: Upon my death, the French can little boast;
25: In yours they will; in you all hopes are lost.
26: Flight cannot stain the honor you have won,
27: But mine it will, that no exploit have done.
28: You fled for vantage, everyone will swear;
29: But if I bow, they’ll say it was for fear.
30: There is no hope that ever I will stay
31: If the first hour I shrink and run away.
32: Here on my knee I beg mortality,
33: Rather than life preserved with infamy.
34: Shall all thy mother’s hopes lie in one tomb?
35: Ay, rather than I’ll shame my mother’s womb.
36: Upon my blessing I command thee go.
37: To fight I will, but not to fly the foe.
38: Part of thy father may be saved in thee.
39: No part of him but will be shame in me.
40: Thou never hadst renown, nor canst not lose it.
41: Yes, your renownèd name; shall flight abuse it?
42: Thy father’s charge shall clear thee from that stain.
43: You cannot witness for me, being slain.
44: If death be so apparent, then both fly.
45: And leave my followers here to fight and die?
46: My age was never tainted with such shame.
47: And shall my youth be guilty of such blame?
48: No more can I be severed from your side
49: Than can yourself yourself in twain divide.
50: Stay, go, do what you will; the like do I,
51: For live I will not, if my father die.
52: Then here I take my leave of thee, fair son,
53: Born to eclipse thy life this afternoon.
54: Come, side by side, together live and die,
55: And soul with soul from France to heaven fly.

1: Saint George, and victory! Fight, soldiers, fight!
2: The Regent hath with Talbot broke his word
3: And left us to the rage of France his sword.
4: Where is John Talbot?—Pause, and take thy breath;
5: I gave thee life and rescued thee from death.
6: O, twice my father, twice am I thy son!
7: The life thou gav’st me first was lost and done
8: Till with thy warlike sword, despite of fate,
9: To my determined time thou gav’st new date.
10: When from the Dauphin’s crest thy sword struck fire,
11: It warmed thy father’s heart with proud desire
12: Of bold-faced victory. Then leaden age,
13: Quickened with youthful spleen and warlike rage,
15: And from the pride of Gallia rescued thee.
16: The ireful Bastard Orleance, that drew blood
17: From thee, my boy, and had the maidenhood
18: Of thy first fight, I soon encounterèd,
19: And, interchanging blows, I quickly shed
20: Some of his bastard blood, and in disgrace
22: And misbegotten blood I spill of thine,
23: Mean and right poor, for that pure blood of mine
24: Which thou didst force from Talbot, my brave boy.
25: Here, purposing the Bastard to destroy,
26: Came in strong rescue. Speak, thy father’s care:
27: Art thou not weary, John? How dost thou fare?
28: Wilt thou yet leave the battle, boy, and fly,
29: Now thou art sealed the son of chivalry?
30: Fly, to revenge my death when I am dead;
31: The help of one stands me in little stead.
32: O, too much folly is it, well I wot,
33: To hazard all our lives in one small boat.
34: If I today die not with Frenchmen’s rage,
35: Tomorrow I shall die with mickle age.
36: By me they nothing gain, and, if I stay,
37: ’Tis but the short’ning of my life one day.
38: In thee thy mother dies, our household’s name,
39: My death’s revenge, thy youth, and England’s fame.
40: All these and more we hazard by thy stay;
41: All these are saved if thou wilt fly away.
42: The sword of Orleance hath not made me smart;
43: These words of yours draw lifeblood from my heart.
44: On that advantage, bought with such a shame,
45: To save a paltry life and slay bright fame,
46: Before young Talbot from old Talbot fly,
47: The coward horse that bears me fall and die!
48: And like me to the peasant boys of France,
49: To be shame’s scorn and subject of mischance!
50: Surely, by all the glory you have won,
51: An if I fly, I am not Talbot’s son.
52: Then talk no more of flight, it is no boot;
53: If son to Talbot, die at Talbot’s foot.
54: Then follow thou thy desp’rate sire of Crete,
55: Thou Icarus; thy life to me is sweet.
56: If thou wilt fight, fight by thy father’s side,
57: And commendable proved, let’s die in pride.

1: Where is my other life? Mine own is gone.
2: O, where’s young Talbot? Where is valiant John?
4: Young Talbot’s valor makes me smile at thee.
5: When he perceived me shrink and on my knee,
6: His bloody sword he brandished over me,
7: And like a hungry lion did commence
8: Rough deeds of rage and stern impatience;
9: But when my angry guardant stood alone,
10: Tend’ring my ruin and assailed of none,
11: Dizzy-eyed fury and great rage of heart
12: Suddenly made him from my side to start
13: Into the clust’ring battle of the French;
14: And in that sea of blood, my boy did drench
15: His over-mounting spirit; and there died
16: My Icarus, my blossom, in his pride.
17: O, my dear lord, lo where your son is borne!
18: Thou antic Death, which laugh’st us here to scorn,
21: Two Talbots, wingèd through the lither sky,
22: In thy despite shall scape mortality.—
23: O, thou whose wounds become hard-favored Death,
24: Speak to thy father ere thou yield thy breath!
25: Brave Death by speaking, whither he will or no.
26: Imagine him a Frenchman and thy foe.—
27: Poor boy, he smiles, methinks, as who should say
28: Had Death been French, then Death had died today.—
30: Come, come, and lay him in his father’s arms;
31: My spirit can no longer bear these harms.
32: Soldiers, adieu! I have what I would have,
33: Now my old arms are young John Talbot’s grave.
34: Had York and Somerset brought rescue in,
35: We should have found a bloody day of this.
36: How the young whelp of Talbot’s, raging wood,
37: Did flesh his puny sword in Frenchmen’s blood!
38: Once I encountered him, and thus I said:
39: Thou maiden youth, be vanquished by a maid.
40: But with a proud majestical high scorn
41: He answered thus: Young Talbot was not born
42: To be the pillage of a giglot wench.
43: So, rushing in the bowels of the French,
44: He left me proudly, as unworthy fight.
45: Doubtless he would have made a noble knight.
46: See where he lies inhearsèd in the arms
47: Of the most bloody nurser of his harms.
48: Hew them to pieces, hack their bones asunder,
49: Whose life was England’s glory, Gallia’s wonder.
50: O, no, forbear! For that which we have fled
51: During the life, let us not wrong it dead.
52: Herald, conduct me to the Dauphin’s tent,
53: To know who hath obtained the glory of the day.
54: On what submissive message art thou sent?
55: Submission, dauphin? ’Tis a mere French word.
56: We English warriors wot not what it means.
57: I come to know what prisoners thou hast ta’en,
58: And to survey the bodies of the dead.
59: For prisoners askst thou? Hell our prison is.
60: But tell me whom thou seek’st.
61: But where’s the great Alcides of the field,
62: Valiant Lord Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury,
63: Created for his rare success in arms
64: Great Earl of Washford, Waterford, and Valence,
65: Lord Talbot of Goodrich and Urchinfield,
66: Lord Strange of Blackmere, Lord Verdon of Alton,
67: Lord Cromwell of Wingfield, Lord Furnival of Sheffield,
69: The thrice victorious Lord of Falconbridge,
70: Knight of the noble Order of Saint George,
71: Worthy Saint Michael, and the Golden Fleece,
72: Great Marshal to Henry the Sixth
73: Of all his wars within the realm of France?
74: Here’s a silly stately style indeed.
75: The Turk, that two-and-fifty kingdoms hath,
76: Writes not so tedious a style as this.
77: Him that thou magnifi’st with all these titles
78: Stinking and flyblown lies here at our feet.
79: Is Talbot slain, the Frenchmen’s only scourge,
80: Your kingdom’s terror and black Nemesis?
81: O, were mine eyeballs into bullets turned
82: That I in rage might shoot them at your faces!
83: O, that I could but call these dead to life,
84: It were enough to fright the realm of France.
85: Were but his picture left amongst you here,
86: It would amaze the proudest of you all.
87: Give me their bodies, that I may bear them hence
88: And give them burial as beseems their worth.
89: I think this upstart is old Talbot’s ghost,
90: He speaks with such a proud commanding spirit.
91: For God’s sake, let him have him. To keep them here,
92: They would but stink and putrefy the air.
95: But from their ashes shall be reared
96: A phoenix that shall make all France afeard.
97: So we be rid of them, do with him what thou wilt.
98: And now to Paris in this conquering vein.
99: All will be ours, now bloody Talbot’s slain.

1: Have you perused the letters from the Pope,
2: The Emperor, and the Earl of Armagnac?
3: I have, my lord, and their intent is this:
4: They humbly sue unto your Excellence
5: To have a godly peace concluded of
6: Between the realms of England and of France.
7: How doth your Grace affect their motion?
8: Well, my good lord, and as the only means
9: To stop effusion of our Christian blood
10: And stablish quietness on every side.
11: Ay, marry, uncle, for I always thought
12: It was both impious and unnatural
13: That such immanity and bloody strife
14: Should reign among professors of one faith.
15: Besides, my lord, the sooner to effect
16: And surer bind this knot of amity,
17: The Earl of Armagnac, near knit to Charles,
18: A man of great authority in France,
19: Proffers his only daughter to your Grace
20: In marriage, with a large and sumptuous dowry.
21: Marriage, uncle? Alas, my years are young;
22: And fitter is my study and my books
23: Than wanton dalliance with a paramour.
24: Yet call th’ Ambassadors and, as you please,
25: So let them have their answers every one.
26: I shall be well content with any choice
27: Tends to God’s glory and my country’s weal.
28: What, is my Lord of Winchester installed
29: And called unto a cardinal’s degree?
30: Then I perceive that will be verified
31: Henry the Fifth did sometime prophesy:
32: If once he come to be a cardinal,
33: He’ll make his cap coequal with the crown.
34: My Lords Ambassadors, your several suits
35: Have been considered and debated on;
36: Your purpose is both good and reasonable,
37: And therefore are we certainly resolved
38: To draw conditions of a friendly peace,
39: Which by my Lord of Winchester we mean
40: Shall be transported presently to France.
41: And for the proffer of my lord your master,
42: I have informed his Highness so at large
43: As, liking of the lady’s virtuous gifts,
44: Her beauty, and the value of her dower,
45: He doth intend she shall be England’s queen.
46: In argument and proof of which contract,
47: Bear her this jewel, pledge of my affection.—
48: And so, my Lord Protector, see them guarded
49: And safely brought to Dover, where, inshipped,
50: Commit them to the fortune of the sea.
51: Stay, my Lord Legate; you shall first receive
52: The sum of money which I promisèd
53: Should be delivered to his Holiness
54: For clothing me in these grave ornaments.
55: I will attend upon your Lordship’s leisure.
56: Now Winchester will not submit, I trow,
57: Or be inferior to the proudest peer.
58: Humphrey of Gloucester, thou shalt well perceive
59: That neither in birth or for authority
60: The Bishop will be overborne by thee.
61: I’ll either make thee stoop and bend thy knee,
62: Or sack this country with a mutiny.

1: These news, my lords, may cheer our drooping spirits:
2: ’Tis said the stout Parisians do revolt
3: And turn again unto the warlike French.
4: Then march to Paris, royal Charles of France,
5: And keep not back your powers in dalliance.
6: Peace be amongst them if they turn to us;
7: Else ruin combat with their palaces!
10: What tidings send our scouts? I prithee speak.
11: The English army that divided was
12: Into two parties is now conjoined in one,
13: And means to give you battle presently.
14: Somewhat too sudden, sirs, the warning is,
15: But we will presently provide for them.
16: I trust the ghost of Talbot is not there.
17: Now he is gone, my lord, you need not fear.
18: Of all base passions, fear is most accursed.
19: Command the conquest, Charles, it shall be thine;
20: Let Henry fret and all the world repine.
21: Then on, my lords, and France be fortunate!

1: The Regent conquers and the Frenchmen fly.
2: Now help, you charming spells and periapts,
3: And you choice spirits that admonish me,
4: And give me signs of future accidents.
5: You speedy helpers, that are substitutes
6: Under the lordly monarch of the north,
7: Appear, and aid me in this enterprise.
8: This speed and quick appearance argues proof
9: Of your accustomed diligence to me.
10: Now, you familiar spirits that are culled
11: Out of the powerful regions under earth,
12: Help me this once, that France may get the field.
13: O, hold me not with silence overlong!
14: Where I was wont to feed you with my blood,
15: I’ll lop a member off and give it you
16: In earnest of a further benefit,
17: So you do condescend to help me now.
18: No hope to have redress? My body shall
19: Pay recompense if you will grant my suit.
21: Entreat you to your wonted furtherance?
22: Then take my soul—my body, soul, and all—
23: Before that England give the French the foil.
24: See, they forsake me. Now the time is come
25: That France must vail her lofty-plumèd crest
26: And let her head fall into England’s lap.
27: My ancient incantations are too weak,
28: And hell too strong for me to buckle with.
29: Now, France, thy glory droopeth to the dust.
30: Damsel of France, I think I have you fast.
31: Unchain your spirits now with spelling charms,
32: And try if they can gain your liberty.
33: A goodly prize, fit for the devil’s grace!
34: See how the ugly witch doth bend her brows
35: As if with Circe she would change my shape.
36: Changed to a worser shape thou canst not be.
37: O, Charles the Dauphin is a proper man;
38: No shape but his can please your dainty eye.
39: A plaguing mischief light on Charles and thee,
40: And may you both be suddenly surprised
41: By bloody hands in sleeping on your beds!
42: Fell banning hag! Enchantress, hold thy tongue.
43: I prithee give me leave to curse awhile.
44: Curse, miscreant, when thou com’st to the stake.
45: Be what thou wilt, thou art my prisoner.
46: O fairest beauty, do not fear nor fly,
47: For I will touch thee but with reverent hands.
48: I kiss these fingers for eternal peace
49: And lay them gently on thy tender side.
50: Who art thou? Say, that I may honor thee.
51: Margaret my name, and daughter to a king,
52: The King of Naples, whosoe’er thou art.
53: An earl I am, and Suffolk am I called.
55: Thou art allotted to be ta’en by me.
56: So doth the swan her downy cygnets save,
57: Keeping them prisoner underneath her wings.
58: Yet if this servile usage once offend,
59: Go and be free again as Suffolk’s friend.
60: I have no power to let her pass.
61: My hand would free her, but my heart says no.
62: As plays the sun upon the glassy streams,
64: So seems this gorgeous beauty to mine eyes.
65: Fain would I woo her, yet I dare not speak.
66: I’ll call for pen and ink and write my mind.
67: Fie, de la Pole, disable not thyself!
68: Hast not a tongue? Is she not here?
69: Wilt thou be daunted at a woman’s sight?
70: Ay. Beauty’s princely majesty is such
71: Confounds the tongue and makes the senses rough.
72: Say, Earl of Suffolk, if thy name be so,
73: What ransom must I pay before I pass?
74: For I perceive I am thy prisoner.
75: How canst thou tell she will deny thy suit
76: Before thou make a trial of her love?
77: Why speak’st thou not? What ransom must I pay?
78: She’s beautiful, and therefore to be wooed;
79: She is a woman, therefore to be won.
80: Wilt thou accept of ransom, yea or no?
81: Fond man, remember that thou hast a wife;
82: Then how can Margaret be thy paramour?
83: I were best to leave him, for he will not hear.
84: There all is marred; there lies a cooling card.
85: He talks at random; sure the man is mad.
86: And yet a dispensation may be had.
87: And yet I would that you would answer me.
88: I’ll win this Lady Margaret. For whom?
89: Why, for my king. Tush, that’s a wooden thing!
90: He talks of wood. It is some carpenter.
91: Yet so my fancy may be satisfied,
92: And peace establishèd between these realms.
93: But there remains a scruple in that, too;
94: For though her father be the King of Naples,
95: Duke of Anjou and Maine, yet is he poor,
96: And our nobility will scorn the match.
97: Hear you, captain? Are you not at leisure?
98: It shall be so, disdain they ne’er so much.
99: Henry is youthful, and will quickly yield.—
100: Madam, I have a secret to reveal.
101: What though I be enthralled, he seems a knight,
102: And will not any way dishonor me.
103: Lady, vouchsafe to listen what I say.
104: Perhaps I shall be rescued by the French,
105: And then I need not crave his courtesy.
106: Sweet madam, give me hearing in a cause.
107: Tush, women have been captivate ere now.
109: I cry you mercy, ’tis but quid for quo.
110: Say, gentle princess, would you not suppose
111: Your bondage happy, to be made a queen?
112: To be a queen in bondage is more vile
113: Than is a slave in base servility,
116: If happy England’s royal king be free.
117: Why, what concerns his freedom unto me?
118: I’ll undertake to make thee Henry’s queen,
119: To put a golden scepter in thy hand
120: And set a precious crown upon thy head,
121: If thou wilt condescend to be my—
124: I am unworthy to be Henry’s wife.
125: No, gentle madam, I unworthy am
126: To woo so fair a dame to be his wife,
127: And have no portion in the choice myself.
128: How say you, madam? Are you so content?
129: An if my father please, I am content.
130: Then call our captains and our colors forth!
131: And, madam, at your father’s castle walls
132: We’ll crave a parley to confer with him.
133: See, Reignier, see thy daughter prisoner!
137: I am a soldier and unapt to weep
138: Or to exclaim on Fortune’s fickleness.
139: Yes, there is remedy enough, my lord:
140: Consent, and, for thy Honor give consent,
141: Thy daughter shall be wedded to my king,
142: Whom I with pain have wooed and won thereto;
144: Hath gained thy daughter princely liberty.
147: That Suffolk doth not flatter, face, or feign.
148: Upon thy princely warrant, I descend
149: To give thee answer of thy just demand.
150: And here I will expect thy coming.
151: Welcome, brave earl, into our territories.
152: Command in Anjou what your Honor pleases.
153: Thanks, Reignier, happy for so sweet a child,
154: Fit to be made companion with a king.
155: What answer makes your Grace unto my suit?
156: Since thou dost deign to woo her little worth
157: To be the princely bride of such a lord,
159: Enjoy mine own, the country Maine and Anjou,
160: Free from oppression or the stroke of war,
161: My daughter shall be Henry’s, if he please.
162: That is her ransom; I deliver her,
163: And those two counties I will undertake
164: Your Grace shall well and quietly enjoy.
165: And I, again in Henry’s royal name
166: As deputy unto that gracious king,
167: Give thee her hand for sign of plighted faith.
168: Reignier of France, I give thee kingly thanks
169: Because this is in traffic of a king.
170: And yet methinks I could be well content
171: To be mine own attorney in this case.—
172: I’ll over then to England with this news,
173: And make this marriage to be solemnized.
174: So farewell, Reignier; set this diamond safe
175: In golden palaces, as it becomes.
176: I do embrace thee, as I would embrace
177: The Christian prince King Henry, were he here.
178: Farewell, my lord; good wishes, praise, and prayers
179: Shall Suffolk ever have of Margaret.
180: Farewell, sweet madam. But, hark you, Margaret,
181: No princely commendations to my king?
182: Such commendations as becomes a maid,
183: A virgin, and his servant, say to him.
184: Words sweetly placed and modestly directed.
185: But, madam, I must trouble you again:
186: No loving token to his Majesty?
187: Yes, my good lord: a pure unspotted heart,
188: Never yet taint with love, I send the King.
190: That for thyself. I will not so presume
191: To send such peevish tokens to a king.
192: O, wert thou for myself! But, Suffolk, stay.
193: Thou mayst not wander in that labyrinth.
194: There Minotaurs and ugly treasons lurk.
195: Solicit Henry with her wondrous praise;
196: Bethink thee on her virtues that surmount
197: And natural graces that extinguish art;
198: Repeat their semblance often on the seas,
199: That, when thou com’st to kneel at Henry’s feet,
200: Thou mayst bereave him of his wits with wonder.

1: Bring forth that sorceress condemned to burn.
2: Ah, Joan, this kills thy father’s heart outright.
3: Have I sought every country far and near,
4: And, now it is my chance to find thee out,
5: Must I behold thy timeless cruel death?
6: Ah, Joan, sweet daughter Joan, I’ll die with thee.
8: I am descended of a gentler blood.
9: Thou art no father nor no friend of mine.
10: Out, out!—My lords, an please you, ’tis not so!
11: I did beget her, all the parish knows;
12: Her mother liveth yet, can testify
13: She was the first fruit of my bach’lorship.
14: Graceless, wilt thou deny thy parentage?
15: This argues what her kind of life hath been,

363: To make commotion, as full well he can,

365: In Ireland have I seen this stubborn Cade
366: Oppose himself against a troop of kerns,
367: And fought so long till that his thighs with darts
368: Were almost like a sharp-quilled porpentine;
369: And in the end being rescued, I have seen
370: Him caper upright like a wild Morisco,
371: Shaking the bloody darts as he his bells.
372: Full often, like a shag-haired crafty kern,
373: Hath he conversèd with the enemy,
374: And undiscovered come to me again
375: And given me notice of their villainies.
376: This devil here shall be my substitute;
377: For that John Mortimer, which now is dead,
378: In face, in gait, in speech he doth resemble.
379: By this, I shall perceive the Commons’ mind,
380: How they affect the house and claim of York.
381: Say he be taken, racked, and torturèd,
382: I know no pain they can inflict upon him
383: Will make him say I moved him to those arms.
384: Say that he thrive, as ’tis great like he will,
385: Why then from Ireland come I with my strength
386: And reap the harvest which that rascal sowed.
387: For, Humphrey being dead, as he shall be,
388: And Henry put apart, the next for me.

1: Run to my lord of Suffolk. Let him know
2: We have dispatched the Duke as he commanded.
3: O, that it were to do! What have we done?
4: Didst ever hear a man so penitent?
6: Now, sirs, have you dispatched this thing?
7: Ay, my good lord, he’s dead.
8: Why, that’s well said. Go, get you to my house;
9: I will reward you for this venturous deed.
10: The King and all the peers are here at hand.
11: Have you laid fair the bed? Is all things well,
15: Go, call our uncle to our presence straight.
16: Say we intend to try his Grace today
17: If he be guilty, as ’tis publishèd.
18: I’ll call him presently, my noble lord.
19: Lords, take your places; and, I pray you all,
20: Proceed no straiter ’gainst our uncle Gloucester
21: Than from true evidence of good esteem
22: He be approved in practice culpable.
23: God forbid any malice should prevail
24: That faultless may condemn a nobleman!
25: Pray God he may acquit him of suspicion!
26: I thank thee, Meg. These words content me much.
27: How now? Why look’st thou pale? Why tremblest thou?
29: Where is our uncle? What’s the matter, Suffolk?
30: Dead in his bed, my lord. Gloucester is dead.
32: God’s secret judgment. I did dream tonight
33: The Duke was dumb and could not speak a word.
34: How fares my lord? Help, lords, the King is dead!
35: Rear up his body. Wring him by the nose.
36: Run, go, help, help! O Henry, ope thine eyes!
37: He doth revive again. Madam, be patient.
40: Comfort, my sovereign! Gracious Henry, comfort!
41: What, doth my lord of Suffolk comfort me?
42: Came he right now to sing a raven’s note,
43: Whose dismal tune bereft my vital powers,
44: And thinks he that the chirping of a wren,
45: By crying comfort from a hollow breast,
46: Can chase away the first-conceivèd sound?
47: Hide not thy poison with such sugared words.
48: Lay not thy hands on me. Forbear, I say!
49: Their touch affrights me as a serpent’s sting.
50: Thou baleful messenger, out of my sight!
52: Sits in grim majesty to fright the world.
53: Look not upon me, for thine eyes are wounding.
54: Yet do not go away. Come, basilisk,
55: And kill the innocent gazer with thy sight;
56: For in the shade of death I shall find joy,
57: In life but double death, now Gloucester’s dead.
58: Why do you rate my lord of Suffolk thus?
59: Although the Duke was enemy to him,
60: Yet he most Christian-like laments his death.
61: And for myself, foe as he was to me,
62: Might liquid tears or heart-offending groans
63: Or blood-consuming sighs recall his life,
64: I would be blind with weeping, sick with groans,
65: Look pale as primrose with blood-drinking sighs,
66: And all to have the noble duke alive.
67: What know I how the world may deem of me?
68: For it is known we were but hollow friends.
69: It may be judged I made the Duke away;
70: So shall my name with slander’s tongue be wounded
71: And princes’ courts be filled with my reproach.
72: This get I by his death. Ay me, unhappy,
73: To be a queen and crowned with infamy!
74: Ah, woe is me for Gloucester, wretched man!
75: Be woe for me, more wretched than he is.
76: What, dost thou turn away and hide thy face?
77: I am no loathsome leper. Look on me.
78: What, art thou, like the adder, waxen deaf?
79: Be poisonous too, and kill thy forlorn queen.
80: Is all thy comfort shut in Gloucester’s tomb?
81: Why, then, Dame Margaret was ne’er thy joy.
82: Erect his statue and worship it,
83: And make my image but an alehouse sign.
84: Was I for this nigh-wracked upon the sea
85: And twice by awkward wind from England’s bank
86: Drove back again unto my native clime?
87: What boded this, but well forewarning wind
88: Did seem to say Seek not a scorpion’s nest,
89: Nor set no footing on this unkind shore?
90: What did I then but cursed the gentle gusts
91: And he that loosed them forth their brazen caves
92: And bid them blow towards England’s blessèd shore
93: Or turn our stern upon a dreadful rock?
94: Yet Aeolus would not be a murderer,
95: But left that hateful office unto thee.
96: The pretty-vaulting sea refused to drown me,
97: Knowing that thou wouldst have me drowned on shore
99: With tears as salt as sea, through thy unkindness.
100: The splitting rocks cow’red in the sinking sands
101: And would not dash me with their ragged sides
102: Because thy flinty heart, more hard than they,
103: Might in thy palace perish Margaret.
104: As far as I could ken thy chalky cliffs,
105: When from thy shore the tempest beat us back,
106: I stood upon the hatches in the storm,
107: And when the dusky sky began to rob
108: My earnest-gaping sight of thy land’s view,
109: I took a costly jewel from my neck—
110: A heart it was, bound in with diamonds—
111: And threw it towards thy land. The sea received it,
112: And so I wished thy body might my heart.
113: And even with this I lost fair England’s view,
114: And bid mine eyes be packing with my heart,
115: And called them blind and dusky spectacles
116: For losing ken of Albion’s wishèd coast.
117: How often have I tempted Suffolk’s tongue,
118: The agent of thy foul inconstancy,
119: To sit and watch me, as Ascanius did
120: When he to madding Dido would unfold
121: His father’s acts commenced in burning Troy!
122: Am I not witched like her, or thou not false like him?
124: Ay me, I can no more. Die, Margaret,
125: For Henry weeps that thou dost live so long.
127: That good Duke Humphrey traitorously is murdered
128: By Suffolk and the Cardinal Beaufort’s means.
129: The Commons, like an angry hive of bees
130: That want their leader, scatter up and down
131: And care not who they sting in his revenge.
132: Myself have calmed their spleenful mutiny,
133: Until they hear the order of his death.
134: That he is dead, good Warwick, ’tis too true;
135: But how he died God knows, not Henry.
136: Enter his chamber, view his breathless corpse,
137: And comment then upon his sudden death.
138: That shall I do, my liege.—Stay, Salisbury,
139: With the rude multitude till I return.
140: O Thou that judgest all things, stay my thoughts,
141: My thoughts that labor to persuade my soul
142: Some violent hands were laid on Humphrey’s life.
143: If my suspect be false, forgive me, God,
144: For judgment only doth belong to Thee.
145: Fain would I go to chafe his paly lips
146: With twenty thousand kisses, and to drain
147: Upon his face an ocean of salt tears,
148: To tell my love unto his dumb deaf trunk
149: And with my fingers feel his hand unfeeling;
150: But all in vain are these mean obsequies.
151: And to survey his dead and earthy image,
152: What were it but to make my sorrow greater?
153: Come hither, gracious sovereign. View this body.
154: That is to see how deep my grave is made,
155: For with his soul fled all my worldly solace;
156: For seeing him, I see my life in death.
157: As surely as my soul intends to live
158: With that dread King that took our state upon Him
159: To free us from His Father’s wrathful curse,
160: I do believe that violent hands were laid
161: Upon the life of this thrice-famèd duke.
162: A dreadful oath, sworn with a solemn tongue!
163: What instance gives Lord Warwick for his vow?
164: See how the blood is settled in his face.
165: Oft have I seen a timely-parted ghost,
166: Of ashy semblance, meager, pale, and bloodless,
167: Being all descended to the laboring heart,
168: Who, in the conflict that it holds with death,
169: Attracts the same for aidance ’gainst the enemy,
170: Which with the heart there cools and ne’er returneth
172: To blush and beautify the cheek again.
173: But see, his face is black and full of blood;
174: His eyeballs further out than when he lived,
175: Staring full ghastly, like a strangled man;
176: His hair upreared, his nostrils stretched with struggling;
178: His hands abroad displayed, as one that grasped
179: And tugged for life and was by strength subdued.
180: Look, on the sheets his hair, you see, is sticking;
181: His well-proportioned beard made rough and rugged,
183: Like to the summer’s corn by tempest lodged.
184: It cannot be but he was murdered here.
185: The least of all these signs were probable.
186: Why, Warwick, who should do the Duke to death?
187: Myself and Beaufort had him in protection,
188: And we, I hope, sir, are no murderers.
189: But both of you were vowed Duke Humphrey’s foes,
190: And you, forsooth, had the good duke to keep.
192: ’Tis like you would not feast him like a friend,
193: And ’tis well seen he found an enemy.
194: Then you, belike, suspect these noblemen
195: As guilty of Duke Humphrey’s timeless death.
196: Who finds the heifer dead and bleeding fresh,
197: And sees fast by a butcher with an ax,
198: But will suspect ’twas he that made the slaughter?
199: Who finds the partridge in the puttock’s nest
200: But may imagine how the bird was dead,
201: Although the kite soar with unbloodied beak?
202: Even so suspicious is this tragedy.
203: Are you the butcher, Suffolk? Where’s your knife?
204: Is Beaufort termed a kite? Where are his talons?
205: I wear no knife to slaughter sleeping men,
206: But here’s a vengeful sword, rusted with ease,
207: That shall be scoured in his rancorous heart
208: That slanders me with murder’s crimson badge.—
209: Say, if thou dar’st, proud lord of Warwickshire,
210: That I am faulty in Duke Humphrey’s death.
211: What dares not Warwick, if false Suffolk dare him?
212: He dares not calm his contumelious spirit
213: Nor cease to be an arrogant controller,
214: Though Suffolk dare him twenty thousand times.
215: Madam, be still—with reverence may I say—
216: For every word you speak in his behalf
217: Is slander to your royal dignity.
219: If ever lady wronged her lord so much,
220: Thy mother took into her blameful bed
221: Some stern untutored churl, and noble stock
222: Was graft with crab-tree slip, whose fruit thou art
223: And never of the Nevilles’ noble race.
224: But that the guilt of murder bucklers thee
225: And I should rob the deathsman of his fee,
226: Quitting thee thereby of ten thousand shames,
227: And that my sovereign’s presence makes me mild,
228: I would, false murd’rous coward, on thy knee
229: Make thee beg pardon for thy passèd speech
230: And say it was thy mother that thou meant’st,
231: That thou thyself wast born in bastardy;
232: And after all this fearful homage done,
233: Give thee thy hire and send thy soul to hell,
235: Thou shalt be waking while I shed thy blood,
236: If from this presence thou dar’st go with me.
237: Away even now, or I will drag thee hence!
238: Unworthy though thou art, I’ll cope with thee
239: And do some service to Duke Humphrey’s ghost.
240: What stronger breastplate than a heart untainted?
241: Thrice is he armed that hath his quarrel just,
242: And he but naked, though locked up in steel,
243: Whose conscience with injustice is corrupted.
245: Why, how now, lords? Your wrathful weapons drawn
247: Here in our presence? Dare you be so bold?
248: Why, what tumultuous clamor have we here?
249: The trait’rous Warwick, with the men of Bury,
250: Set all upon me, mighty sovereign.
251: Sirs, stand apart. The King shall know your mind.—
252: Dread lord, the Commons send you word by me,
253: Unless Lord Suffolk straight be done to death
255: They will by violence tear him from your palace
256: And torture him with grievous ling’ring death.
257: They say, by him the good duke Humphrey died;
258: They say, in him they fear your Highness’ death;
259: And mere instinct of love and loyalty,
260: Free from a stubborn opposite intent,
261: As being thought to contradict your liking,
262: Makes them thus forward in his banishment.
263: They say, in care of your most royal person,
264: That if your Highness should intend to sleep,
265: And charge that no man should disturb your rest,
266: In pain of your dislike or pain of death,
267: Yet, notwithstanding such a strait edict,
268: Were there a serpent seen with forkèd tongue
269: That slyly glided towards your Majesty,
270: It were but necessary you were waked,
271: Lest, being suffered in that harmful slumber,
272: The mortal worm might make the sleep eternal.
273: And therefore do they cry, though you forbid,
274: That they will guard you, whe’er you will or no,
275: From such fell serpents as false Suffolk is,
276: With whose envenomèd and fatal sting
277: Your loving uncle, twenty times his worth,
278: They say, is shamefully bereft of life.
279: An answer from the King, my lord of Salisbury!
280: ’Tis like the Commons, rude unpolished hinds,
281: Could send such message to their sovereign!
282: But you, my lord, were glad to be employed,
284: To show how quaint an orator you are.
285: But all the honor Salisbury hath won
286: Is that he was the lord ambassador
287: Sent from a sort of tinkers to the King.
288: An answer from the King, or we will all break in.
289: Go, Salisbury, and tell them all from me,
290: I thank them for their tender loving care;
291: And, had I not been cited so by them,
292: Yet did I purpose as they do entreat.
293: For, sure, my thoughts do hourly prophesy
294: Mischance unto my state by Suffolk’s means.
295: And therefore, by His Majesty I swear,
296: Whose far unworthy deputy I am,
297: He shall not breathe infection in this air
298: But three days longer, on the pain of death.
299: O Henry, let me plead for gentle Suffolk!
300: Ungentle queen to call him gentle Suffolk!
301: No more, I say. If thou dost plead for him,
302: Thou wilt but add increase unto my wrath.
303: Had I but said, I would have kept my word;
304: But when I swear, it is irrevocable.
305: If, after three days’ space, thou here be’st found
307: On any ground that I am ruler of,
308: The world shall not be ransom for thy life.—
309: Come, Warwick, come, good Warwick, go with me.
310: I have great matters to impart to thee.
311: Mischance and sorrow go along with you!
313: Be playfellows to keep you company!
314: There’s two of you; the devil make a third,
315: And threefold vengeance tend upon your steps!
317: And let thy Suffolk take his heavy leave.
318: Fie, coward woman and soft-hearted wretch!
319: Hast thou not spirit to curse thine enemies?
320: A plague upon them! Wherefore should I curse them?
322: Could curses kill, as doth the mandrake’s groan,
323: I would invent as bitter searching terms,
324: As curst, as harsh, and horrible to hear,
325: Delivered strongly through my fixèd teeth,
326: With full as many signs of deadly hate,
327: As lean-faced Envy in her loathsome cave.
328: My tongue should stumble in mine earnest words;
329: Mine eyes should sparkle like the beaten flint;
330: Mine hair be fixed on end, as one distract;
331: Ay, every joint should seem to curse and ban;
332: And even now my burdened heart would break
333: Should I not curse them. Poison be their drink!
334: Gall, worse than gall, the daintiest that they taste;
335: Their sweetest shade, a grove of cypress trees;
337: Their softest touch, as smart as lizards’ stings!
338: Their music, frightful as the serpent’s hiss,
339: And boding screech owls make the consort full!
340: All the foul terrors in dark-seated hell—
341: Enough, sweet Suffolk, thou torment’st thyself,
342: And these dread curses, like the sun ’gainst glass,
343: Or like an over-chargèd gun, recoil
344: And turn the force of them upon thyself.
345: You bade me ban, and will you bid me leave?
346: Now, by the ground that I am banished from,
347: Well could I curse away a winter’s night,
348: Though standing naked on a mountain top
349: Where biting cold would never let grass grow,
350: And think it but a minute spent in sport.
351: O, let me entreat thee cease! Give me thy hand,
352: That I may dew it with my mournful tears;
353: Nor let the rain of heaven wet this place
354: To wash away my woeful monuments.
355: O, could this kiss be printed in thy hand,
356: That thou mightst think upon these by the seal,
357: Through whom a thousand sighs are breathed for thee!
359: So, get thee gone, that I may know my grief;
360: ’Tis but surmised whiles thou art standing by,
361: As one that surfeits thinking on a want.
362: I will repeal thee, or, be well assured,
364: And banishèd I am, if but from thee.
365: Go, speak not to me. Even now be gone!
366: O, go not yet! Even thus two friends condemned
367: Embrace and kiss and take ten thousand leaves,
368: Loather a hundred times to part than die.
369: Yet now farewell, and farewell life with thee.
370: Thus is poor Suffolk ten times banishèd,
371: Once by the King, and three times thrice by thee.
372: ’Tis not the land I care for, wert thou thence.
374: So Suffolk had thy heavenly company;
375: For where thou art, there is the world itself,
376: With every several pleasure in the world;
377: And where thou art not, desolation.
378: I can no more. Live thou to joy thy life;
379: Myself no joy in naught but that thou liv’st.
380: Whither goes Vaux so fast? What news, I prithee?
382: That Cardinal Beaufort is at point of death;
383: For suddenly a grievous sickness took him
384: That makes him gasp and stare and catch the air,
385: Blaspheming God and cursing men on Earth.
386: Sometimes he talks as if Duke Humphrey’s ghost
387: Were by his side; sometimes he calls the King
388: And whispers to his pillow, as to him,
389: The secrets of his overchargèd soul.
390: And I am sent to tell his Majesty
391: That even now he cries aloud for him.
392: Go, tell this heavy message to the King.
393: Ay me! What is this world? What news are these!
394: But wherefore grieve I at an hour’s poor loss,
395: Omitting Suffolk’s exile, my soul’s treasure?
396: Why only, Suffolk, mourn I not for thee,
397: And with the southern clouds contend in tears—
398: Theirs for the earth’s increase, mine for my sorrows’?
400: Now get thee hence. The King, thou know’st, is coming;
402: If thou be found by me, thou art but dead.
403: If I depart from thee, I cannot live;
404: And in thy sight to die, what were it else
405: But like a pleasant slumber in thy lap?
406: Here could I breathe my soul into the air,
407: As mild and gentle as the cradle babe
408: Dying with mother’s dug between its lips;
409: Where, from thy sight, I should be raging mad
410: And cry out for thee to close up mine eyes,
411: To have thee with thy lips to stop my mouth.
412: So shouldst thou either turn my flying soul,
413: Or I should breathe it so into thy body,
414: And then it lived in sweet Elysium.
415: To die by thee were but to die in jest;
416: From thee to die were torture more than death.
417: O, let me stay, befall what may befall!
418: Away! Though parting be a fretful corrosive,
419: It is applièd to a deathful wound.
420: To France, sweet Suffolk. Let me hear from thee,
421: For wheresoe’er thou art in this world’s globe,
422: I’ll have an Iris that shall find thee out.
424: And take my heart with thee.
425: A jewel locked into the woefull’st cask
426: That ever did contain a thing of worth!
427: Even as a splitted bark, so sunder we.
428: This way fall I to death.

1: How fares my lord? Speak, Beaufort, to thy sovereign.
2: If thou be’st Death, I’ll give thee England’s treasure,
3: Enough to purchase such another island,
4: So thou wilt let me live and feel no pain.
5: Ah, what a sign it is of evil life,
6: Where Death’s approach is seen so terrible!
7: Beaufort, it is thy sovereign speaks to thee.
8: Bring me unto my trial when you will.
9: Died he not in his bed? Where should he die?
10: Can I make men live, whe’er they will or no?
11: O, torture me no more! I will confess.
12: Alive again? Then show me where he is.
13: I’ll give a thousand pound to look upon him.
14: He hath no eyes! The dust hath blinded them.
15: Comb down his hair. Look, look. It stands upright,
16: Like lime-twigs set to catch my wingèd soul.
17: Give me some drink, and bid the apothecary
18: Bring the strong poison that I bought of him.
19: O, Thou eternal mover of the heavens,
20: Look with a gentle eye upon this wretch!
21: O, beat away the busy meddling fiend
22: That lays strong siege unto this wretch’s soul,
23: And from his bosom purge this black despair!
24: See how the pangs of death do make him grin!
25: Disturb him not. Let him pass peaceably.
26: Peace to his soul, if God’s good pleasure be!—
27: Lord Card’nal, if thou think’st on heaven’s bliss,
28: Hold up thy hand; make signal of thy hope.
29: He dies and makes no sign. O, God forgive him!
30: So bad a death argues a monstrous life.
31: Forbear to judge, for we are sinners all.
32: Close up his eyes, and draw the curtain close,
33: And let us all to meditation.

1: The gaudy, blabbing, and remorseful day
2: Is crept into the bosom of the sea,
3: And now loud-howling wolves arouse the jades
4: That drag the tragic melancholy night,
5: Who, with their drowsy, slow, and flagging wings
6: Clip dead men’s graves, and from their misty jaws
7: Breathe foul contagious darkness in the air.
8: Therefore bring forth the soldiers of our prize;
9: For, whilst our pinnace anchors in the Downs,
10: Here shall they make their ransom on the sand,
11: Or with their blood stain this discolored shore.—
12: Master, this prisoner freely give I thee.—
13: And, thou that art his mate, make boot of this.—
14: The other, Walter Whitmore, is thy share.
15: What is my ransom, master? Let me know.
16: A thousand crowns, or else lay down your head.
17: And so much shall you give, or off goes yours.
18: What, think you much to pay two thousand crowns,
19: And bear the name and port of gentlemen?—
20: Cut both the villains’ throats—for die you shall;
21: The lives of those which we have lost in fight
22: Be counterpoised with such a petty sum!
23: I’ll give it, sir, and therefore spare my life.
24: And so will I, and write home for it straight.
25: I lost mine eye in laying the prize aboard,
26: And therefore to revenge it shalt thou die;
27: And so should these, if I might have my will.
28: Be not so rash. Take ransom; let him live.
29: Look on my George; I am a gentleman.
30: Rate me at what thou wilt, thou shalt be paid.
31: And so am I. My name is Walter Whitmore.
32: How now, why starts thou? What, doth death affright?
34: Thy name affrights me, in whose sound is death.
35: A cunning man did calculate my birth
36: And told me that by water I should die.
37: Yet let not this make thee be bloody-minded;
38: Thy name is Gualtier, being rightly sounded.
39: Gualtier or Walter, which it is, I care not.
40: Never yet did base dishonor blur our name
41: But with our sword we wiped away the blot.
42: Therefore, when merchantlike I sell revenge,
43: Broke be my sword, my arms torn and defaced,
44: And I proclaimed a coward through the world!
45: Stay, Whitmore, for thy prisoner is a prince,
46: The Duke of Suffolk, William de la Pole.
47: The Duke of Suffolk muffled up in rags?
48: Ay, but these rags are no part of the Duke.
49: Jove sometimes went disguised, and why not I?
50: But Jove was never slain, as thou shalt be.
51: Obscure and lousy swain, King Henry’s blood,
53: Must not be shed by such a jaded groom.
54: Hast thou not kissed thy hand and held my stirrup?
55: Bareheaded plodded by my footcloth mule,
56: And thought thee happy when I shook my head?
57: How often hast thou waited at my cup,
58: Fed from my trencher, kneeled down at the board,
59: When I have feasted with Queen Margaret?
60: Remember it, and let it make thee crestfall’n,
61: Ay, and allay this thy abortive pride.
62: How in our voiding lobby hast thou stood
63: And duly waited for my coming forth?
64: This hand of mine hath writ in thy behalf,
65: And therefore shall it charm thy riotous tongue.
66: Speak, captain, shall I stab the forlorn swain?
67: First let my words stab him as he hath me.
68: Base slave, thy words are blunt, and so art thou.
69: Convey him hence, and on our longboat’s side,
71: Thou dar’st not for thy own.
75: Ay, kennel, puddle, sink, whose filth and dirt
76: Troubles the silver spring where England drinks!
77: Now will I dam up this thy yawning mouth
78: For swallowing the treasure of the realm.
79: Thy lips that kissed the Queen shall sweep the ground,
81: And thou that smiledst at good Duke Humphrey’s death
83: Against the senseless winds shall grin in vain,
84: Who in contempt shall hiss at thee again.
85: And wedded be thou to the hags of hell
86: For daring to affy a mighty lord
87: Unto the daughter of a worthless king,
88: Having neither subject, wealth, nor diadem.
89: By devilish policy art thou grown great,
91: With gobbets of thy mother’s bleeding heart.
92: By thee Anjou and Maine were sold to France.
93: The false revolting Normans thorough thee
94: Disdain to call us lord, and Picardy
95: Hath slain their governors, surprised our forts,
96: And sent the ragged soldiers wounded home.

22: Or gather wealth, I care not with what envy.
23: Sufficeth that I have maintains my state
24: And sends the poor well pleasèd from my gate.
25: Here’s the lord of the soil come to seize
26: me for a stray, for entering his fee-simple without
27: leave.—Ah, villain, thou wilt betray me and get a
28: thousand crowns of the King by carrying my head
29: to him; but I’ll make thee eat iron like an ostrich
30: and swallow my sword like a great pin, ere thou
32: Why, rude companion, whatsoe’er thou be,
33: I know thee not. Why, then, should I betray thee?
34: Is ’t not enough to break into my garden
35: And, like a thief, to come to rob my grounds,
36: Climbing my walls in spite of me the owner,
37: But thou wilt brave me with these saucy terms?
38: Brave thee? Ay, by the best blood that ever was
39: broached, and beard thee too. Look on me well: I
40: have eat no meat these five days, yet come thou
41: and thy five men, and if I do not leave you all as
42: dead as a doornail, I pray God I may never eat
44: Nay, it shall ne’er be said, while England stands,
45: That Alexander Iden, an esquire of Kent,
46: Took odds to combat a poor famished man.
47: Oppose thy steadfast gazing eyes to mine;
48: See if thou canst outface me with thy looks.
49: Set limb to limb, and thou art far the lesser;
50: Thy hand is but a finger to my fist,
51: Thy leg a stick comparèd with this truncheon.
52: My foot shall fight with all the strength thou hast;
53: And if mine arm be heavèd in the air,
54: Thy grave is digged already in the earth.
55: As for words, whose greatness answers words,
56: Let this my sword report what speech forbears.
57: By my valor, the most complete champion that
58: ever I heard! Steel, if thou turn the edge or cut not
59: out the burly-boned clown in chines of beef ere
60: thou sleep in thy sheath, I beseech God on my
61: knees thou mayst be turned to hobnails.
62: O, I am slain! Famine, and no other, hath slain me.
63: Let ten thousand devils come against me, and give
64: me but the ten meals I have lost, and I’d defy them
65: all. Wither, garden, and be henceforth a burying
66: place to all that do dwell in this house, because the
67: unconquered soul of Cade is fled.
68: Is ’t Cade that I have slain, that monstrous traitor?
69: Sword, I will hallow thee for this thy deed,
70: And hang thee o’er my tomb when I am dead.
71: Ne’er shall this blood be wipèd from thy point,
72: But thou shalt wear it as a herald’s coat
73: To emblaze the honor that thy master got.
74: Iden, farewell, and be proud of thy victory. Tell
75: Kent from me she hath lost her best man, and
76: exhort all the world to be cowards; for I, that never
77: feared any, am vanquished by famine, not by valor.
78: How much thou wrong’st me, heaven be my judge!
79: Die, damnèd wretch, the curse of her that bare thee!
80: And as I thrust thy body in with my sword,
81: So wish I, I might thrust thy soul to hell.
82: Hence will I drag thee headlong by the heels
83: Unto a dunghill, which shall be thy grave,
84: And there cut off thy most ungracious head,
85: Which I will bear in triumph to the King,
86: Leaving thy trunk for crows to feed upon.

1: From Ireland thus comes York to claim his right
2: And pluck the crown from feeble Henry’s head.
