3: Ring, bells, aloud! Burn, bonfires, clear and bright
4: To entertain great England’s lawful king!
5: Ah, sancta maiestas, who would not buy thee dear?
6: Let them obey that knows not how to rule.
7: This hand was made to handle naught but gold.
8: I cannot give due action to my words
9: Except a sword or scepter balance it.
10: A scepter shall it have, have I a soul,
11: On which I’ll toss the fleur-de-luce of France.
12: Whom have we here? Buckingham, to disturb me?
14: The King hath sent him, sure. I must dissemble.
15: York, if thou meanest well, I greet thee well.
16: Humphrey of Buckingham, I accept thy greeting.
17: Art thou a messenger, or come of pleasure?
18: A messenger from Henry, our dread liege,
19: To know the reason of these arms in peace;
20: Or why thou, being a subject as I am,
21: Against thy oath and true allegiance sworn,
22: Should raise so great a power without his leave,
23: Or dare to bring thy force so near the court.
24: Scarce can I speak, my choler is so great.
25: O, I could hew up rocks and fight with flint,
26: I am so angry at these abject terms!
28: On sheep or oxen could I spend my fury.
29: I am far better born than is the King,
30: More like a king, more kingly in my thoughts.
31: But I must make fair weather yet awhile,
32: Till Henry be more weak and I more strong.—
34: That I have given no answer all this while.
35: My mind was troubled with deep melancholy.
36: The cause why I have brought this army hither
37: Is to remove proud Somerset from the King,
38: Seditious to his Grace and to the state.
39: That is too much presumption on thy part.
40: But if thy arms be to no other end,
41: The King hath yielded unto thy demand:
42: The Duke of Somerset is in the Tower.
43: Upon thine honor, is he prisoner?
44: Upon mine honor, he is prisoner.
45: Then, Buckingham, I do dismiss my powers.—
46: Soldiers, I thank you all. Disperse yourselves.
47: Meet me tomorrow in Saint George’s field;
48: You shall have pay and everything you wish.
49: And let my sovereign, virtuous Henry,
50: Command my eldest son, nay, all my sons,
51: As pledges of my fealty and love;
52: I’ll send them all as willing as I live.
53: Lands, goods, horse, armor, anything I have
54: Is his to use, so Somerset may die.
55: York, I commend this kind submission.
56: We twain will go into his Highness’ tent.
57: Buckingham, doth York intend no harm to us
58: That thus he marcheth with thee arm in arm?
60: York doth present himself unto your Highness.
61: Then what intends these forces thou dost bring?
62: To heave the traitor Somerset from hence
63: And fight against that monstrous rebel Cade,
64: Who since I heard to be discomfited.
65: If one so rude and of so mean condition
66: May pass into the presence of a king,
67: Lo, I present your Grace a traitor’s head,
68: The head of Cade, whom I in combat slew.
69: The head of Cade? Great God, how just art Thou!
70: O, let me view his visage, being dead,
71: That living wrought me such exceeding trouble.
72: Tell me, my friend, art thou the man that slew him?
73: I was, an ’t like your Majesty.
74: How art thou called? And what is thy degree?
76: A poor esquire of Kent that loves his king.
77: So please it you, my lord, ’twere not amiss
78: He were created knight for his good service.
80: We give thee for reward a thousand marks,
81: And will that thou henceforth attend on us.
82: May Iden live to merit such a bounty,
83: And never live but true unto his liege!
84: See, Buckingham, Somerset comes with th’ Queen.
85: Go bid her hide him quickly from the Duke.
86: For thousand Yorks he shall not hide his head,
87: But boldly stand and front him to his face.
88: How now? Is Somerset at liberty?
89: Then, York, unloose thy long-imprisoned thoughts,
90: And let thy tongue be equal with thy heart.
91: Shall I endure the sight of Somerset?—
92: False king, why hast thou broken faith with me,
93: Knowing how hardly I can brook abuse?
94: King did I call thee? No, thou art not king,
95: Not fit to govern and rule multitudes,
96: Which dar’st not—no, nor canst not—rule a traitor.
97: That head of thine doth not become a crown;
98: Thy hand is made to grasp a palmer’s staff,
99: And not to grace an awful princely scepter.
100: That gold must round engirt these brows of mine,
101: Whose smile and frown, like to Achilles’ spear,
102: Is able with the change to kill and cure.
103: Here is a hand to hold a scepter up
104: And with the same to act controlling laws.
105: Give place. By heaven, thou shalt rule no more
106: O’er him whom heaven created for thy ruler.
107: O monstrous traitor! I arrest thee, York,
108: Of capital treason ’gainst the King and crown.
109: Obey, audacious traitor. Kneel for grace.
110: Wouldst have me kneel? First let me ask of these
111: If they can brook I bow a knee to man.
112: Sirrah, call in my sons to be my bail.
114: I know, ere they will have me go to ward,
115: They’ll pawn their swords for my enfranchisement.
116: Call hither Clifford; bid him come amain,
117: To say if that the bastard boys of York
118: Shall be the surety for their traitor father.
120: Outcast of Naples, England’s bloody scourge!
121: The sons of York, thy betters in their birth,
122: Shall be their father’s bail, and bane to those
123: That for my surety will refuse the boys.
124: See where they come; I’ll warrant they’ll make it good.
126: And here comes Clifford to deny their bail.
127: Health and all happiness to my lord the King.
128: I thank thee, Clifford. Say, what news with thee?
129: Nay, do not fright us with an angry look.
130: We are thy sovereign, Clifford; kneel again.
131: For thy mistaking so, we pardon thee.
132: This is my king, York; I do not mistake,
133: But thou mistakes me much to think I do.—
134: To Bedlam with him! Is the man grown mad?
135: Ay, Clifford, a bedlam and ambitious humor
136: Makes him oppose himself against his king.
137: He is a traitor. Let him to the Tower,
138: And chop away that factious pate of his.
139: He is arrested, but will not obey.
140: His sons, he says, shall give their words for him.
142: Ay, noble father, if our words will serve.
143: And if words will not, then our weapons shall.
144: Why, what a brood of traitors have we here!
145: Look in a glass, and call thy image so.
146: I am thy king and thou a false-heart traitor.
147: Call hither to the stake my two brave bears,
148: That, with the very shaking of their chains,
149: They may astonish these fell-lurking curs.
150: Bid Salisbury and Warwick come to me.
152: Are these thy bears? We’ll bait thy bears to death
153: And manacle the bearherd in their chains,
154: If thou dar’st bring them to the baiting place.
155: Oft have I seen a hot o’erweening cur
156: Run back and bite because he was withheld,
157: Who, being suffered with the bear’s fell paw,
158: Hath clapped his tail between his legs and cried;
159: And such a piece of service will you do
160: If you oppose yourselves to match Lord Warwick.
161: Hence, heap of wrath, foul indigested lump,
162: As crooked in thy manners as thy shape!
163: Nay, we shall heat you thoroughly anon.
164: Take heed, lest by your heat you burn yourselves.
165: Why, Warwick, hath thy knee forgot to bow?—
166: Old Salisbury, shame to thy silver hair,
167: Thou mad misleader of thy brainsick son!
168: What, wilt thou on thy deathbed play the ruffian
169: And seek for sorrow with thy spectacles?
170: O, where is faith? O, where is loyalty?
171: If it be banished from the frosty head,
172: Where shall it find a harbor in the earth?
173: Wilt thou go dig a grave to find out war,
174: And shame thine honorable age with blood?
175: Why art thou old and want’st experience?
176: Or wherefore dost abuse it, if thou hast it?
177: For shame! In duty bend thy knee to me
178: That bows unto the grave with mickle age.
179: My lord, I have considered with myself
180: The title of this most renownèd duke,
181: And in my conscience do repute his Grace
182: The rightful heir to England’s royal seat.
183: Hast thou not sworn allegiance unto me?
185: Canst thou dispense with heaven for such an oath?
186: It is great sin to swear unto a sin,
187: But greater sin to keep a sinful oath.
188: Who can be bound by any solemn vow
189: To do a murd’rous deed, to rob a man,
190: To force a spotless virgin’s chastity,
191: To reave the orphan of his patrimony,
192: To wring the widow from her customed right,
193: And have no other reason for this wrong
194: But that he was bound by a solemn oath?
195: A subtle traitor needs no sophister.
196: Call Buckingham, and bid him arm himself.
197: Call Buckingham and all the friends thou hast,
198: I am resolved for death or dignity.
199: The first, I warrant thee, if dreams prove true.
200: You were best to go to bed and dream again,
201: To keep thee from the tempest of the field.
202: I am resolved to bear a greater storm
203: Than any thou canst conjure up today;
204: And that I’ll write upon thy burgonet,
205: Might I but know thee by thy house’s badge.
206: Now, by my father’s badge, old Neville’s crest,
207: The rampant bear chained to the ragged staff,
208: This day I’ll wear aloft my burgonet—
209: As on a mountaintop the cedar shows
210: That keeps his leaves in spite of any storm—
211: Even to affright thee with the view thereof.
212: And from thy burgonet I’ll rend thy bear
213: And tread it under foot with all contempt,
214: Despite the bearherd that protects the bear.
215: And so to arms, victorious father,
216: To quell the rebels and their complices.
217: Fie! Charity, for shame! Speak not in spite,
218: For you shall sup with Jesu Christ tonight.
219: Foul stigmatic, that’s more than thou canst tell!
220: If not in heaven, you’ll surely sup in hell.

2: An if thou dost not hide thee from the bear,
3: Now, when the angry trumpet sounds alarum
4: And dead men’s cries do fill the empty air,
5: Clifford, I say, come forth and fight with me;
6: Proud northern lord, Clifford of Cumberland,
7: Warwick is hoarse with calling thee to arms.
8: How now, my noble lord? What, all afoot?
9: The deadly-handed Clifford slew my steed,
10: But match to match I have encountered him
11: And made a prey for carrion kites and crows
12: Even of the bonny beast he loved so well.
13: Of one or both of us the time is come.
14: Hold, Warwick! Seek thee out some other chase,
15: For I myself must hunt this deer to death.
16: Then, nobly, York! ’Tis for a crown thou fight’st.—
17: As I intend, Clifford, to thrive today,
18: It grieves my soul to leave thee unassailed.
19: What seest thou in me, York? Why dost thou pause?
20: With thy brave bearing should I be in love,
21: But that thou art so fast mine enemy.
22: Nor should thy prowess want praise and esteem,
23: But that ’tis shown ignobly and in treason.
24: So let it help me now against thy sword
25: As I in justice and true right express it!
26: My soul and body on the action both!
27: A dreadful lay! Address thee instantly.
29: Thus war hath given thee peace, for thou art still.
30: Peace with his soul, heaven, if it be thy will!
31: Shame and confusion! All is on the rout.
32: Fear frames disorder, and disorder wounds
33: Where it should guard. O war, thou son of hell,
34: Whom angry heavens do make their minister,
35: Throw in the frozen bosoms of our part
36: Hot coals of vengeance! Let no soldier fly.
37: He that is truly dedicate to war
38: Hath no self-love; nor he that loves himself
39: Hath not essentially, but by circumstance,
40: O, let the vile world end
42: And the premised flames of the last day
44: Now let the general trumpet blow his blast,
46: To cease! Wast thou ordained, dear father,
47: To lose thy youth in peace, and to achieve
48: The silver livery of advisèd age,
49: And, in thy reverence and thy chair-days, thus
50: To die in ruffian battle? Even at this sight
51: My heart is turned to stone, and while ’tis mine,
52: It shall be stony. York not our old men spares;
53: No more will I their babes. Tears virginal
54: Shall be to me even as the dew to fire;
55: And beauty, that the tyrant oft reclaims,
56: Shall to my flaming wrath be oil and flax.
57: Henceforth I will not have to do with pity.
58: Meet I an infant of the house of York,
59: Into as many gobbets will I cut it
60: As wild Medea young Absyrtis did.
61: In cruelty will I seek out my fame.
62: Come, thou new ruin of old Clifford’s house;
63: As did Aeneas old Anchises bear,
64: So bear I thee upon my manly shoulders.
65: But then Aeneas bare a living load,
66: Nothing so heavy as these woes of mine.
68: For underneath an alehouse’ paltry sign,
69: The Castle in Saint Albans, Somerset
70: Hath made the wizard famous in his death.
71: Sword, hold thy temper! Heart, be wrathful still!
72: Priests pray for enemies, but princes kill.
73: Away, my lord! You are slow. For shame, away!
74: Can we outrun the heavens? Good Margaret, stay!
75: What are you made of? You’ll nor fight nor fly.
76: Now is it manhood, wisdom, and defense
77: To give the enemy way, and to secure us
78: By what we can, which can no more but fly.
79: If you be ta’en, we then should see the bottom
80: Of all our fortunes; but if we haply scape,
81: As well we may—if not through your neglect—
82: We shall to London get, where you are loved
83: And where this breach now in our fortunes made
85: But that my heart’s on future mischief set,
86: I would speak blasphemy ere bid you fly;
87: But fly you must. Uncurable discomfit
88: Reigns in the hearts of all our present parts.
89: Away, for your relief! And we will live
90: To see their day and them our fortune give.

1: Of Salisbury, who can report of him,
2: That winter lion, who in rage forgets
3: Agèd contusions and all brush of time,
4: And, like a gallant in the brow of youth,
5: Repairs him with occasion? This happy day
6: Is not itself, nor have we won one foot,
9: Three times today I holp him to his horse,
10: Three times bestrid him. Thrice I led him off,
11: Persuaded him from any further act;
12: But still, where danger was, still there I met him,
13: And, like rich hangings in a homely house,
14: So was his will in his old feeble body.
15: But, noble as he is, look where he comes.
16: Now, by my sword, well hast thou fought today!
17: By th’ Mass, so did we all. I thank you, Richard.
18: God knows how long it is I have to live,
19: And it hath pleased Him that three times today
20: You have defended me from imminent death.
21: Well, lords, we have not got that which we have;
22: ’Tis not enough our foes are this time fled,
23: Being opposites of such repairing nature.
24: I know our safety is to follow them;
25: For, as I hear, the King is fled to London
26: To call a present court of Parliament.
27: Let us pursue him ere the writs go forth.—
28: What says Lord Warwick? Shall we after them?
29: After them? Nay, before them, if we can.
30: Now, by my hand, lords, ’twas a glorious day.
31: Saint Albans battle won by famous York
32: Shall be eternized in all age to come.—
33: Sound drum and trumpets, and to London all;
34: And more such days as these to us befall!

1: I wonder how the King escaped our hands.
2: While we pursued the horsemen of the north,
3: He slyly stole away and left his men;
4: Whereat the great lord of Northumberland,
5: Whose warlike ears could never brook retreat,
6: Cheered up the drooping army; and himself,
7: Lord Clifford, and Lord Stafford, all abreast,
8: Charged our main battle’s front and, breaking in,
9: Were by the swords of common soldiers slain.
10: Lord Stafford’s father, Duke of Buckingham,
11: Is either slain or wounded dangerous.
12: I cleft his beaver with a downright blow.
13: That this is true, father, behold his blood.
14: And, brother, here’s the Earl of Wiltshire’s blood,
15: Whom I encountered as the battles joined.
16: Speak thou for me, and tell them what I did.
17: Richard hath best deserved of all my sons.
18: But is your Grace dead, my lord of Somerset?
19: Such hope have all the line of John of Gaunt!
20: Thus do I hope to shake King Henry’s head.
21: And so do I, victorious prince of York.
22: Before I see thee seated in that throne
23: Which now the house of Lancaster usurps,
24: I vow by heaven these eyes shall never close.
25: This is the palace of the fearful king,
26: And this the regal seat. Possess it, York,
27: For this is thine and not King Henry’s heirs’.
28: Assist me, then, sweet Warwick, and I will,
29: For hither we have broken in by force.
30: We’ll all assist you. He that flies shall die.
31: Thanks, gentle Norfolk. Stay by me, my lords.—
32: And soldiers, stay and lodge by me this night.
33: And when the King comes, offer him no violence
34: Unless he seek to thrust you out perforce.
35: The Queen this day here holds her parliament,
36: But little thinks we shall be of her council.
37: By words or blows, here let us win our right.
38: Armed as we are, let’s stay within this house.
39: The Bloody Parliament shall this be called
40: Unless Plantagenet, Duke of York, be king
41: And bashful Henry deposed, whose cowardice
42: Hath made us bywords to our enemies.
43: Then leave me not, my lords; be resolute.
44: I mean to take possession of my right.
45: Neither the King nor he that loves him best,
46: The proudest he that holds up Lancaster,
47: Dares stir a wing if Warwick shake his bells.
48: I’ll plant Plantagenet, root him up who dares.
49: Resolve thee, Richard; claim the English crown.
50: My lords, look where the sturdy rebel sits,
51: Even in the chair of state! Belike he means,
52: Backed by the power of Warwick, that false peer,
53: To aspire unto the crown and reign as king.
54: Earl of Northumberland, he slew thy father,
55: And thine, Lord Clifford, and you both have vowed revenge
57: On him, his sons, his favorites, and his friends.
58: If I be not, heavens be revenged on me!
59: The hope thereof makes Clifford mourn in steel.
60: What, shall we suffer this? Let’s pluck him down.
61: My heart for anger burns. I cannot brook it.
62: Be patient, gentle Earl of Westmorland.
63: Patience is for poltroons such as he.
64: He durst not sit there had your father lived.
65: My gracious lord, here in the Parliament
66: Let us assail the family of York.
67: Well hast thou spoken, cousin. Be it so.
68: Ah, know you not the city favors them,
69: And they have troops of soldiers at their beck?
70: But when the Duke is slain, they’ll quickly fly.
71: Far be the thought of this from Henry’s heart,
72: To make a shambles of the Parliament House!
73: Cousin of Exeter, frowns, words, and threats
74: Shall be the war that Henry means to use.—
75: Thou factious Duke of York, descend my throne
76: And kneel for grace and mercy at my feet.
79: For shame, come down. He made thee Duke of York.
81: It was my inheritance, as the earldom was.
82: Thy father was a traitor to the crown.
83: Exeter, thou art a traitor to the crown
85: Whom should he follow but his natural king?
86: True, Clifford, that’s Richard, Duke of York.
87: And shall I stand, and thou sit in my throne?
88: It must and shall be so. Content thyself.
89: Be Duke of Lancaster. Let him be king.
90: He is both king and Duke of Lancaster,
91: And that the lord of Westmorland shall maintain.
92: And Warwick shall disprove it. You forget
93: That we are those which chased you from the field
94: And slew your fathers and, with colors spread,
95: Marched through the city to the palace gates.
96: Yes, Warwick, I remember it to my grief;
97: And by his soul, thou and thy house shall rue it.
98: Plantagenet, of thee and these thy sons,
99: Thy kinsmen, and thy friends, I’ll have more lives
100: Than drops of blood were in my father’s veins.
101: Urge it no more, lest that, instead of words,
102: I send thee, Warwick, such a messenger
103: As shall revenge his death before I stir.
104: Poor Clifford, how I scorn his worthless threats!
105: Will you we show our title to the crown?
106: If not, our swords shall plead it in the field.
107: What title hast thou, traitor, to the crown?
108: Thy father was as thou art, Duke of York;
109: Thy grandfather, Roger Mortimer, Earl of March.
110: I am the son of Henry the Fifth,
111: Who made the Dauphin and the French to stoop
112: And seized upon their towns and provinces.
113: Talk not of France, sith thou hast lost it all.
114: The Lord Protector lost it and not I.
115: When I was crowned, I was but nine months old.
116: You are old enough now, and yet, methinks, you lose.—
118: Father, tear the crown from the usurper’s head.
119: Sweet father, do so. Set it on your head.
120: Good brother, as thou lov’st and honorest arms,
121: Let’s fight it out and not stand caviling thus.
122: Sound drums and trumpets, and the King will fly.
124: Peace thou, and give King Henry leave to speak!
125: Plantagenet shall speak first. Hear him, lords,
126: And be you silent and attentive too,
127: For he that interrupts him shall not live.
128: Think’st thou that I will leave my kingly throne,
129: Wherein my grandsire and my father sat?
130: No. First shall war unpeople this my realm;
131: Ay, and their colors, often borne in France,
132: And now in England to our heart’s great sorrow,
133: Shall be my winding-sheet. Why faint you, lords?
134: My title’s good, and better far than his.
135: Prove it, Henry, and thou shalt be king.
136: Henry the Fourth by conquest got the crown.
138: I know not what to say; my title’s weak.—
139: Tell me, may not a king adopt an heir?
141: An if he may, then am I lawful king;
142: For Richard, in the view of many lords,
143: Resigned the crown to Henry the Fourth,
144: Whose heir my father was, and I am his.
145: He rose against him, being his sovereign,
146: And made him to resign his crown perforce.
147: Suppose, my lords, he did it unconstrained,
148: Think you ’twere prejudicial to his crown?
149: No, for he could not so resign his crown
150: But that the next heir should succeed and reign.
151: Art thou against us, Duke of Exeter?
152: His is the right, and therefore pardon me.
153: Why whisper you, my lords, and answer not?
154: My conscience tells me he is lawful king.
155: All will revolt from me and turn to him.
156: Plantagenet, for all the claim thou lay’st,
157: Think not that Henry shall be so deposed.
158: Deposed he shall be, in despite of all.
159: Thou art deceived. ’Tis not thy southern power
160: Of Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, nor of Kent,
161: Which makes thee thus presumptuous and proud,
162: Can set the Duke up in despite of me.
163: King Henry, be thy title right or wrong,
164: Lord Clifford vows to fight in thy defense.
165: May that ground gape and swallow me alive
166: Where I shall kneel to him that slew my father.
167: O Clifford, how thy words revive my heart!
168: Henry of Lancaster, resign thy crown.—
169: What mutter you, or what conspire you, lords?
170: Do right unto this princely Duke of York,
171: Or I will fill the house with armèd men,
172: And over the chair of state, where now he sits,
173: Write up his title with usurping blood.
174: My lord of Warwick, hear but one word:
175: Let me for this my lifetime reign as king.
176: Confirm the crown to me and to mine heirs,
177: And thou shalt reign in quiet while thou liv’st.
179: Enjoy the kingdom after my decease.
180: What wrong is this unto the Prince your son!
181: What good is this to England and himself!
183: How hast thou injured both thyself and us!
184: I cannot stay to hear these articles.
186: Come, cousin, let us tell the Queen these news.
188: In whose cold blood no spark of honor bides.
189: Be thou a prey unto the house of York,
190: And die in bands for this unmanly deed.
191: In dreadful war mayst thou be overcome,
192: Or live in peace abandoned and despised!
193: Turn this way, Henry, and regard them not.
194: They seek revenge and therefore will not yield.
196: Why should you sigh, my lord?
197: Not for myself, Lord Warwick, but my son,
199: But be it as it may.
200: The crown to thee and to thine heirs forever,
201: Conditionally, that here thou take an oath
202: To cease this civil war and, whilst I live,
203: To honor me as thy king and sovereign,
204: And neither by treason nor hostility
205: To seek to put me down and reign thyself.
206: This oath I willingly take and will perform.
207: Long live King Henry! Plantagenet, embrace him.
208: And long live thou and these thy forward sons!
209: Now York and Lancaster are reconciled.
210: Accursed be he that seeks to make them foes.
211: Farewell, my gracious lord. I’ll to my castle.
212: And I’ll keep London with my soldiers.
213: And I to Norfolk with my followers.
214: And I unto the sea, from whence I came.
215: And I with grief and sorrow to the court.
216: Here comes the Queen, whose looks bewray her anger.
220: Nay, go not from me. I will follow thee.
221: Be patient, gentle queen, and I will stay.
222: Who can be patient in such extremes?
223: Ah, wretched man, would I had died a maid
224: And never seen thee, never borne thee son,
225: Seeing thou hast proved so unnatural a father.
226: Hath he deserved to lose his birthright thus?
227: Hadst thou but loved him half so well as I,
228: Or felt that pain which I did for him once,
229: Or nourished him as I did with my blood,
230: Thou wouldst have left thy dearest heart-blood there,
232: Rather than have made that savage duke thine heir
235: If you be king, why should not I succeed?
236: Pardon me, Margaret.—Pardon me, sweet son.
237: The Earl of Warwick and the Duke enforced me.
238: Enforced thee? Art thou king and wilt be forced?
239: I shame to hear thee speak. Ah, timorous wretch,
240: Thou hast undone thyself, thy son, and me,
241: And giv’n unto the house of York such head
242: As thou shalt reign but by their sufferance!
243: To entail him and his heirs unto the crown,
244: What is it but to make thy sepulcher
245: And creep into it far before thy time?
246: Warwick is Chancellor and the lord of Callice;
247: Stern Falconbridge commands the Narrow Seas;
248: The Duke is made Protector of the realm;
249: And yet shalt thou be safe? Such safety finds
250: The trembling lamb environèd with wolves.
251: Had I been there, which am a silly woman,
252: The soldiers should have tossed me on their pikes
253: Before I would have granted to that act.
254: But thou preferr’st thy life before thine honor.
255: And seeing thou dost, I here divorce myself
256: Both from thy table, Henry, and thy bed,
257: Until that act of Parliament be repealed
259: The northern lords that have forsworn thy colors
260: Will follow mine if once they see them spread;
261: And spread they shall be, to thy foul disgrace
262: And utter ruin of the house of York.
263: Thus do I leave thee.—Come, son, let’s away.
264: Our army is ready. Come, we’ll after them.
265: Stay, gentle Margaret, and hear me speak.
266: Thou hast spoke too much already. Get thee gone.
267: Gentle son Edward, thou wilt stay with me?
268: Ay, to be murdered by his enemies!
269: When I return with victory from the field,
270: I’ll see your Grace. Till then, I’ll follow her.
271: Come, son, away. We may not linger thus.
272: Poor queen! How love to me and to her son
273: Hath made her break out into terms of rage!
274: Revenged may she be on that hateful duke,
275: Whose haughty spirit, wingèd with desire,
276: Will cost my crown, and like an empty eagle
277: Tire on the flesh of me and of my son.
278: The loss of those three lords torments my heart.
279: I’ll write unto them and entreat them fair.
280: Come, cousin, you shall be the messenger.
281: And I, I hope, shall reconcile them all.

1: Brother, though I be youngest, give me leave.
2: No, I can better play the orator.
3: But I have reasons strong and forcible.
4: Why, how now, sons and brother, at a strife?
5: What is your quarrel? How began it first?
6: No quarrel, but a slight contention.
8: About that which concerns your Grace and us:
9: The crown of England, father, which is yours.
10: Mine, boy? Not till King Henry be dead.
11: Your right depends not on his life or death.
12: Now you are heir; therefore enjoy it now.
13: By giving the house of Lancaster leave to breathe,
14: It will outrun you, father, in the end.
15: I took an oath that he should quietly reign.
16: But for a kingdom any oath may be broken.
17: I would break a thousand oaths to reign one year.
18: No, God forbid your Grace should be forsworn.
19: I shall be, if I claim by open war.
20: I’ll prove the contrary, if you’ll hear me speak.
21: Thou canst not, son; it is impossible.
22: An oath is of no moment, being not took
23: Before a true and lawful magistrate
24: That hath authority over him that swears.
25: Henry had none, but did usurp the place.
26: Then, seeing ’twas he that made you to depose,
27: Your oath, my lord, is vain and frivolous.
28: Therefore, to arms! And, father, do but think
29: How sweet a thing it is to wear a crown,
31: And all that poets feign of bliss and joy.
32: Why do we linger thus? I cannot rest
33: Until the white rose that I wear be dyed
34: Even in the lukewarm blood of Henry’s heart.
35: Richard, enough. I will be king or die.—
36: Brother, thou shalt to London presently,
37: And whet on Warwick to this enterprise.—
38: Thou, Richard, shalt to the Duke of Norfolk
39: And tell him privily of our intent.—
40: You, Edward, shall unto my Lord Cobham,
41: With whom the Kentishmen will willingly rise;
42: In them I trust, for they are soldiers
43: Witty, courteous, liberal, full of spirit.
44: While you are thus employed, what resteth more
45: But that I seek occasion how to rise,
46: And yet the King not privy to my drift,
47: Nor any of the house of Lancaster.
48: But stay, what news? Why com’st thou in such post?
49: The Queen with all the northern earls and lords
50: Intend here to besiege you in your castle.
51: She is hard by with twenty thousand men.
52: And therefore fortify your hold, my lord.
53: Ay, with my sword. What, think’st thou that we fear them?—
55: Edward and Richard, you shall stay with me;
56: My brother Montague shall post to London.
57: Let noble Warwick, Cobham, and the rest,
58: Whom we have left Protectors of the King,
60: And trust not simple Henry nor his oaths.
61: Brother, I go. I’ll win them, fear it not.
62: And thus most humbly I do take my leave.
63: Sir John and Sir Hugh Mortimer, mine uncles,
64: You are come to Sandal in a happy hour.
65: The army of the Queen mean to besiege us.
66: She shall not need; we’ll meet her in the field.
68: Ay, with five hundred, father, for a need.
69: A woman’s general; what should we fear?
70: I hear their drums. Let’s set our men in order,
71: And issue forth and bid them battle straight.
72: Five men to twenty: though the odds be great,
73: I doubt not, uncle, of our victory.
74: Many a battle have I won in France
75: Whenas the enemy hath been ten to one.
76: Why should I not now have the like success?

1: Ah, whither shall I fly to scape their hands?
2: Ah, tutor, look where bloody Clifford comes.
3: Chaplain, away. Thy priesthood saves thy life.
4: As for the brat of this accursèd duke,
5: Whose father slew my father, he shall die.
6: And I, my lord, will bear him company.
8: Ah, Clifford, murder not this innocent child,
9: Lest thou be hated both of God and man.
10: How now? Is he dead already? Or is it fear
11: That makes him close his eyes? I’ll open them.
12: So looks the pent-up lion o’er the wretch
13: That trembles under his devouring paws;
14: And so he walks, insulting o’er his prey;
15: And so he comes to rend his limbs asunder.
16: Ah, gentle Clifford, kill me with thy sword
17: And not with such a cruel threat’ning look.
18: Sweet Clifford, hear me speak before I die.
19: I am too mean a subject for thy wrath.
20: Be thou revenged on men, and let me live.
21: In vain thou speak’st, poor boy. My father’s blood
22: Hath stopped the passage where thy words should enter.
24: Then let my father’s blood open it again;
25: He is a man and, Clifford, cope with him.
26: Had I thy brethren here, their lives and thine
27: Were not revenge sufficient for me.
28: No, if I digged up thy forefathers’ graves
29: And hung their rotten coffins up in chains,
30: It could not slake mine ire nor ease my heart.
31: The sight of any of the house of York
32: Is as a fury to torment my soul,
33: And till I root out their accursèd line
34: And leave not one alive, I live in hell.
36: O, let me pray before I take my death!
37: To thee I pray: sweet Clifford, pity me!
38: Such pity as my rapier’s point affords.
39: I never did thee harm. Why wilt thou slay me?
42: Thou hast one son; for his sake pity me,
43: Lest in revenge thereof, sith God is just,
44: He be as miserably slain as I.
45: Ah, let me live in prison all my days,
46: And when I give occasion of offense
47: Then let me die, for now thou hast no cause.
48: No cause? Thy father slew my father; therefore die.
49: Di faciant laudis summa sit ista tuae!
51: And this thy son’s blood, cleaving to my blade,
52: Shall rust upon my weapon till thy blood,
53: Congealed with this, do make me wipe off both.

1: The army of the Queen hath got the field.
2: My uncles both are slain in rescuing me;
3: And all my followers to the eager foe
4: Turn back and fly like ships before the wind,
5: Or lambs pursued by hunger-starvèd wolves.
6: My sons, God knows what hath bechancèd them;
7: But this I know: they have demeaned themselves
8: Like men borne to renown by life or death.
9: Three times did Richard make a lane to me
10: And thrice cried Courage, father, fight it out!
11: And full as oft came Edward to my side,
12: With purple falchion painted to the hilt
13: In blood of those that had encountered him;
14: And when the hardiest warriors did retire,
15: Richard cried Charge, and give no foot of ground!
16: And cried A crown or else a glorious tomb;
17: A scepter or an earthly sepulcher!
18: With this we charged again; but, out alas,
19: We budged again, as I have seen a swan
20: With bootless labor swim against the tide
21: And spend her strength with over-matching waves.
22: Ah, hark, the fatal followers do pursue,
23: And I am faint and cannot fly their fury;
24: And were I strong, I would not shun their fury.
25: The sands are numbered that makes up my life.
26: Here must I stay, and here my life must end.
28: I dare your quenchless fury to more rage.
29: I am your butt, and I abide your shot.
30: Yield to our mercy, proud Plantagenet.
31: Ay, to such mercy as his ruthless arm
32: With downright payment showed unto my father.
33: Now Phaëton hath tumbled from his car
34: And made an evening at the noontide prick.
35: My ashes, as the Phoenix’, may bring forth
36: A bird that will revenge upon you all;
37: And in that hope I throw mine eyes to heaven,
38: Scorning whate’er you can afflict me with.
39: Why come you not? What, multitudes, and fear?
40: So cowards fight when they can fly no further;
41: So doves do peck the falcon’s piercing talons;
42: So desperate thieves, all hopeless of their lives,
44: O Clifford, but bethink thee once again
45: And in thy thought o’errun my former time;
46: And, if thou canst for blushing, view this face
47: And bite thy tongue that slanders him with cowardice
48: Whose frown hath made thee faint and fly ere this.
49: I will not bandy with thee word for word,
50: But buckler with thee blows twice two for one.
51: Hold, valiant Clifford, for a thousand causes
52: I would prolong a while the traitor’s life.—
53: Wrath makes him deaf; speak thou, Northumberland.
54: Hold, Clifford, do not honor him so much
55: To prick thy finger, though to wound his heart.
56: What valor were it when a cur doth grin
57: For one to thrust his hand between his teeth,
58: When he might spurn him with his foot away?
59: It is war’s prize to take all vantages,
60: And ten to one is no impeach of valor.
61: Ay, ay, so strives the woodcock with the gin.
62: So doth the coney struggle in the net.
63: So triumph thieves upon their conquered booty;
64: So true men yield with robbers, so o’ermatched.
65: What would your Grace have done unto him now?
67: Come, make him stand upon this molehill here
68: That raught at mountains with outstretchèd arms,
69: Yet parted but the shadow with his hand.
70: What, was it you that would be England’s king?
71: Was ’t you that reveled in our parliament
72: And made a preachment of your high descent?
73: Where are your mess of sons to back you now,
74: The wanton Edward and the lusty George?
75: And where’s that valiant crookback prodigy,
76: Dickie, your boy, that with his grumbling voice
77: Was wont to cheer his dad in mutinies?
78: Or, with the rest, where is your darling Rutland?
79: Look, York, I stained this napkin with the blood
80: That valiant Clifford with his rapier’s point
81: Made issue from the bosom of the boy;
82: And if thine eyes can water for his death,
83: I give thee this to dry thy cheeks withal.
84: Alas, poor York, but that I hate thee deadly
85: I should lament thy miserable state.
86: I prithee grieve to make me merry, York.
87: What, hath thy fiery heart so parched thine entrails
88: That not a tear can fall for Rutland’s death?
89: Why art thou patient, man? Thou shouldst be mad;
90: And I, to make thee mad, do mock thee thus.
91: Stamp, rave, and fret, that I may sing and dance.
92: Thou would’st be fee’d, I see, to make me sport.—
93: York cannot speak unless he wear a crown.
95: And, lords, bow low to him.
96: Hold you his hands whilst I do set it on.
97: Ay, marry, sir, now looks he like a king.
98: Ay, this is he that took King Henry’s chair,
99: And this is he was his adopted heir.
100: But how is it that great Plantagenet
101: Is crowned so soon and broke his solemn oath?—
102: As I bethink me, you should not be king
103: Till our King Henry had shook hands with Death.
104: And will you pale your head in Henry’s glory
105: And rob his temples of the diadem
106: Now, in his life, against your holy oath?
107: O, ’tis a fault too too unpardonable.
108: Off with the crown and, with the crown, his head;
109: And whilst we breathe, take time to do him dead.
110: That is my office, for my father’s sake.
111: Nay, stay, let’s hear the orisons he makes.
112: She-wolf of France, but worse than wolves of France,
114: Whose tongue more poisons than the adder’s tooth:
115: How ill-beseeming is it in thy sex
116: To triumph like an Amazonian trull
117: Upon their woes whom Fortune captivates.
118: But that thy face is vizard-like, unchanging,
119: Made impudent with use of evil deeds,
120: I would assay, proud queen, to make thee blush.
121: To tell thee whence thou cam’st, of whom derived,
122: Were shame enough to shame thee, wert thou not shameless.
124: Thy father bears the type of King of Naples,
125: Of both the Sicils, and Jerusalem,
126: Yet not so wealthy as an English yeoman.
127: Hath that poor monarch taught thee to insult?
128: It needs not, nor it boots thee not, proud queen,
129: Unless the adage must be verified
130: That beggars mounted run their horse to death.
131: ’Tis beauty that doth oft make women proud,
132: But God He knows thy share thereof is small.
133: ’Tis virtue that doth make them most admired;
134: The contrary doth make thee wondered at.
135: ’Tis government that makes them seem divine;
136: The want thereof makes thee abominable.
137: Thou art as opposite to every good
138: As the Antipodes are unto us
139: Or as the south to the Septentrion.
140: O, tiger’s heart wrapped in a woman’s hide,
141: How couldst thou drain the lifeblood of the child
142: To bid the father wipe his eyes withal,
143: And yet be seen to bear a woman’s face?
144: Women are soft, mild, pitiful, and flexible;
145: Thou, stern, obdurate, flinty, rough, remorseless.
146: Bidd’st thou me rage? Why, now thou hast thy wish.
147: Wouldst have me weep? Why, now thou hast thy will;
148: For raging wind blows up incessant showers,
149: And when the rage allays, the rain begins.
150: These tears are my sweet Rutland’s obsequies,
151: And every drop cries vengeance for his death
152: ’Gainst thee, fell Clifford, and thee, false Frenchwoman!
154: Beshrew me, but his passions moves me so
155: That hardly can I check my eyes from tears.
156: That face of his the hungry cannibals
157: Would not have touched, would not have stained with blood;
159: But you are more inhuman, more inexorable,
160: O, ten times more than tigers of Hyrcania.
161: See, ruthless queen, a hapless father’s tears.
162: This cloth thou dipped’st in blood of my sweet boy,
163: And I with tears do wash the blood away.
164: Keep thou the napkin and go boast of this;
165: And if thou tell’st the heavy story right,
166: Upon my soul, the hearers will shed tears.
167: Yea, even my foes will shed fast-falling tears
168: And say Alas, it was a piteous deed.
169: There, take the crown and, with the crown, my curse,
171: And in thy need such comfort come to thee
172: As now I reap at thy too cruel hand.—
173: Hard-hearted Clifford, take me from the world,
174: My soul to heaven, my blood upon your heads.
175: Had he been slaughterman to all my kin,
176: I should not for my life but weep with him
177: To see how inly sorrow gripes his soul.
178: What, weeping ripe, my Lord Northumberland?
179: Think but upon the wrong he did us all,
180: And that will quickly dry thy melting tears.
181: Here’s for my oath; here’s for my father’s death!
182: And here’s to right our gentle-hearted king.
183: Open thy gate of mercy, gracious God.
184: My soul flies through these wounds to seek out Thee.
185: Off with his head, and set it on York gates,
186: So York may overlook the town of York.

1: I wonder how our princely father scaped,
2: Or whether he be scaped away or no
4: Had he been ta’en, we should have heard the news;
5: Had he been slain, we should have heard the news;
6: Or had he scaped, methinks we should have heard
7: The happy tidings of his good escape.
8: How fares my brother? Why is he so sad?
9: I cannot joy until I be resolved
10: Where our right valiant father is become.
11: I saw him in the battle range about
12: And watched him how he singled Clifford forth.
13: Methought he bore him in the thickest troop
14: As doth a lion in a herd of neat,
15: Or as a bear encompassed round with dogs,
16: Who having pinched a few and made them cry,
17: The rest stand all aloof and bark at him;
18: So fared our father with his enemies;
19: So fled his enemies my warlike father.
20: Methinks ’tis prize enough to be his son.
21: See how the morning opes her golden gates
22: And takes her farewell of the glorious sun.
23: How well resembles it the prime of youth,
24: Trimmed like a younker, prancing to his love!
25: Dazzle mine eyes, or do I see three suns?
26: Three glorious suns, each one a perfect sun,
27: Not separated with the racking clouds
28: But severed in a pale clear-shining sky.
29: See, see, they join, embrace, and seem to kiss,
30: As if they vowed some league inviolable.
31: Now are they but one lamp, one light, one sun;
32: In this, the heaven figures some event.
33: ’Tis wondrous strange, the like yet never heard of.
34: I think it cites us, brother, to the field,
35: That we, the sons of brave Plantagenet,
36: Each one already blazing by our meeds,
37: Should notwithstanding join our lights together
38: And overshine the earth, as this the world.
39: Whate’er it bodes, henceforward will I bear
40: Upon my target three fair shining suns.
41: Nay, bear three daughters: by your leave I speak it,
42: You love the breeder better than the male.
43: But what art thou whose heavy looks foretell
44: Some dreadful story hanging on thy tongue?
45: Ah, one that was a woeful looker-on
46: Whenas the noble Duke of York was slain,
47: Your princely father and my loving lord.
48: O, speak no more, for I have heard too much!
49: Say how he died, for I will hear it all.
50: Environèd he was with many foes,
51: And stood against them, as the hope of Troy
52: Against the Greeks that would have entered Troy.
53: But Hercules himself must yield to odds;
54: And many strokes, though with a little axe,
55: Hews down and fells the hardest-timbered oak.
56: By many hands your father was subdued,
57: But only slaughtered by the ireful arm
58: Of unrelenting Clifford and the Queen,
59: Who crowned the gracious duke in high despite,
60: Laughed in his face; and when with grief he wept,
61: The ruthless queen gave him to dry his cheeks
62: A napkin steepèd in the harmless blood
63: Of sweet young Rutland, by rough Clifford slain.
64: And after many scorns, many foul taunts,
65: They took his head and on the gates of York
66: They set the same, and there it doth remain,
67: The saddest spectacle that e’er I viewed.
68: Sweet Duke of York, our prop to lean upon,
69: Now thou art gone, we have no staff, no stay.
70: O Clifford, boist’rous Clifford, thou hast slain
71: The flower of Europe for his chivalry;
72: And treacherously hast thou vanquished him,
73: For hand to hand he would have vanquished thee.
74: Now my soul’s palace is become a prison;
75: Ah, would she break from hence, that this my body
76: Might in the ground be closèd up in rest,
77: For never henceforth shall I joy again.
78: Never, O never, shall I see more joy!
79: I cannot weep, for all my body’s moisture
80: Scarce serves to quench my furnace-burning heart;
81: Nor can my tongue unload my heart’s great burden,
82: For selfsame wind that I should speak withal
83: Is kindling coals that fires all my breast
84: And burns me up with flames that tears would quench.
86: To weep is to make less the depth of grief:
87: Tears, then, for babes; blows and revenge for me.
88: Richard, I bear thy name. I’ll venge thy death
89: Or die renownèd by attempting it.
90: His name that valiant duke hath left with thee;
91: His dukedom and his chair with me is left.
92: Nay, if thou be that princely eagle’s bird,
93: Show thy descent by gazing ’gainst the sun;
94: For chair and dukedom, throne and kingdom say;
96: Either that is thine or else thou wert not his.
97: How now, fair lords? What fare, what news abroad?
98: Great lord of Warwick, if we should recount
99: Our baleful news, and at each word’s deliverance
100: Stab poniards in our flesh till all were told,
101: The words would add more anguish than the wounds.
102: O valiant lord, the Duke of York is slain.
104: Which held thee dearly as his soul’s redemption
105: Is by the stern Lord Clifford done to death.
106: Ten days ago I drowned these news in tears.
107: And now to add more measure to your woes,
108: I come to tell you things sith then befall’n.
109: After the bloody fray at Wakefield fought,
110: Where your brave father breathed his latest gasp,
111: Tidings, as swiftly as the posts could run,
112: Were brought me of your loss and his depart.
113: I, then in London, keeper of the King,
114: Mustered my soldiers, gathered flocks of friends,
115: Marched toward Saint Albans to intercept the Queen,
117: Bearing the King in my behalf along;
118: For by my scouts I was advertisèd
119: That she was coming with a full intent
120: To dash our late decree in Parliament
121: Touching King Henry’s oath and your succession.
122: Short tale to make, we at Saint Albans met,
123: Our battles joined, and both sides fiercely fought.
124: But whether ’twas the coldness of the King,
125: Who looked full gently on his warlike queen,
126: That robbed my soldiers of their heated spleen,
127: Or whether ’twas report of her success
128: Or more than common fear of Clifford’s rigor,
129: Who thunders to his captives blood and death,
130: I cannot judge; but to conclude with truth,
131: Their weapons like to lightning came and went;
132: Our soldiers’, like the night owl’s lazy flight
133: Or like an idle thresher with a flail,
134: Fell gently down, as if they struck their friends.
135: I cheered them up with justice of our cause,
136: With promise of high pay and great rewards,
137: But all in vain; they had no heart to fight,
138: And we, in them, no hope to win the day,
139: So that we fled: the King unto the Queen;
140: Lord George your brother, Norfolk, and myself
141: In haste, posthaste, are come to join with you;
142: For in the Marches here we heard you were,
143: Making another head to fight again.
144: Where is the Duke of Norfolk, gentle Warwick?
145: And when came George from Burgundy to England?
146: Some six miles off the Duke is with the soldiers,
147: And, for your brother, he was lately sent
148: From your kind aunt, Duchess of Burgundy,
149: With aid of soldiers to this needful war.
150: ’Twas odds, belike, when valiant Warwick fled.
151: Oft have I heard his praises in pursuit,
152: But ne’er till now his scandal of retire.
153: Nor now my scandal, Richard, dost thou hear?
154: For thou shalt know this strong right hand of mine
155: Can pluck the diadem from faint Henry’s head
156: And wring the awful scepter from his fist,
157: Were he as famous and as bold in war
158: As he is famed for mildness, peace, and prayer.
159: I know it well, Lord Warwick; blame me not.
160: ’Tis love I bear thy glories make me speak.
161: But in this troublous time, what’s to be done?
162: Shall we go throw away our coats of steel
163: And wrap our bodies in black mourning gowns,
164: Numb’ring our Ave Marys with our beads?
165: Or shall we on the helmets of our foes
166: Tell our devotion with revengeful arms?
167: If for the last, say Ay, and to it, lords.
168: Why, therefore Warwick came to seek you out,
169: And therefore comes my brother Montague.
170: Attend me, lords: the proud insulting queen,
171: With Clifford and the haught Northumberland
172: And of their feather many more proud birds,
173: Have wrought the easy-melting king like wax.
174: He swore consent to your succession,
175: His oath enrollèd in the Parliament.
176: And now to London all the crew are gone
177: To frustrate both his oath and what beside
178: May make against the house of Lancaster.
179: Their power, I think, is thirty thousand strong.
180: Now, if the help of Norfolk and myself,
181: With all the friends that thou, brave Earl of March,
182: Amongst the loving Welshmen canst procure,
183: Will but amount to five and twenty thousand,
184: Why, via, to London will we march,
185: And once again bestride our foaming steeds,
186: And once again cry Charge! upon our foes,
187: But never once again turn back and fly.
188: Ay, now methinks I hear great Warwick speak.
189: Ne’er may he live to see a sunshine day
190: That cries Retire! if Warwick bid him stay.
191: Lord Warwick, on thy shoulder will I lean,
192: And when thou fail’st—as God forbid the hour!—
193: Must Edward fall, which peril heaven forfend.
194: No longer Earl of March, but Duke of York;
195: The next degree is England’s royal throne:
196: For King of England shalt thou be proclaimed
197: In every borough as we pass along,
198: And he that throws not up his cap for joy
199: Shall for the fault make forfeit of his head.
201: Stay we no longer dreaming of renown,
202: But sound the trumpets and about our task.
203: Then, Clifford, were thy heart as hard as steel,
204: As thou hast shown it flinty by thy deeds,
205: I come to pierce it or to give thee mine.
206: Then strike up drums! God and Saint George for us!
208: The Duke of Norfolk sends you word by me,
209: The Queen is coming with a puissant host,
210: And craves your company for speedy counsel.
211: Why, then it sorts. Brave warriors, let’s away!

1: Welcome, my lord, to this brave town of York.
2: Yonder’s the head of that arch-enemy
3: That sought to be encompassed with your crown.
4: Doth not the object cheer your heart, my lord?
5: Ay, as the rocks cheer them that fear their wrack!
6: To see this sight, it irks my very soul.
7: Withhold revenge, dear God! ’Tis not my fault,
8: Nor wittingly have I infringed my vow.
9: My gracious liege, this too much lenity
10: And harmful pity must be laid aside.
11: To whom do lions cast their gentle looks?
12: Not to the beast that would usurp their den.
13: Whose hand is that the forest bear doth lick?
14: Not his that spoils her young before her face.
15: Who scapes the lurking serpent’s mortal sting?
16: Not he that sets his foot upon her back.
17: The smallest worm will turn, being trodden on,
18: And doves will peck in safeguard of their brood.
19: Ambitious York did level at thy crown,
20: Thou smiling while he knit his angry brows.
21: He, but a duke, would have his son a king
22: And raise his issue like a loving sire;
23: Thou being a king, blest with a goodly son,
24: Didst yield consent to disinherit him,
25: Which argued thee a most unloving father.
27: And though man’s face be fearful to their eyes,
28: Yet in protection of their tender ones,
29: Who hath not seen them, even with those wings
30: Which sometime they have used with fearful flight,
31: Make war with him that climbed unto their nest,
32: Offering their own lives in their young’s defense?
33: For shame, my liege, make them your precedent.
34: Were it not pity that this goodly boy
35: Should lose his birthright by his father’s fault,
36: And long hereafter say unto his child
37: What my great-grandfather and grandsire got,
38: My careless father fondly gave away?
39: Ah, what a shame were this! Look on the boy,
40: And let his manly face, which promiseth
41: Successful fortune, steel thy melting heart
42: To hold thine own and leave thine own with him.
43: Full well hath Clifford played the orator,
45: But, Clifford, tell me, didst thou never hear
46: That things ill got had ever bad success?
47: And happy always was it for that son
48: Whose father for his hoarding went to hell?
49: I’ll leave my son my virtuous deeds behind,
50: And would my father had left me no more;
51: For all the rest is held at such a rate
52: As brings a thousandfold more care to keep
53: Than in possession any jot of pleasure.
54: Ah, cousin York, would thy best friends did know
55: How it doth grieve me that thy head is here.
56: My lord, cheer up your spirits; our foes are nigh,
57: And this soft courage makes your followers faint.
58: You promised knighthood to our forward son.
59: Unsheathe your sword and dub him presently.—
62: And learn this lesson: draw thy sword in right.
63: My gracious father, by your kingly leave,
64: I’ll draw it as apparent to the crown
65: And in that quarrel use it to the death.
66: Why, that is spoken like a toward prince.
68: For with a band of thirty thousand men
69: Comes Warwick backing of the Duke of York,
70: And in the towns as they do march along
71: Proclaims him king, and many fly to him.
72: Deraign your battle, for they are at hand.
73: I would your Highness would depart the field.
74: The Queen hath best success when you are absent.
75: Ay, good my lord, and leave us to our fortune.
76: Why, that’s my fortune too; therefore I’ll stay.
77: Be it with resolution, then, to fight.
78: My royal father, cheer these noble lords
79: And hearten those that fight in your defense.
80: Unsheathe your sword, good father; cry Saint George!
82: Now, perjured Henry, wilt thou kneel for grace
83: And set thy diadem upon my head,
84: Or bide the mortal fortune of the field?
85: Go rate thy minions, proud insulting boy.
86: Becomes it thee to be thus bold in terms
87: Before thy sovereign and thy lawful king?
88: I am his king, and he should bow his knee.
89: I was adopted heir by his consent.
90: Since when, his oath is broke; for, as I hear,
91: You that are king, though he do wear the crown,
92: Have caused him, by new act of Parliament,
93: To blot out me and put his own son in.
95: Who should succeed the father but the son?
96: Are you there, butcher? O, I cannot speak!
97: Ay, crookback, here I stand to answer thee,
98: Or any he, the proudest of thy sort.
99: ’Twas you that killed young Rutland, was it not?
100: Ay, and old York, and yet not satisfied.
101: For God’s sake, lords, give signal to the fight!
102: What sayst thou, Henry? Wilt thou yield the crown?
103: Why, how now, long-tongued Warwick, dare you speak?
105: When you and I met at Saint Albans last,
106: Your legs did better service than your hands.
107: Then ’twas my turn to fly, and now ’tis thine.
108: You said so much before, and yet you fled.
109: ’Twas not your valor, Clifford, drove me thence.
110: No, nor your manhood that durst make you stay.
112: Break off the parley, for scarce I can refrain
113: The execution of my big-swoll’n heart
114: Upon that Clifford, that cruel child-killer.
115: I slew thy father; call’st thou him a child?
116: Ay, like a dastard and a treacherous coward,
117: As thou didst kill our tender brother Rutland.
118: But ere sunset I’ll make thee curse the deed.
119: Have done with words, my lords, and hear me speak.
121: Defy them, then, or else hold close thy lips.
122: I prithee, give no limits to my tongue.
123: I am a king and privileged to speak.
124: My liege, the wound that bred this meeting here
125: Cannot be cured by words; therefore, be still.
127: By Him that made us all, I am resolved
128: That Clifford’s manhood lies upon his tongue.
129: Say, Henry, shall I have my right or no?
130: A thousand men have broke their fasts today
131: That ne’er shall dine unless thou yield the crown.
132: If thou deny, their blood upon thy head,
133: For York in justice puts his armor on.
134: If that be right which Warwick says is right,
135: There is no wrong, but everything is right.
136: Whoever got thee, there thy mother stands,
137: For well I wot thou hast thy mother’s tongue.
138: But thou art neither like thy sire nor dam,
139: But like a foul misshapen stigmatic,
140: Marked by the Destinies to be avoided,
141: As venom toads or lizards’ dreadful stings.
142: Iron of Naples, hid with English gilt,
143: Whose father bears the title of a king,
144: As if a channel should be called the sea,
145: Sham’st thou not, knowing whence thou art extraught,
147: To let thy tongue detect thy baseborn heart?
148: A wisp of straw were worth a thousand crowns
149: To make this shameless callet know herself.—
150: Helen of Greece was fairer far than thou,
151: Although thy husband may be Menelaus;
152: And ne’er was Agamemnon’s brother wronged
153: By that false woman as this king by thee.
154: His father reveled in the heart of France,
155: And tamed the King, and made the Dauphin stoop;
156: And had he matched according to his state,
157: He might have kept that glory to this day.
158: But when he took a beggar to his bed
159: And graced thy poor sire with his bridal day,
160: Even then that sunshine brewed a shower for him
161: That washed his father’s fortunes forth of France
162: And heaped sedition on his crown at home.
163: For what hath broached this tumult but thy pride?
164: Hadst thou been meek, our title still had slept,
165: And we, in pity of the gentle king,
166: Had slipped our claim until another age.
167: But when we saw our sunshine made thy spring,
168: And that thy summer bred us no increase,
169: We set the axe to thy usurping root;
170: And though the edge hath something hit ourselves,
171: Yet know thou, since we have begun to strike,
172: We’ll never leave till we have hewn thee down
173: Or bathed thy growing with our heated bloods.
174: And in this resolution, I defy thee,
176: Since thou denied’st the gentle king to speak.—
177: Sound, trumpets! Let our bloody colors wave;
178: And either victory or else a grave!
180: No, wrangling woman, we’ll no longer stay.
181: These words will cost ten thousand lives this day.

1: Forspent with toil, as runners with a race,
2: I lay me down a little while to breathe,
3: For strokes received and many blows repaid
4: Have robbed my strong-knit sinews of their strength;
5: And spite of spite, needs must I rest awhile.
6: Smile, gentle heaven, or strike, ungentle death,
7: For this world frowns and Edward’s sun is clouded.
8: How now, my lord, what hap? What hope of good?
9: Our hap is loss, our hope but sad despair;
10: Our ranks are broke, and ruin follows us.
11: What counsel give you? Whither shall we fly?
12: Bootless is flight; they follow us with wings,
13: And weak we are and cannot shun pursuit.
14: Ah, Warwick, why hast thou withdrawn thyself?
15: Thy brother’s blood the thirsty earth hath drunk,
16: Broached with the steely point of Clifford’s lance,
17: And in the very pangs of death he cried,
18: Like to a dismal clangor heard from far,
19: Warwick, revenge! Brother, revenge my death!
20: So, underneath the belly of their steeds,
21: That stained their fetlocks in his smoking blood,
22: The noble gentleman gave up the ghost.
23: Then let the earth be drunken with our blood!
24: I’ll kill my horse because I will not fly.
25: Why stand we like soft-hearted women here,
26: Wailing our losses whiles the foe doth rage,
27: And look upon, as if the tragedy
28: Were played in jest by counterfeiting actors?
29: Here on my knee I vow to God above
30: I’ll never pause again, never stand still,
31: Till either death hath closed these eyes of mine
32: Or Fortune given me measure of revenge.
33: O Warwick, I do bend my knee with thine,
34: And in this vow do chain my soul to thine
35: And, ere my knee rise from the Earth’s cold face,
36: I throw my hands, mine eyes, my heart to Thee,
37: Thou setter up and plucker down of kings,
38: Beseeching Thee, if with Thy will it stands
39: That to my foes this body must be prey,
40: Yet that Thy brazen gates of heaven may ope
41: And give sweet passage to my sinful soul.
42: Now, lords, take leave until we meet again,
43: Where’er it be, in heaven or in Earth.
44: Brother, give me thy hand.—And, gentle Warwick,
45: Let me embrace thee in my weary arms.
46: I that did never weep now melt with woe
47: That winter should cut off our springtime so.
48: Away, away! Once more, sweet lords, farewell.
49: Yet let us all together to our troops
50: And give them leave to fly that will not stay,
51: And call them pillars that will stand to us;
52: And, if we thrive, promise them such rewards
53: As victors wear at the Olympian Games.
54: This may plant courage in their quailing breasts,
55: For yet is hope of life and victory.
56: Forslow no longer; make we hence amain.

1: Now, Clifford, I have singled thee alone.
2: Suppose this arm is for the Duke of York,
3: And this for Rutland, both bound to revenge,
4: Wert thou environed with a brazen wall.
5: Now, Richard, I am with thee here alone.
6: This is the hand that stabbed thy father York,
7: And this the hand that slew thy brother Rutland,
8: And here’s the heart that triumphs in their death
9: And cheers these hands that slew thy sire and brother
10: To execute the like upon thyself.
12: Nay, Warwick, single out some other chase,
13: For I myself will hunt this wolf to death.

1: This battle fares like to the morning’s war,
2: When dying clouds contend with growing light,
3: What time the shepherd, blowing of his nails,
4: Can neither call it perfect day nor night.
5: Now sways it this way, like a mighty sea
6: Forced by the tide to combat with the wind;
7: Now sways it that way, like the selfsame sea
8: Forced to retire by fury of the wind.
9: Sometime the flood prevails, and then the wind;
10: Now one the better, then another best,
11: Both tugging to be victors, breast to breast,
13: So is the equal poise of this fell war.
14: Here on this molehill will I sit me down.
15: To whom God will, there be the victory;
16: For Margaret my queen and Clifford too
17: Have chid me from the battle, swearing both
18: They prosper best of all when I am thence.
19: Would I were dead, if God’s good will were so,
20: For what is in this world but grief and woe?
21: O God! Methinks it were a happy life
22: To be no better than a homely swain,
23: To sit upon a hill as I do now,
24: To carve out dials quaintly, point by point,
25: Thereby to see the minutes how they run:
26: How many makes the hour full complete,
27: How many hours brings about the day,
28: How many days will finish up the year,
29: How many years a mortal man may live.
30: When this is known, then to divide the times:
31: So many hours must I tend my flock,
32: So many hours must I take my rest,
33: So many hours must I contemplate,
34: So many hours must I sport myself,
35: So many days my ewes have been with young,
36: So many weeks ere the poor fools will ean,
37: So many years ere I shall shear the fleece;
38: So minutes, hours, days, months, and years,
39: Passed over to the end they were created,
40: Would bring white hairs unto a quiet grave.
41: Ah, what a life were this! How sweet, how lovely!
42: Gives not the hawthorn bush a sweeter shade
43: To shepherds looking on their silly sheep
44: Than doth a rich embroidered canopy
45: To kings that fear their subjects’ treachery?
46: O yes, it doth, a thousandfold it doth.
47: And to conclude, the shepherd’s homely curds,
48: His cold thin drink out of his leather bottle,
49: His wonted sleep under a fresh tree’s shade,
50: All which secure and sweetly he enjoys,
51: Is far beyond a prince’s delicates—
52: His viands sparkling in a golden cup,
53: His body couchèd in a curious bed—
54: When care, mistrust, and treason waits on him.
55: Ill blows the wind that profits nobody.
56: This man, whom hand to hand I slew in fight,
57: May be possessèd with some store of crowns,
58: And I, that haply take them from him now,
59: May yet ere night yield both my life and them
60: To some man else, as this dead man doth me.
61: Who’s this? O God! It is my father’s face,
62: Whom in this conflict I unwares have killed.
63: O heavy times, begetting such events!
64: From London by the King was I pressed forth.
65: My father, being the Earl of Warwick’s man,
66: Came on the part of York, pressed by his master.
67: And I, who at his hands received my life,
68: Have by my hands of life bereavèd him.
69: Pardon me, God, I knew not what I did;
70: And pardon, father, for I knew not thee.
71: My tears shall wipe away these bloody marks,
72: And no more words till they have flowed their fill.
73: O piteous spectacle! O bloody times!
74: Whiles lions war and battle for their dens,
75: Poor harmless lambs abide their enmity.
76: Weep, wretched man. I’ll aid thee tear for tear,
77: And let our hearts and eyes, like civil war,
78: Be blind with tears and break, o’ercharged with grief.
79: Thou that so stoutly hath resisted me,
80: Give me thy gold, if thou hast any gold,
81: For I have bought it with an hundred blows.
82: But let me see: is this our foeman’s face?
83: Ah, no, no, no, it is mine only son!
84: Ah, boy, if any life be left in thee,
85: Throw up thine eye! See, see, what showers arise,
86: Blown with the windy tempest of my heart
87: Upon thy wounds, that kills mine eye and heart!
88: O, pity God this miserable age!
89: What stratagems, how fell, how butcherly,
91: This deadly quarrel daily doth beget!
92: O, boy, thy father gave thee life too soon,
93: And hath bereft thee of thy life too late!
94: Woe above woe, grief more than common grief!
95: O, that my death would stay these ruthful deeds!
96: O pity, pity, gentle heaven, pity!
97: The red rose and the white are on his face,
98: The fatal colors of our striving houses;
99: The one his purple blood right well resembles,
100: The other his pale cheeks methinks presenteth.
101: Wither one rose and let the other flourish;
102: If you contend, a thousand lives must wither.
103: How will my mother for a father’s death
104: Take on with me and ne’er be satisfied!
105: How will my wife for slaughter of my son
106: Shed seas of tears and ne’er be satisfied!
107: How will the country for these woeful chances
108: Misthink the King and not be satisfied!
109: Was ever son so rued a father’s death?
110: Was ever father so bemoaned his son?
111: Was ever king so grieved for subjects’ woe?
112: Much is your sorrow, mine ten times so much.
113: I’ll bear thee hence, where I may weep my fill.
114: These arms of mine shall be thy winding-sheet;
115: My heart, sweet boy, shall be thy sepulcher,
116: For from my heart thine image ne’er shall go.
117: My sighing breast shall be thy funeral bell;
118: And so obsequious will thy father be
119: E’en for the loss of thee, having no more,
120: As Priam was for all his valiant sons.
121: I’ll bear thee hence, and let them fight that will,
122: For I have murdered where I should not kill.
123: Sad-hearted men, much overgone with care,
124: Here sits a king more woeful than you are.
125: Fly, father, fly, for all your friends are fled,
126: And Warwick rages like a chafèd bull.
127: Away, for Death doth hold us in pursuit.
128: Mount you, my lord; towards Berwick post amain.
129: Edward and Richard, like a brace of greyhounds
130: Having the fearful flying hare in sight,
131: With fiery eyes sparkling for very wrath
132: And bloody steel grasped in their ireful hands,
133: Are at our backs, and therefore hence amain.
134: Away, for Vengeance comes along with them.
135: Nay, stay not to expostulate, make speed;
136: Or else come after; I’ll away before.
137: Nay, take me with thee, good sweet Exeter;
138: Not that I fear to stay, but love to go
139: Whither the Queen intends. Forward, away!

1: Here burns my candle out; ay, here it dies,
2: Which whiles it lasted gave King Henry light.
3: O Lancaster, I fear thy overthrow
4: More than my body’s parting with my soul!
5: My love and fear glued many friends to thee;
6: And now I fall, thy tough commixtures melts,
8: And whither fly the gnats but to the sun?
9: And who shines now but Henry’s enemies?
10: O Phoebus, hadst thou never given consent
11: That Phaëton should check thy fiery steeds,
12: Thy burning car never had scorched the Earth!
13: And Henry, hadst thou swayed as kings should do,
14: Or as thy father and his father did,
15: Giving no ground unto the house of York,
16: They never then had sprung like summer flies;
17: I and ten thousand in this luckless realm
18: Had left no mourning widows for our death,
19: And thou this day hadst kept thy chair in peace.
20: For what doth cherish weeds but gentle air?
21: And what makes robbers bold but too much lenity?
22: Bootless are plaints, and cureless are my wounds;
23: No way to fly, no strength to hold out flight.
24: The foe is merciless and will not pity,
25: For at their hands I have deserved no pity.
26: The air hath got into my deadly wounds,
27: And much effuse of blood doth make me faint.
28: Come, York and Richard, Warwick and the rest.
29: I stabbed your fathers’ bosoms; split my breast.
30: Now breathe we, lords. Good fortune bids us pause
31: And smooth the frowns of war with peaceful looks.
32: Some troops pursue the bloody-minded queen
33: That led calm Henry, though he were a king,
34: As doth a sail filled with a fretting gust
35: Command an argosy to stem the waves.
36: But think you, lords, that Clifford fled with them?
38: For, though before his face I speak the words,
39: Your brother Richard marked him for the grave,
40: And wheresoe’er he is, he’s surely dead.
41: Whose soul is that which takes her heavy leave?
42: A deadly groan, like life and death’s departing.
43: See who it is; and, now the battle’s ended,
44: If friend or foe, let him be gently used.
45: Revoke that doom of mercy, for ’tis Clifford,
46: Who not contented that he lopped the branch
47: In hewing Rutland when his leaves put forth,
48: But set his murd’ring knife unto the root
49: From whence that tender spray did sweetly spring,
50: I mean our princely father, Duke of York.
51: From off the gates of York fetch down the head,
52: Your father’s head, which Clifford placèd there;
53: Instead whereof let this supply the room.
54: Measure for measure must be answerèd.
55: Bring forth that fatal screech owl to our house
56: That nothing sung but death to us and ours;
57: Now death shall stop his dismal threat’ning sound,
58: And his ill-boding tongue no more shall speak.
59: I think his understanding is bereft.—
60: Speak, Clifford, dost thou know who speaks to thee?—
62: Dark cloudy death o’ershades his beams of life,
63: And he nor sees nor hears us what we say.
64: O, would he did—and so, perhaps, he doth!
66: Because he would avoid such bitter taunts
67: Which in the time of death he gave our father.
68: If so thou think’st, vex him with eager words.
69: Clifford, ask mercy and obtain no grace.
71: Clifford, devise excuses for thy faults.
72: While we devise fell tortures for thy faults.
73: Thou didst love York, and I am son to York.
74: Thou pitied’st Rutland; I will pity thee.
75: Where’s Captain Margaret to fence you now?
76: They mock thee, Clifford; swear as thou wast wont.
77: What, not an oath? Nay, then, the world goes hard
78: When Clifford cannot spare his friends an oath.
79: I know by that he’s dead; and, by my soul,
80: If this right hand would buy but two hours’ life
81: That I in all despite might rail at him,
82: This hand should chop it off, and with the issuing blood
84: Stifle the villain whose unstaunchèd thirst
85: York and young Rutland could not satisfy.
86: Ay, but he’s dead. Off with the traitor’s head,
87: And rear it in the place your father’s stands.
88: And now to London with triumphant march,
89: There to be crownèd England’s royal king,
90: From whence shall Warwick cut the sea to France
91: And ask the Lady Bona for thy queen;
92: So shalt thou sinew both these lands together,
93: And having France thy friend, thou shalt not dread
94: The scattered foe that hopes to rise again;
95: For though they cannot greatly sting to hurt,
96: Yet look to have them buzz to offend thine ears.
97: First will I see the coronation,
98: And then to Brittany I’ll cross the sea
99: To effect this marriage, so it please my lord.
100: Even as thou wilt, sweet Warwick, let it be;
101: For in thy shoulder do I build my seat,
102: And never will I undertake the thing
103: Wherein thy counsel and consent is wanting.—
104: Richard, I will create thee Duke of Gloucester,
105: And George, of Clarence. Warwick as ourself
106: Shall do and undo as him pleaseth best.
107: Let me be Duke of Clarence, George of Gloucester,
108: For Gloucester’s dukedom is too ominous.
110: Richard, be Duke of Gloucester. Now to London,
111: To see these honors in possession.

1: Under this thick-grown brake we’ll shroud ourselves,
2: For through this laund anon the deer will come;
3: And in this covert will we make our stand,
4: Culling the principal of all the deer.
5: I’ll stay above the hill, so both may shoot.
6: That cannot be. The noise of thy crossbow
7: Will scare the herd, and so my shoot is lost.
8: Here stand we both, and aim we at the best.
9: And for the time shall not seem tedious,
10: I’ll tell thee what befell me on a day
11: In this self place where now we mean to stand.
12: Here comes a man; let’s stay till he be past.
13: From Scotland am I stol’n, even of pure love,
14: To greet mine own land with my wishful sight.
15: No, Harry, Harry, ’tis no land of thine!
16: Thy place is filled, thy scepter wrung from thee,
17: Thy balm washed off wherewith thou wast anointed.
18: No bending knee will call thee Caesar now,
19: No humble suitors press to speak for right,
20: No, not a man comes for redress of thee;
21: For how can I help them an not myself?
22: Ay, here’s a deer whose skin’s a keeper’s fee.
23: This is the quondam king. Let’s seize upon him.
24: Let me embrace the sour adversaries,
25: For wise men say it is the wisest course.
26: Why linger we? Let us lay hands upon him.
27: Forbear awhile; we’ll hear a little more.
28: My queen and son are gone to France for aid,
29: And, as I hear, the great commanding Warwick
30: Is thither gone to crave the French king’s sister
31: To wife for Edward. If this news be true,
32: Poor queen and son, your labor is but lost,
33: For Warwick is a subtle orator,
34: And Lewis a prince soon won with moving words.
35: By this account, then, Margaret may win him,
36: For she’s a woman to be pitied much.
37: Her sighs will make a batt’ry in his breast,
38: Her tears will pierce into a marble heart.
39: The tiger will be mild whiles she doth mourn,
40: And Nero will be tainted with remorse
41: To hear and see her plaints, her brinish tears.
42: Ay, but she’s come to beg, Warwick to give;
43: She on his left side craving aid for Henry;
44: He on his right asking a wife for Edward.
45: She weeps and says her Henry is deposed;
46: He smiles and says his Edward is installed;
47: That she, poor wretch, for grief can speak no more,
48: Whiles Warwick tells his title, smooths the wrong,
50: And in conclusion wins the King from her
51: With promise of his sister and what else
52: To strengthen and support King Edward’s place.
53: O Margaret, thus ’twill be, and thou, poor soul,
54: Art then forsaken, as thou went’st forlorn.
55: Say, what art thou that talk’st of kings and queens?
56: More than I seem, and less than I was born to:
57: A man at least, for less I should not be;
58: And men may talk of kings, and why not I?
59: Ay, but thou talk’st as if thou wert a king.
60: Why, so I am in mind, and that’s enough.
61: But if thou be a king, where is thy crown?
62: My crown is in my heart, not on my head;
63: Not decked with diamonds and Indian stones,
64: Nor to be seen. My crown is called content;
65: A crown it is that seldom kings enjoy.
66: Well, if you be a king crowned with content,
67: Your crown content and you must be contented
68: To go along with us. For, as we think,
69: You are the king King Edward hath deposed;
70: And we his subjects sworn in all allegiance
71: Will apprehend you as his enemy.
72: But did you never swear and break an oath?
73: No, never such an oath, nor will not now.
74: Where did you dwell when I was King of England?
75: Here in this country, where we now remain.
76: I was anointed king at nine months old.
77: My father and my grandfather were kings,
78: And you were sworn true subjects unto me.
79: And tell me, then, have you not broke your oaths?
80: No, for we were subjects but while you were king.
81: Why, am I dead? Do I not breathe a man?
82: Ah, simple men, you know not what you swear.
83: Look as I blow this feather from my face
84: And as the air blows it to me again,
85: Obeying with my wind when I do blow
86: And yielding to another when it blows,
87: Commanded always by the greater gust,
88: Such is the lightness of you common men.
89: But do not break your oaths, for of that sin
90: My mild entreaty shall not make you guilty.
91: Go where you will, the King shall be commanded,
92: And be you kings: command, and I’ll obey.
93: We are true subjects to the King, King Edward.
94: So would you be again to Henry
95: If he were seated as King Edward is.
96: We charge you in God’s name and the King’s
97: To go with us unto the officers.
98: In God’s name, lead. Your king’s name be obeyed,
99: And what God will, that let your king perform.
100: And what he will, I humbly yield unto.

1: Brother of Gloucester, at Saint Albans field

13: Before the King will grant her humble suit.
14: He knows the game; how true he keeps the wind!
16: Widow, we will consider of your suit,
17: And come some other time to know our mind.
18: Right gracious lord, I cannot brook delay.
19: May it please your Highness to resolve me now,
20: And what your pleasure is shall satisfy me.

45: What you command that rests in me to do.

48: Ay, but thou canst do what I mean to ask.
49: Why, then, I will do what your Grace commands.
50: He plies her hard, and much rain wears the marble.
51: As red as fire! Nay, then, her wax must melt.

53: An easy task; ’tis but to love a king.
54: That’s soon performed because I am a subject.
55: Why, then, thy husband’s lands I freely give thee.

57: The match is made; she seals it with a cursy.
