59: The fruits of love I mean, my loving liege.
60: Ay, but, I fear me, in another sense.
61: What love, think’st thou, I sue so much to get?
62: My love till death, my humble thanks, my prayers,
63: That love which virtue begs and virtue grants.
64: No, by my troth, I did not mean such love.
65: Why, then, you mean not as I thought you did.

71: Why, then, thou shalt not have thy husband’s lands.

82: The widow likes him not; she knits her brows.
83: He is the bluntest wooer in Christendom.
84: Her looks doth argue her replete with modesty;
85: Her words doth show her wit incomparable;
87: One way or other, she is for a king,

91: I am a subject fit to jest withal,
92: But far unfit to be a sovereign.

95: And that is, to enjoy thee for my love.
96: And that is more than I will yield unto.

99: You cavil, widow; I did mean my queen.
100: ’Twill grieve your Grace my sons should call you father.
102: No more than when my daughters call thee mother.
103: Thou art a widow and thou hast some children,

115: That would be ten days’ wonder at the least.
116: That’s a day longer than a wonder lasts.
117: By so much is the wonder in extremes.
118: Well, jest on, brothers. I can tell you both

120: My gracious lord, Henry, your foe, is taken
121: And brought your prisoner to your palace gate.
122: See that he be conveyed unto the Tower.
123: And go we, brothers, to the man that took him,
125: Widow, go you along.—Lords, use her honorably.
126: Ay, Edward will use women honorably!
127: Would he were wasted—marrow, bones, and all—
128: That from his loins no hopeful branch may spring
129: To cross me from the golden time I look for.
130: And yet, between my soul’s desire and me,
132: Is Clarence, Henry, and his son, young Edward,
133: And all the unlooked-for issue of their bodies
134: To take their rooms ere I can place myself.
135: A cold premeditation for my purpose.
136: Why, then, I do but dream on sovereignty
137: Like one that stands upon a promontory
138: And spies a far-off shore where he would tread,
139: Wishing his foot were equal with his eye,
140: And chides the sea that sunders him from thence,
141: Saying he’ll lade it dry to have his way.
142: So do I wish the crown, being so far off,
143: And so I chide the means that keeps me from it,
144: And so, I say, I’ll cut the causes off,
146: My eye’s too quick, my heart o’erweens too much,
147: Unless my hand and strength could equal them.
148: Well, say there is no kingdom then for Richard,
149: What other pleasure can the world afford?
150: I’ll make my heaven in a lady’s lap
151: And deck my body in gay ornaments,
152: And ’witch sweet ladies with my words and looks.
153: O miserable thought, and more unlikely
154: Than to accomplish twenty golden crowns!
155: Why, Love forswore me in my mother’s womb,
156: And, for I should not deal in her soft laws,
157: She did corrupt frail Nature with some bribe
158: To shrink mine arm up like a withered shrub;
159: To make an envious mountain on my back,
160: Where sits Deformity to mock my body;
161: To shape my legs of an unequal size;
162: To disproportion me in every part,
163: Like to a chaos, or an unlicked bear-whelp,
164: That carries no impression like the dam.
165: And am I then a man to be beloved?
166: O monstrous fault to harbor such a thought!
167: Then, since this Earth affords no joy to me
168: But to command, to check, to o’erbear such
169: As are of better person than myself,
170: I’ll make my heaven to dream upon the crown,
171: And, whiles I live, t’ account this world but hell
172: Until my misshaped trunk that bears this head
173: Be round impalèd with a glorious crown.
174: And yet I know not how to get the crown,
175: For many lives stand between me and home;
176: And I, like one lost in a thorny wood,
177: That rents the thorns and is rent with the thorns,
178: Seeking a way and straying from the way,
179: Not knowing how to find the open air,
180: But toiling desperately to find it out,
181: Torment myself to catch the English crown.
182: And from that torment I will free myself
183: Or hew my way out with a bloody axe.
184: Why, I can smile, and murder whiles I smile,
185: And cry Content to that which grieves my heart,
186: And wet my cheeks with artificial tears,
187: And frame my face to all occasions.
188: I’ll drown more sailors than the mermaid shall;
189: I’ll slay more gazers than the basilisk;
190: I’ll play the orator as well as Nestor,
191: Deceive more slyly than Ulysses could,
192: And, like a Sinon, take another Troy.
193: I can add colors to the chameleon,
194: Change shapes with Proteus for advantages,
195: And set the murderous Machiavel to school.
196: Can I do this and cannot get a crown?
197: Tut, were it farther off, I’ll pluck it down.

1: Fair Queen of England, worthy Margaret,
2: Sit down with us. It ill befits thy state
3: And birth that thou shouldst stand while Lewis doth sit.
5: No, mighty King of France. Now Margaret
6: Must strike her sail and learn awhile to serve
7: Where kings command. I was, I must confess,
8: Great Albion’s queen in former golden days,
9: But now mischance hath trod my title down
10: And with dishonor laid me on the ground,
11: Where I must take like seat unto my fortune
12: And to my humble seat conform myself.
13: Why, say, fair queen, whence springs this deep despair?
15: From such a cause as fills mine eyes with tears
16: And stops my tongue, while heart is drowned in cares.
17: Whate’er it be, be thou still like thyself,
18: And sit thee by our side.
20: To Fortune’s yoke, but let thy dauntless mind
21: Still ride in triumph over all mischance.
22: Be plain, Queen Margaret, and tell thy grief.
23: It shall be eased if France can yield relief.
24: Those gracious words revive my drooping thoughts
25: And give my tongue-tied sorrows leave to speak.
26: Now therefore be it known to noble Lewis
27: That Henry, sole possessor of my love,
28: Is, of a king, become a banished man
29: And forced to live in Scotland a forlorn;
30: While proud ambitious Edward, Duke of York,
31: Usurps the regal title and the seat
33: This is the cause that I, poor Margaret,
34: With this my son, Prince Edward, Henry’s heir,
35: Am come to crave thy just and lawful aid;
36: And if thou fail us, all our hope is done.
37: Scotland hath will to help but cannot help;
38: Our people and our peers are both misled,
39: Our treasure seized, our soldiers put to flight,
40: And, as thou seest, ourselves in heavy plight.
41: Renownèd queen, with patience calm the storm
42: While we bethink a means to break it off.
43: The more we stay, the stronger grows our foe.
44: The more I stay, the more I’ll succor thee.
45: O, but impatience waiteth on true sorrow.
46: And see where comes the breeder of my sorrow.
47: What’s he approacheth boldly to our presence?
48: Our Earl of Warwick, Edward’s greatest friend.
49: Welcome, brave Warwick. What brings thee to France?
50: Ay, now begins a second storm to rise,
51: For this is he that moves both wind and tide.
52: From worthy Edward, King of Albion,
53: My lord and sovereign and thy vowèd friend,
54: I come in kindness and unfeignèd love,
55: First, to do greetings to thy royal person,
56: And then to crave a league of amity,
57: And, lastly, to confirm that amity
58: With nuptial knot, if thou vouchsafe to grant
59: That virtuous Lady Bona, thy fair sister,
60: To England’s king in lawful marriage.
61: If that go forward, Henry’s hope is done.
62: And, gracious madam, in our king’s behalf,
63: I am commanded, with your leave and favor,
64: Humbly to kiss your hand, and with my tongue
65: To tell the passion of my sovereign’s heart,
66: Where fame, late ent’ring at his heedful ears,
67: Hath placed thy beauty’s image and thy virtue.
68: King Lewis and Lady Bona, hear me speak
69: Before you answer Warwick. His demand
70: Springs not from Edward’s well-meant honest love,
71: But from deceit, bred by necessity;
72: For how can tyrants safely govern home
73: Unless abroad they purchase great alliance?
74: To prove him tyrant, this reason may suffice:
75: That Henry liveth still; but were he dead,
76: Yet here Prince Edward stands, King Henry’s son.
77: Look, therefore, Lewis, that by this league and marriage
79: Thou draw not on thy danger and dishonor;
80: For though usurpers sway the rule awhile,
81: Yet heav’ns are just, and time suppresseth wrongs.
84: Because thy father Henry did usurp,
85: And thou no more art prince than she is queen.
86: Then Warwick disannuls great John of Gaunt,
87: Which did subdue the greatest part of Spain;
88: And after John of Gaunt, Henry the Fourth,
89: Whose wisdom was a mirror to the wisest;
90: And after that wise prince, Henry the Fifth,
91: Who by his prowess conquerèd all France.
92: From these our Henry lineally descends.
93: Oxford, how haps it in this smooth discourse
94: You told not how Henry the Sixth hath lost
95: All that which Henry the Fifth had gotten.
96: Methinks these peers of France should smile at that.
97: But, for the rest: you tell a pedigree
98: Of threescore and two years, a silly time
99: To make prescription for a kingdom’s worth.
100: Why, Warwick, canst thou speak against thy liege,
101: Whom thou obeyed’st thirty and six years,
102: And not bewray thy treason with a blush?
103: Can Oxford, that did ever fence the right,
104: Now buckler falsehood with a pedigree?
105: For shame, leave Henry, and call Edward king.
106: Call him my king, by whose injurious doom
107: My elder brother, the Lord Aubrey Vere,
108: Was done to death? And more than so, my father,
109: Even in the downfall of his mellowed years,
110: When nature brought him to the door of death?
111: No, Warwick, no. While life upholds this arm,
112: This arm upholds the house of Lancaster.
113: And I the house of York.
114: Queen Margaret, Prince Edward, and Oxford,
115: Vouchsafe, at our request, to stand aside
116: While I use further conference with Warwick.
117: Heavens grant that Warwick’s words bewitch him not.
119: Now, Warwick, tell me, even upon thy conscience,
120: Is Edward your true king? For I were loath
121: To link with him that were not lawful chosen.
122: Thereon I pawn my credit and mine honor.
123: But is he gracious in the people’s eye?
124: The more that Henry was unfortunate.
125: Then further, all dissembling set aside,
126: Tell me for truth the measure of his love
129: As may beseem a monarch like himself.
130: Myself have often heard him say and swear
131: That this his love was an eternal plant,
132: Whereof the root was fixed in virtue’s ground,
133: The leaves and fruit maintained with beauty’s sun,
134: Exempt from envy but not from disdain,

136: Now, sister, let us hear your firm resolve.
137: Your grant or your denial shall be mine.
138: Yet I confess that often ere this day,
140: When I have heard your king’s desert recounted,
141: Mine ear hath tempted judgment to desire.

143: And now forthwith shall articles be drawn
144: Touching the jointure that your king must make,
145: Which with her dowry shall be counterpoised.—
146: Draw near, Queen Margaret, and be a witness
147: That Bona shall be wife to the English king.
148: To Edward, but not to the English king.
149: Deceitful Warwick, it was thy device
150: By this alliance to make void my suit.
151: Before thy coming, Lewis was Henry’s friend.
152: And still is friend to him and Margaret.

154: As may appear by Edward’s good success,

156: From giving aid which late I promisèd.

162: You have a father able to maintain you,
163: And better ’twere you troubled him than France.
165: Proud setter-up and puller-down of kings!

168: Thy sly conveyance and thy lord’s false love,
169: For both of you are birds of selfsame feather.
170: Warwick, this is some post to us or thee.
171: My lord ambassador, these letters are for you,
172: Sent from your brother, Marquess Montague.
173: These from our king unto your Majesty.
174: And, madam, these for you—from whom, I know not.
176: I like it well that our fair queen and mistress
177: Smiles at her news, while Warwick frowns at his.
178: Nay, mark how Lewis stamps as he were nettled.
179: I hope all’s for the best.
180: Warwick, what are thy news? And yours, fair queen?
181: Mine, such as fill my heart with unhoped joys.
182: Mine, full of sorrow and heart’s discontent.
183: What, has your king married the Lady Grey,
184: And now, to soothe your forgery and his,
185: Sends me a paper to persuade me patience?
186: Is this th’ alliance that he seeks with France?
187: Dare he presume to scorn us in this manner?
188: I told your Majesty as much before.
189: This proveth Edward’s love and Warwick’s honesty.
190: King Lewis, I here protest in sight of heaven
191: And by the hope I have of heavenly bliss,
192: That I am clear from this misdeed of Edward’s—
193: No more my king, for he dishonors me,
194: But most himself, if he could see his shame.
195: Did I forget that by the house of York
196: My father came untimely to his death?
197: Did I let pass th’ abuse done to my niece?
198: Did I impale him with the regal crown?
199: Did I put Henry from his native right?
200: And am I guerdoned at the last with shame?
201: Shame on himself, for my desert is honor!
202: And to repair my honor lost for him,
203: I here renounce him and return to Henry.
204: My noble queen, let former grudges pass,
205: And henceforth I am thy true servitor.
206: I will revenge his wrong to Lady Bona
207: And replant Henry in his former state.
208: Warwick, these words have turned my hate to love,
209: And I forgive and quite forget old faults,
210: And joy that thou becom’st King Henry’s friend.
211: So much his friend, ay, his unfeignèd friend,
212: That if King Lewis vouchsafe to furnish us
213: With some few bands of chosen soldiers,
214: I’ll undertake to land them on our coast
215: And force the tyrant from his seat by war.
216: ’Tis not his new-made bride shall succor him.
217: And as for Clarence, as my letters tell me,
218: He’s very likely now to fall from him
219: For matching more for wanton lust than honor,
220: Or than for strength and safety of our country.
221: Dear brother, how shall Bona be revenged
222: But by thy help to this distressèd queen?
223: Renownèd prince, how shall poor Henry live
224: Unless thou rescue him from foul despair?
225: My quarrel and this English queen’s are one.
226: And mine, fair Lady Bona, joins with yours.
227: And mine with hers and thine and Margaret’s.
228: Therefore at last I firmly am resolved
230: Let me give humble thanks for all, at once.
231: Then, England’s messenger, return in post,
232: And tell false Edward, thy supposèd king,
233: That Lewis of France is sending over maskers
234: To revel it with him and his new bride.
235: Thou seest what’s passed; go fear thy king withal.
236: Tell him, in hope he’ll prove a widower shortly,
237: I wear the willow garland for his sake.
238: Tell him my mourning weeds are laid aside
239: And I am ready to put armor on.
240: Tell him from me that he hath done me wrong,
241: And therefore I’ll uncrown him ere ’t be long.
245: Thou and Oxford with five thousand men
246: Shall cross the seas and bid false Edward battle;
247: And as occasion serves, this noble queen
248: And prince shall follow with a fresh supply.
249: Yet ere thou go, but answer me one doubt:
250: What pledge have we of thy firm loyalty?
251: This shall assure my constant loyalty:
252: That if our queen and this young prince agree,
253: I’ll join mine eldest daughter, and my joy,
254: To him forthwith in holy wedlock bands.
255: Yes, I agree, and thank you for your motion.
256: Son Edward, she is fair and virtuous.
257: Therefore, delay not; give thy hand to Warwick,
258: And with thy hand, thy faith irrevocable,
259: That only Warwick’s daughter shall be thine.
260: Yes, I accept her, for she well deserves it,
261: And here, to pledge my vow, I give my hand.
262: Why stay we now? These soldiers shall be levied,
263: And thou, Lord Bourbon, our High Admiral,
264: Shall waft them over with our royal fleet.
265: I long till Edward fall by war’s mischance
266: For mocking marriage with a dame of France.
267: I came from Edward as ambassador,
268: But I return his sworn and mortal foe.
269: Matter of marriage was the charge he gave me,
270: But dreadful war shall answer his demand.
271: Had he none else to make a stale but me?
272: Then none but I shall turn his jest to sorrow.
273: I was the chief that raised him to the crown,
274: And I’ll be chief to bring him down again:
275: Not that I pity Henry’s misery,
276: But seek revenge on Edward’s mockery.

1: Now tell me, brother Clarence, what think you
2: Of this new marriage with the Lady Grey?
3: Hath not our brother made a worthy choice?
4: Alas, you know ’tis far from hence to France.
5: How could he stay till Warwick made return?
6: My lords, forbear this talk. Here comes the King.
8: I mind to tell him plainly what I think.
9: Now, brother of Clarence, how like you our choice,
10: That you stand pensive, as half malcontent?
11: As well as Lewis of France or the Earl of Warwick,
12: Which are so weak of courage and in judgment
13: That they’ll take no offense at our abuse.
14: Suppose they take offense without a cause,
15: They are but Lewis and Warwick; I am Edward,
16: Your king and Warwick’s, and must have my will.
17: And shall have your will because our king.
18: Yet hasty marriage seldom proveth well.
19: Yea, brother Richard, are you offended too?
21: No, God forbid that I should wish them severed
22: Whom God hath joined together. Ay, and ’twere pity
23: To sunder them that yoke so well together.
24: Setting your scorns and your mislike aside,
25: Tell me some reason why the Lady Grey
26: Should not become my wife and England’s queen?
27: And you too, Somerset and Montague,
29: Then this is mine opinion: that King Lewis
30: Becomes your enemy for mocking him
31: About the marriage of the Lady Bona.
32: And Warwick, doing what you gave in charge,
33: Is now dishonorèd by this new marriage.
34: What if both Lewis and Warwick be appeased
35: By such invention as I can devise?
36: Yet to have joined with France in such alliance
37: Would more have strengthened this our commonwealth
39: ’Gainst foreign storms than any home-bred marriage.
40: Why, knows not Montague that of itself
41: England is safe, if true within itself?
42: But the safer when ’tis backed with France.
43: ’Tis better using France than trusting France.
44: Let us be backed with God and with the seas
45: Which He hath giv’n for fence impregnable,
46: And with their helps only defend ourselves.
47: In them and in ourselves our safety lies.
48: For this one speech, Lord Hastings well deserves
49: To have the heir of the Lord Hungerford.
50: Ay, what of that? It was my will and grant,
51: And for this once my will shall stand for law.
52: And yet methinks your Grace hath not done well
53: To give the heir and daughter of Lord Scales
54: Unto the brother of your loving bride.
55: She better would have fitted me or Clarence;
56: But in your bride you bury brotherhood.
57: Or else you would not have bestowed the heir
58: Of the Lord Bonville on your new wife’s son,
59: And leave your brothers to go speed elsewhere.
60: Alas, poor Clarence, is it for a wife
61: That thou art malcontent? I will provide thee.
62: In choosing for yourself you showed your judgment,
63: Which, being shallow, you shall give me leave
64: To play the broker in mine own behalf.
65: And to that end, I shortly mind to leave you.
66: Leave me or tarry, Edward will be king
67: And not be tied unto his brother’s will.
68: My lords, before it pleased his Majesty
69: To raise my state to title of a queen,
70: Do me but right and you must all confess
71: That I was not ignoble of descent,
72: And meaner than myself have had like fortune.
73: But as this title honors me and mine,
74: So your dislikes, to whom I would be pleasing,
75: Doth cloud my joys with danger and with sorrow.
76: My love, forbear to fawn upon their frowns.
77: What danger or what sorrow can befall thee
78: So long as Edward is thy constant friend
79: And their true sovereign, whom they must obey?
80: Nay, whom they shall obey, and love thee too,
81: Unless they seek for hatred at my hands;
82: Which if they do, yet will I keep thee safe,
83: And they shall feel the vengeance of my wrath.
84: I hear, yet say not much, but think the more.
85: Now, messenger, what letters or what news from France?
87: My sovereign liege, no letters and few words
88: But such as I without your special pardon
90: Go to, we pardon thee. Therefore, in brief,
91: Tell me their words as near as thou canst guess them.
92: What answer makes King Lewis unto our letters?
93: At my depart, these were his very words:
94: Go tell false Edward, the supposèd king,
95: That Lewis of France is sending over maskers
96: To revel it with him and his new bride.
97: Is Lewis so brave? Belike he thinks me Henry.
98: But what said Lady Bona to my marriage?
99: These were her words, uttered with mild disdain:
100: Tell him, in hope he’ll prove a widower shortly,
101: I’ll wear the willow garland for his sake.
102: I blame not her; she could say little less;
103: She had the wrong. But what said Henry’s queen?
104: For I have heard that she was there in place.
105: Tell him, quoth she, my mourning weeds are done,
107: And I am ready to put armor on.
108: Belike she minds to play the Amazon.
109: But what said Warwick to these injuries?
110: He, more incensed against your Majesty
111: Than all the rest, discharged me with these words:
112: Tell him from me that he hath done me wrong,
113: And therefore I’ll uncrown him ere ’t be long.
114: Ha! Durst the traitor breathe out so proud words?
115: Well, I will arm me, being thus forewarned.
116: They shall have wars and pay for their presumption.
117: But say, is Warwick friends with Margaret?
118: Ay, gracious sovereign, they are so linked in friendship
120: That young Prince Edward marries Warwick’s daughter.
122: Belike the elder; Clarence will have the younger.—
123: Now, brother king, farewell, and sit you fast,
124: For I will hence to Warwick’s other daughter,
125: That, though I want a kingdom, yet in marriage
126: I may not prove inferior to yourself.
127: You that love me and Warwick, follow me.
128: Not I. My thoughts aim at a further matter:
129: I stay not for the love of Edward, but the crown.
130: Clarence and Somerset both gone to Warwick?
131: Yet am I armed against the worst can happen,
132: And haste is needful in this desp’rate case.
133: Pembroke and Stafford, you in our behalf
134: Go levy men and make prepare for war.
135: They are already, or quickly will be, landed.
136: Myself in person will straight follow you.
137: But ere I go, Hastings and Montague,
138: Resolve my doubt: you twain, of all the rest,
139: Are near to Warwick by blood and by alliance.
140: Tell me if you love Warwick more than me.
141: If it be so, then both depart to him.
142: I rather wish you foes than hollow friends.
143: But if you mind to hold your true obedience,
144: Give me assurance with some friendly vow,
145: That I may never have you in suspect.
146: So God help Montague as he proves true!
147: And Hastings as he favors Edward’s cause!
148: Now, brother Richard, will you stand by us?
149: Ay, in despite of all that shall withstand you.
150: Why, so. Then am I sure of victory.
151: Now therefore let us hence and lose no hour
152: Till we meet Warwick with his foreign power.

1: Trust me, my lord, all hitherto goes well.
2: The common people by numbers swarm to us.
3: But see where Somerset and Clarence comes.—
4: Speak suddenly, my lords: are we all friends?
6: Then, gentle Clarence, welcome unto Warwick,
7: And welcome, Somerset. I hold it cowardice
8: To rest mistrustful where a noble heart
9: Hath pawned an open hand in sign of love;
10: Else might I think that Clarence, Edward’s brother,
11: Were but a feignèd friend to our proceedings.
12: But welcome, sweet Clarence; my daughter shall be thine.
14: And now, what rests but, in night’s coverture
16: His soldiers lurking in the town about,
17: And but attended by a simple guard,
18: We may surprise and take him at our pleasure?
19: Our scouts have found the adventure very easy;
20: That, as Ulysses and stout Diomed
21: With sleight and manhood stole to Rhesus’ tents
22: And brought from thence the Thracian fatal steeds,
23: So we, well covered with the night’s black mantle,
24: At unawares may beat down Edward’s guard
25: And seize himself. I say not slaughter him,
26: For I intend but only to surprise him.
27: You that will follow me to this attempt,
28: Applaud the name of Henry with your leader.
29: Why then, let’s on our way in silent sort.
30: For Warwick and his friends, God and Saint George!

1: Come on, my masters, each man take his stand.
2: The King by this is set him down to sleep.
3: What, will he not to bed?
4: Why, no, for he hath made a solemn vow
5: Never to lie and take his natural rest
6: Till Warwick or himself be quite suppressed.
7: Tomorrow, then, belike shall be the day,
8: If Warwick be so near as men report.
9: But say, I pray, what nobleman is that
10: That with the King here resteth in his tent?
11: ’Tis the Lord Hastings, the King’s chiefest friend.
12: O, is it so? But why commands the King
13: That his chief followers lodge in towns about him,
14: While he himself keeps in the cold field?
15: ’Tis the more honor, because more dangerous.
16: Ay, but give me worship and quietness;
17: I like it better than a dangerous honor.
18: If Warwick knew in what estate he stands,
19: ’Tis to be doubted he would waken him.
20: Unless our halberds did shut up his passage.
21: Ay, wherefore else guard we his royal tent
22: But to defend his person from night foes?
23: This is his tent, and see where stand his guard.
24: Courage, my masters. Honor, now or never!
25: But follow me, and Edward shall be ours.
28: What are they that fly there?
30: Let them go. Here is the Duke.
32: Why, Warwick, when we parted, thou call’dst me king.
33: Ay, but the case is altered.
34: When you disgraced me in my embassade,
35: Then I degraded you from being king
36: And come now to create you Duke of York.
37: Alas, how should you govern any kingdom
38: That know not how to use ambassadors,
39: Nor how to be contented with one wife,
40: Nor how to use your brothers brotherly,
41: Nor how to study for the people’s welfare,
42: Nor how to shroud yourself from enemies?
43: Yea, brother of Clarence, art thou here too?
44: Nay, then, I see that Edward needs must down.
45: Yet, Warwick, in despite of all mischance,
46: Of thee thyself and all thy complices,
47: Edward will always bear himself as king.
48: Though Fortune’s malice overthrow my state,
49: My mind exceeds the compass of her wheel.
50: Then for his mind be Edward England’s king,
51: But Henry now shall wear the English crown
52: And be true king indeed, thou but the shadow.—
53: My lord of Somerset, at my request,
54: See that forthwith Duke Edward be conveyed
55: Unto my brother, Archbishop of York.
56: When I have fought with Pembroke and his fellows,
57: I’ll follow you and tell what answer
58: Lewis and the Lady Bona send to him.—
59: Now for awhile farewell, good Duke of York.
60: What Fates impose, that men must needs abide;
61: It boots not to resist both wind and tide.
62: What now remains, my lords, for us to do
63: But march to London with our soldiers?
64: Ay, that’s the first thing that we have to do,
65: To free King Henry from imprisonment
66: And see him seated in the regal throne.

1: Madam, what makes you in this sudden change?
2: Why, brother Rivers, are you yet to learn
3: What late misfortune is befall’n King Edward?
4: What, loss of some pitched battle against Warwick?
5: No, but the loss of his own royal person.
7: Ay, almost slain, for he is taken prisoner,
8: Either betrayed by falsehood of his guard
9: Or by his foe surprised at unawares;
10: And, as I further have to understand,
11: Is new committed to the Bishop of York,
12: Fell Warwick’s brother and by that our foe.
13: These news I must confess are full of grief;
14: Yet, gracious madam, bear it as you may.
15: Warwick may lose that now hath won the day.
16: Till then fair hope must hinder life’s decay;
17: And I the rather wean me from despair
18: For love of Edward’s offspring in my womb.
19: This is it that makes me bridle passion
20: And bear with mildness my misfortune’s cross.
21: Ay, ay, for this I draw in many a tear
22: And stop the rising of blood-sucking sighs,
23: Lest with my sighs or tears I blast or drown
24: King Edward’s fruit, true heir to th’ English crown.
25: But, madam, where is Warwick then become?
26: I am informèd that he comes towards London
27: To set the crown once more on Henry’s head.
28: Guess thou the rest: King Edward’s friends must down.
30: But to prevent the tyrant’s violence—
31: For trust not him that hath once broken faith—
32: I’ll hence forthwith unto the sanctuary
33: To save at least the heir of Edward’s right.
34: There shall I rest secure from force and fraud.
35: Come, therefore, let us fly while we may fly.
36: If Warwick take us, we are sure to die.

1: Now, my Lord Hastings and Sir William Stanley,
2: Leave off to wonder why I drew you hither
3: Into this chiefest thicket of the park.
4: Thus stands the case: you know our king, my brother,
5: Is prisoner to the Bishop here, at whose hands
6: He hath good usage and great liberty,
7: And, often but attended with weak guard,
8: Comes hunting this way to disport himself.
9: I have advertised him by secret means
10: That, if about this hour he make this way
11: Under the color of his usual game,
12: He shall here find his friends with horse and men
13: To set him free from his captivity.
14: This way, my lord, for this way lies the game.
15: Nay, this way, man. See where the huntsmen stand.—
16: Now, brother of Gloucester, Lord Hastings, and the rest,
18: Stand you thus close to steal the Bishop’s deer?
19: Brother, the time and case requireth haste.
20: Your horse stands ready at the park corner.
22: To Lynn, my lord, and shipped from thence to Flanders.
24: Well guessed, believe me, for that was my meaning.
25: Stanley, I will requite thy forwardness.
26: But wherefore stay we? ’Tis no time to talk.
27: Huntsman, what sayst thou? Wilt thou go along?
28: Better do so than tarry and be hanged.
29: Come then, away! Let’s ha’ no more ado.
30: Bishop, farewell; shield thee from Warwick’s frown,
31: And pray that I may repossess the crown.

1: Master lieutenant, now that God and friends
2: Have shaken Edward from the regal seat
3: And turned my captive state to liberty,
4: My fear to hope, my sorrows unto joys,
5: At our enlargement what are thy due fees?
6: Subjects may challenge nothing of their sov’reigns,
7: But, if an humble prayer may prevail,
8: I then crave pardon of your Majesty.
9: For what, lieutenant? For well using me?
10: Nay, be thou sure I’ll well requite thy kindness,
11: For that it made my imprisonment a pleasure,
12: Ay, such a pleasure as encagèd birds
13: Conceive when, after many moody thoughts,
14: At last by notes of household harmony
15: They quite forget their loss of liberty.—
16: But, Warwick, after God thou sett’st me free,
17: And chiefly, therefore, I thank God and thee.
18: He was the author, thou the instrument.
19: Therefore, that I may conquer Fortune’s spite
20: By living low where Fortune cannot hurt me,
21: And that the people of this blessèd land
22: May not be punished with my thwarting stars,
23: Warwick, although my head still wear the crown,
24: I here resign my government to thee,
25: For thou art fortunate in all thy deeds.
26: Your Grace hath still been famed for virtuous
27: And now may seem as wise as virtuous
28: By spying and avoiding Fortune’s malice,
29: For few men rightly temper with the stars.
30: Yet, in this one thing let me blame your Grace:
31: For choosing me when Clarence is in place.
32: No, Warwick, thou art worthy of the sway,
33: To whom the heav’ns in thy nativity
34: Adjudged an olive branch and laurel crown
35: As likely to be blest in peace and war;
36: And therefore I yield thee my free consent.
37: And I choose Clarence only for Protector.
38: Warwick and Clarence, give me both your hands.
39: Now join your hands, and with your hands your hearts,
42: I make you both Protectors of this land,
43: While I myself will lead a private life
44: And in devotion spend my latter days,
45: To sin’s rebuke and my Creator’s praise.
46: What answers Clarence to his sovereign’s will?
47: That he consents, if Warwick yield consent,
48: For on thy fortune I repose myself.
49: Why, then, though loath, yet must I be content.
50: We’ll yoke together like a double shadow
51: To Henry’s body, and supply his place—
52: I mean, in bearing weight of government—
53: While he enjoys the honor and his ease.
54: And, Clarence, now then it is more than needful
55: Forthwith that Edward be pronounced a traitor
56: And all his lands and goods be confiscate.
57: What else? And that succession be determinèd.
58: Ay, therein Clarence shall not want his part.
59: But with the first of all your chief affairs
60: Let me entreat—for I command no more—
61: That Margaret your queen and my son Edward
62: Be sent for, to return from France with speed,
63: For till I see them here, by doubtful fear
64: My joy of liberty is half eclipsed.
65: It shall be done, my sovereign, with all speed.
66: My lord of Somerset, what youth is that
67: Of whom you seem to have so tender care?
68: My liege, it is young Henry, Earl of Richmond.
71: Suggest but truth to my divining thoughts,
72: This pretty lad will prove our country’s bliss.
73: His looks are full of peaceful majesty,
74: His head by nature framed to wear a crown,
75: His hand to wield a scepter, and himself
76: Likely in time to bless a regal throne.
77: Make much of him, my lords, for this is he
78: Must help you more than you are hurt by me.
80: That Edward is escapèd from your brother
81: And fled, as he hears since, to Burgundy.
82: Unsavory news! But how made he escape?
83: He was conveyed by Richard, Duke of Gloucester,
84: And the Lord Hastings, who attended him
85: In secret ambush on the forest side
86: And from the Bishop’s huntsmen rescued him,
87: For hunting was his daily exercise.
88: My brother was too careless of his charge.
89: But let us hence, my sovereign, to provide
90: A salve for any sore that may betide.
91: My lord, I like not of this flight of Edward’s,
92: For doubtless Burgundy will yield him help,
93: And we shall have more wars before ’t be long.
95: Did glad my heart with hope of this young Richmond,
97: So doth my heart misgive me in these conflicts
98: What may befall him, to his harm and ours.
99: Therefore, Lord Oxford, to prevent the worst,
100: Forthwith we’ll send him hence to Brittany
101: Till storms be past of civil enmity.
102: Ay, for if Edward repossess the crown,
103: ’Tis like that Richmond, with the rest, shall down.
104: It shall be so. He shall to Brittany.
105: Come, therefore, let’s about it speedily.

1: Now, brother Richard, Lord Hastings, and the rest:
2: Yet thus far Fortune maketh us amends,
3: And says that once more I shall interchange
4: My wanèd state for Henry’s regal crown.
5: Well have we passed, and now re-passed, the seas,
6: And brought desirèd help from Burgundy.
7: What then remains, we being thus arrived
8: From Ravenspurgh Haven before the gates of York,
9: But that we enter as into our dukedom?
10: The gates made fast? Brother, I like not this.
11: For many men that stumble at the threshold
12: Are well foretold that danger lurks within.
13: Tush, man, abodements must not now affright us.
14: By fair or foul means we must enter in,
15: For hither will our friends repair to us.
16: My liege, I’ll knock once more to summon them.
17: My lords, we were forewarnèd of your coming,
18: And shut the gates for safety of ourselves,
19: For now we owe allegiance unto Henry.
20: But, master mayor, if Henry be your king,
21: Yet Edward, at the least, is Duke of York.
22: True, my good lord, I know you for no less.
23: Why, and I challenge nothing but my dukedom,
24: As being well content with that alone.
25: But when the fox hath once got in his nose,
26: He’ll soon find means to make the body follow.
27: Why, master mayor, why stand you in a doubt?
28: Open the gates. We are King Henry’s friends.
29: Ay, say you so? The gates shall then be opened.
30: A wise stout captain, and soon persuaded.
31: The good old man would fain that all were well,
32: So ’twere not long of him; but being entered,
33: I doubt not, I, but we shall soon persuade
34: Both him and all his brothers unto reason.
35: So, master mayor, these gates must not be shut
36: But in the night or in the time of war.
37: What, fear not, man, but yield me up the keys.
38: For Edward will defend the town and thee
39: And all those friends that deign to follow me.
40: Brother, this is Sir John Montgomery,
41: Our trusty friend, unless I be deceived.
42: Welcome, Sir John. But why come you in arms?
43: To help King Edward in his time of storm,
44: As every loyal subject ought to do.
45: Thanks, good Montgomery. But we now forget
46: Our title to the crown, and only claim
47: Our dukedom, till God please to send the rest.
48: Then fare you well, for I will hence again.
49: I came to serve a king and not a duke.—
50: Drummer, strike up, and let us march away.
51: Nay, stay, Sir John, a while, and we’ll debate
52: By what safe means the crown may be recovered.
53: What talk you of debating? In few words,
54: If you’ll not here proclaim yourself our king,
55: I’ll leave you to your fortune and be gone
56: To keep them back that come to succor you.
57: Why shall we fight if you pretend no title?
58: Why, brother, wherefore stand you on nice points?
59: When we grow stronger, then we’ll make our claim.
60: Till then ’tis wisdom to conceal our meaning.
61: Away with scrupulous wit! Now arms must rule.
62: And fearless minds climb soonest unto crowns.
63: Brother, we will proclaim you out of hand;
64: The bruit thereof will bring you many friends.
65: Then be it as you will, for ’tis my right,
66: And Henry but usurps the diadem.
67: Ay, now my sovereign speaketh like himself,
68: And now will I be Edward’s champion.
69: Sound, trumpet! Edward shall be here proclaimed.—
70: Come, fellow soldier, make thou proclamation.
71: Edward the Fourth, by the Grace of
72: God, King of England and France, and Lord of
74: And whosoe’er gainsays King Edward’s right,
75: By this I challenge him to single fight.
77: Thanks, brave Montgomery, and thanks unto you all.
78: If fortune serve me, I’ll requite this kindness.
79: Now, for this night let’s harbor here in York,
80: And when the morning sun shall raise his car
81: Above the border of this horizon,
82: We’ll forward towards Warwick and his mates;
83: For well I wot that Henry is no soldier.
84: Ah, froward Clarence, how evil it beseems thee
85: To flatter Henry and forsake thy brother!
86: Yet, as we may, we’ll meet both thee and Warwick.
87: Come on, brave soldiers; doubt not of the day;
88: And that once gotten, doubt not of large pay.

1: What counsel, lords? Edward from Belgia,
2: With hasty Germans and blunt Hollanders,
3: Hath passed in safety through the Narrow Seas,
4: And with his troops doth march amain to London,
5: And many giddy people flock to him.
6: Let’s levy men and beat him back again.
7: A little fire is quickly trodden out,
8: Which, being suffered, rivers cannot quench.
9: In Warwickshire I have true-hearted friends,
10: Not mutinous in peace yet bold in war.
11: Those will I muster up; and thou, son Clarence,
12: Shalt stir up in Suffolk, Norfolk, and in Kent
13: The knights and gentlemen to come with thee.—
15: Northampton, and in Leicestershire shalt find
16: Men well inclined to hear what thou command’st.—
17: And thou, brave Oxford, wondrous well beloved,
18: In Oxfordshire shalt muster up thy friends.—
19: My sovereign, with the loving citizens,
20: Like to his island girt in with the ocean,
21: Or modest Dian circled with her nymphs,
22: Shall rest in London till we come to him.
23: Fair lords, take leave, and stand not to reply.—
25: Farewell, my Hector and my Troy’s true hope.
26: In sign of truth, I kiss your Highness’ hand.
28: Comfort, my lord; and so I take my leave.
29: And thus I seal my truth, and bid adieu.
30: Sweet Oxford and my loving Montague
31: And all at once, once more a happy farewell.
32: Farewell, sweet lords. Let’s meet at Coventry.
33: Here at the palace will I rest awhile.
34: Cousin of Exeter, what thinks your Lordship?
35: Methinks the power that Edward hath in field
36: Should not be able to encounter mine.
37: The doubt is that he will seduce the rest.
38: That’s not my fear. My meed hath got me fame.
39: I have not stopped mine ears to their demands,
40: Nor posted off their suits with slow delays.
41: My pity hath been balm to heal their wounds,
42: My mildness hath allayed their swelling griefs,
43: My mercy dried their water-flowing tears.
44: I have not been desirous of their wealth
45: Nor much oppressed them with great subsidies,
46: Nor forward of revenge, though they much erred.
47: Then why should they love Edward more than me?
48: No, Exeter, these graces challenge grace;
49: And when the lion fawns upon the lamb,
50: The lamb will never cease to follow him.
51: Hark, hark, my lord, what shouts are these?
52: Seize on the shamefaced Henry, bear him hence,
53: And once again proclaim us King of England.—
54: You are the fount that makes small brooks to flow.
55: Now stops thy spring; my sea shall suck them dry
56: And swell so much the higher by their ebb.—
57: Hence with him to the Tower. Let him not speak.
58: And, lords, towards Coventry bend we our course,
60: The sun shines hot, and if we use delay,
61: Cold biting winter mars our hoped-for hay.
62: Away betimes, before his forces join,
63: And take the great-grown traitor unawares.
64: Brave warriors, march amain towards Coventry.

1: Where is the post that came from valiant Oxford?—
2: How far hence is thy lord, mine honest fellow?
3: By this at Dunsmore, marching hitherward.
4: How far off is our brother Montague?
5: Where is the post that came from Montague?
6: By this at Daintry, with a puissant troop.
7: Say, Somerville, what says my loving son?
8: And, by thy guess, how nigh is Clarence now?
9: At Southam I did leave him with his forces
10: And do expect him here some two hours hence.
11: Then Clarence is at hand; I hear his drum.
12: It is not his, my lord; here Southam lies.
13: The drum your Honor hears marcheth from Warwick.
14: Who should that be? Belike unlooked-for friends.
15: They are at hand, and you shall quickly know.
16: Go, Trumpet, to the walls, and sound a parle.
17: See how the surly Warwick mans the wall.
18: O unbid spite, is sportful Edward come?
19: Where slept our scouts, or how are they seduced,
20: That we could hear no news of his repair?
21: Now, Warwick, wilt thou ope the city gates,
22: Speak gentle words, and humbly bend thy knee?
23: Call Edward king, and at his hands beg mercy,
24: And he shall pardon thee these outrages.
25: Nay, rather wilt thou draw thy forces hence,
26: Confess who set thee up and plucked thee down,
27: Call Warwick patron, and be penitent,
28: And thou shalt still remain the Duke of York.
29: I thought at least he would have said the King.
30: Or did he make the jest against his will?
31: Is not a dukedom, sir, a goodly gift?
32: Ay, by my faith, for a poor earl to give.
33: I’ll do thee service for so good a gift.
34: ’Twas I that gave the kingdom to thy brother.
35: Why, then, ’tis mine, if but by Warwick’s gift.
36: Thou art no Atlas for so great a weight;
37: And, weakling, Warwick takes his gift again,
38: And Henry is my king, Warwick his subject.
39: But Warwick’s king is Edward’s prisoner.
40: And, gallant Warwick, do but answer this:
41: What is the body when the head is off?
42: Alas, that Warwick had no more forecast,
43: But whiles he thought to steal the single ten,
44: The King was slyly fingered from the deck.
45: You left poor Henry at the Bishop’s palace,
46: And ten to one you’ll meet him in the Tower.
47: ’Tis even so; yet you are Warwick still.
48: Come, Warwick, take the time; kneel down, kneel down.
50: Nay, when? Strike now, or else the iron cools.
51: I had rather chop this hand off at a blow
52: And with the other fling it at thy face
53: Than bear so low a sail to strike to thee.
54: Sail how thou canst, have wind and tide thy friend,
55: This hand, fast wound about thy coal-black hair,
56: Shall, whiles thy head is warm and new cut off,
57: Write in the dust this sentence with thy blood:
58: Wind-changing Warwick now can change no more.
59: O, cheerful colors, see where Oxford comes!
61: The gates are open; let us enter too.
62: So other foes may set upon our backs.
63: Stand we in good array, for they no doubt
64: Will issue out again and bid us battle.
65: If not, the city being but of small defense,
66: We’ll quickly rouse the traitors in the same.
67: O welcome, Oxford, for we want thy help.
69: Thou and thy brother both shall buy this treason
70: Even with the dearest blood your bodies bear!
71: The harder matched, the greater victory.
72: My mind presageth happy gain and conquest.
74: Two of thy name, both dukes of Somerset,
75: Have sold their lives unto the house of York,
76: And thou shalt be the third, if this sword hold.
77: And lo, where George of Clarence sweeps along,
78: Of force enough to bid his brother battle,
79: With whom an upright zeal to right prevails
80: More than the nature of a brother’s love.—
81: Come, Clarence, come; thou wilt, if Warwick call.
82: Father of Warwick, know you what this means?
83: Look, here I throw my infamy at thee.
84: I will not ruinate my father’s house,
85: Who gave his blood to lime the stones together
86: And set up Lancaster. Why, trowest thou, Warwick,
87: That Clarence is so harsh, so blunt, unnatural,
88: To bend the fatal instruments of war
89: Against his brother and his lawful king?
90: Perhaps thou wilt object my holy oath.
91: To keep that oath were more impiety
92: Than Jephthah when he sacrificed his daughter.
93: I am so sorry for my trespass made
94: That, to deserve well at my brother’s hands,
95: I here proclaim myself thy mortal foe,
96: With resolution, wheresoe’er I meet thee—
97: As I will meet thee if thou stir abroad—
98: To plague thee for thy foul misleading me.
99: And so, proud-hearted Warwick, I defy thee
100: And to my brother turn my blushing cheeks.—
101: Pardon me, Edward, I will make amends.—
102: And, Richard, do not frown upon my faults,
103: For I will henceforth be no more unconstant.
104: Now, welcome more, and ten times more beloved,
105: Than if thou never hadst deserved our hate.
106: Welcome, good Clarence; this is brother-like.
107: O, passing traitor, perjured and unjust.
108: What, Warwick, wilt thou leave the town and fight?
109: Or shall we beat the stones about thine ears?
110: Alas, I am not cooped here for defense.
111: I will away towards Barnet presently
112: And bid thee battle, Edward, if thou dar’st.
113: Yes, Warwick, Edward dares, and leads the way.—
114: Lords, to the field! Saint George and victory!

1: So, lie thou there. Die thou, and die our fear,
2: For Warwick was a bug that feared us all.
3: Now, Montague, sit fast. I seek for thee,
4: That Warwick’s bones may keep thine company.
5: Ah, who is nigh? Come to me, friend or foe,
6: And tell me who is victor, York or Warwick?
7: Why ask I that? My mangled body shows,
8: My blood, my want of strength, my sick heart shows
9: That I must yield my body to the earth
10: And, by my fall, the conquest to my foe.
11: Thus yields the cedar to the axe’s edge,
12: Whose arms gave shelter to the princely eagle,
13: Under whose shade the ramping lion slept,
14: Whose top branch overpeered Jove’s spreading tree
15: And kept low shrubs from winter’s pow’rful wind.
16: These eyes, that now are dimmed with death’s black veil,
18: Have been as piercing as the midday sun
19: To search the secret treasons of the world.
20: The wrinkles in my brows, now filled with blood,
21: Were likened oft to kingly sepulchers,
22: For who lived king but I could dig his grave?
23: And who durst smile when Warwick bent his brow?
24: Lo, now my glory smeared in dust and blood!
25: My parks, my walks, my manors that I had
26: Even now forsake me; and of all my lands
27: Is nothing left me but my body’s length.
28: Why, what is pomp, rule, reign, but earth and dust?
29: And live we how we can, yet die we must.
30: Ah, Warwick, Warwick, wert thou as we are,
31: We might recover all our loss again.
32: The Queen from France hath brought a puissant power;
34: Even now we heard the news. Ah, could’st thou fly—
35: Why, then, I would not fly. Ah, Montague,
36: If thou be there, sweet brother, take my hand
37: And with thy lips keep in my soul awhile.
38: Thou lov’st me not, for, brother, if thou didst,
39: Thy tears would wash this cold congealèd blood
40: That glues my lips and will not let me speak.
41: Come quickly, Montague, or I am dead.
42: Ah, Warwick, Montague hath breathed his last,
43: And to the latest gasp cried out for Warwick,
44: And said Commend me to my valiant brother.
45: And more he would have said, and more he spoke,
46: Which sounded like a cannon in a vault,
47: That mought not be distinguished, but at last
48: I well might hear, delivered with a groan,
50: Sweet rest his soul! Fly, lords, and save yourselves,
51: For Warwick bids you all farewell to meet in heaven.
52: Away, away, to meet the Queen’s great power!

1: Thus far our fortune keeps an upward course,
2: And we are graced with wreaths of victory.
3: But in the midst of this bright-shining day,
4: I spy a black suspicious threat’ning cloud
5: That will encounter with our glorious sun
6: Ere he attain his easeful western bed.
7: I mean, my lords, those powers that the Queen
8: Hath raised in Gallia have arrived our coast
9: And, as we hear, march on to fight with us.
10: A little gale will soon disperse that cloud
11: And blow it to the source from whence it came;
12: Thy very beams will dry those vapors up,
13: For every cloud engenders not a storm.
14: The Queen is valued thirty thousand strong,
15: And Somerset, with Oxford, fled to her.
16: If she have time to breathe, be well assured
17: Her faction will be full as strong as ours.
18: We are advertised by our loving friends
19: That they do hold their course toward Tewkesbury.
20: We having now the best at Barnet Field
21: Will thither straight, for willingness rids way,
22: And, as we march, our strength will be augmented
23: In every county as we go along.
24: Strike up the drum, cry Courage! and away.

1: Great lords, wise men ne’er sit and wail their loss
2: But cheerly seek how to redress their harms.
3: What though the mast be now blown overboard,
4: The cable broke, the holding-anchor lost,
5: And half our sailors swallowed in the flood?
6: Yet lives our pilot still. Is ’t meet that he
7: Should leave the helm and, like a fearful lad,
8: With tearful eyes add water to the sea
9: And give more strength to that which hath too much,
10: Whiles in his moan the ship splits on the rock,
11: Which industry and courage might have saved?
12: Ah, what a shame, ah, what a fault were this!
13: Say Warwick was our anchor; what of that?
14: And Montague our topmast; what of him?
15: Our slaughtered friends the tackles; what of these?
16: Why, is not Oxford here another anchor?
18: The friends of France our shrouds and tacklings?
19: And, though unskillful, why not Ned and I
20: For once allowed the skillful pilot’s charge?
21: We will not from the helm to sit and weep,
22: But keep our course, though the rough wind say no,
23: From shelves and rocks that threaten us with wrack.
24: As good to chide the waves as speak them fair.
25: And what is Edward but a ruthless sea?
26: What Clarence but a quicksand of deceit?
27: And Richard but a ragged fatal rock—
28: All these the enemies to our poor bark?
29: Say you can swim: alas, ’tis but awhile;
30: Tread on the sand: why, there you quickly sink;
31: Bestride the rock: the tide will wash you off
32: Or else you famish; that’s a threefold death.
33: This speak I, lords, to let you understand,
34: If case some one of you would fly from us,
35: That there’s no hoped-for mercy with the brothers
36: More than with ruthless waves, with sands and rocks.
37: Why, courage then! What cannot be avoided
38: ’Twere childish weakness to lament or fear.
39: Methinks a woman of this valiant spirit
40: Should, if a coward heard her speak these words,
42: And make him, naked, foil a man-at-arms.
43: I speak not this as doubting any here,
44: For did I but suspect a fearful man,
45: He should have leave to go away betimes,
46: Lest in our need he might infect another
47: And make him of like spirit to himself.
48: If any such be here, as God forbid,
49: Let him depart before we need his help.
50: Women and children of so high a courage,
51: And warriors faint? Why, ’twere perpetual shame!
52: O, brave young prince, thy famous grandfather
53: Doth live again in thee. Long mayst thou live
54: To bear his image and renew his glories!
55: And he that will not fight for such a hope,
56: Go home to bed and, like the owl by day,
57: If he arise, be mocked and wondered at.
59: And take his thanks that yet hath nothing else.
60: Prepare you, lords, for Edward is at hand,
61: Ready to fight. Therefore be resolute.
62: I thought no less. It is his policy
63: To haste thus fast to find us unprovided.
64: But he’s deceived. We are in readiness.
65: This cheers my heart to see your forwardness.
66: Here pitch our battle; hence we will not budge.
67: Brave followers, yonder stands the thorny wood
68: Which by the heavens’ assistance and your strength
69: Must by the roots be hewn up yet ere night.
70: I need not add more fuel to your fire,
71: For, well I wot, you blaze to burn them out.
72: Give signal to the fight, and to it, lords!
73: Lords, knights, and gentlemen, what I should say
74: My tears gainsay, for every word I speak
75: You see I drink the water of my eye.
76: Therefore, no more but this: Henry, your sovereign,
77: Is prisoner to the foe, his state usurped,
78: His realm a slaughterhouse, his subjects slain,
79: His statutes cancelled and his treasure spent,
80: And yonder is the wolf that makes this spoil.
81: You fight in justice. Then, in God’s name, lords,
82: Be valiant, and give signal to the fight!

1: Now here a period of tumultuous broils.
2: Away with Oxford to Hames Castle straight.
3: For Somerset, off with his guilty head.
4: Go bear them hence. I will not hear them speak.
5: For my part, I’ll not trouble thee with words.
6: Nor I, but stoop with patience to my fortune.
7: So part we sadly in this troublous world
8: To meet with joy in sweet Jerusalem.
9: Is proclamation made that who finds Edward
10: Shall have a high reward, and he his life?
11: It is, and lo where youthful Edward comes.
12: Bring forth the gallant; let us hear him speak.
13: What, can so young a thorn begin to prick?—
14: Edward, what satisfaction canst thou make
15: For bearing arms, for stirring up my subjects,
16: And all the trouble thou hast turned me to?
17: Speak like a subject, proud ambitious York.
18: Suppose that I am now my father’s mouth:
19: Resign thy chair, and where I stand, kneel thou,
20: Whilst I propose the selfsame words to thee
21: Which, traitor, thou wouldst have me answer to.
22: Ah, that thy father had been so resolved!
23: That you might still have worn the petticoat
24: And ne’er have stol’n the breech from Lancaster.
25: Let Aesop fable in a winter’s night;
26: His currish riddles sorts not with this place.
27: By heaven, brat, I’ll plague you for that word.
28: Ay, thou wast born to be a plague to men.
29: For God’s sake, take away this captive scold.
30: Nay, take away this scolding crookback, rather.
31: Peace, willful boy, or I will charm your tongue.
32: Untutored lad, thou art too malapert.
33: I know my duty. You are all undutiful.
34: Lascivious Edward, and thou perjured George,
35: And thou misshapen Dick, I tell you all
36: I am your better, traitors as you are,
37: And thou usurp’st my father’s right and mine.
38: Take that, the likeness of this railer here!
39: Sprawl’st thou? Take that to end thy agony!
40: And there’s for twitting me with perjury.
43: Hold, Richard, hold, for we have done too much.
44: Why should she live to fill the world with words?
45: What, doth she swoon? Use means for her recovery.
46: Clarence, excuse me to the King my brother.
47: I’ll hence to London on a serious matter.
48: Ere you come there, be sure to hear some news.
51: O Ned, sweet Ned, speak to thy mother, boy.
52: Canst thou not speak? O traitors, murderers!
53: They that stabbed Caesar shed no blood at all,
54: Did not offend, nor were not worthy blame,
55: If this foul deed were by to equal it.
56: He was a man; this, in respect, a child,
57: And men ne’er spend their fury on a child.
58: What’s worse than murderer, that I may name it?
59: No, no, my heart will burst an if I speak,
60: And I will speak, that so my heart may burst.
62: How sweet a plant have you untimely cropped!
63: You have no children, butchers. If you had,
64: The thought of them would have stirred up remorse.
65: But if you ever chance to have a child,
66: Look in his youth to have him so cut off
67: As, deathsmen, you have rid this sweet young prince.
68: Away with her. Go bear her hence perforce.
69: Nay, never bear me hence! Dispatch me here.
70: Here sheathe thy sword; I’ll pardon thee my death.
71: What, wilt thou not?—Then, Clarence, do it thou.
72: By heaven, I will not do thee so much ease.
73: Good Clarence, do! Sweet Clarence, do thou do it.
74: Didst thou not hear me swear I would not do it?
75: Ay, but thou usest to forswear thyself.
77: What, wilt thou not? Where is that devil’s butcher, Richard,
79: Hard-favored Richard? Richard, where art thou?
80: Thou art not here. Murder is thy alms-deed;
81: Petitioners for blood thou ne’er putt’st back.
82: I charge you bear her hence.
84: So come to you and yours as to this prince!
86: To London all in post, and, as I guess,
87: To make a bloody supper in the Tower.
88: He’s sudden if a thing comes in his head.
89: Now march we hence. Discharge the common sort
90: With pay and thanks, and let’s away to London
91: And see our gentle queen how well she fares.
92: By this I hope she hath a son for me.

1: Good day, my lord. What, at your book so hard?
2: Ay, my good lord—my lord, I should say rather.
3: ’Tis sin to flatter; good was little better:
4: Good Gloucester and good devil were alike,
5: And both preposterous: therefore, not good lord.
6: Sirrah, leave us to ourselves; we must confer.
7: So flies the reckless shepherd from the wolf;
8: So first the harmless sheep doth yield his fleece
9: And next his throat unto the butcher’s knife.
10: What scene of death hath Roscius now to act?
11: Suspicion always haunts the guilty mind;
12: The thief doth fear each bush an officer.
13: The bird that hath been limèd in a bush,
14: With trembling wings misdoubteth every bush;
15: And I, the hapless male to one sweet bird,
16: Have now the fatal object in my eye
17: Where my poor young was limed, was caught, and killed.
19: Why, what a peevish fool was that of Crete
20: That taught his son the office of a fowl!
21: And yet, for all his wings, the fool was drowned.
22: I Daedalus, my poor boy Icarus,
23: Thy father Minos, that denied our course;
24: The sun that seared the wings of my sweet boy
25: Thy brother Edward, and thyself the sea
26: Whose envious gulf did swallow up his life.
27: Ah, kill me with thy weapon, not with words!
28: My breast can better brook thy dagger’s point
29: Than can my ears that tragic history.
30: But wherefore dost thou come? Is ’t for my life?
31: Think’st thou I am an executioner?
32: A persecutor I am sure thou art.
34: Why, then, thou art an executioner.
35: Thy son I killed for his presumption.
36: Hadst thou been killed when first thou didst presume,
37: Thou hadst not lived to kill a son of mine.
38: And thus I prophesy: that many a thousand
39: Which now mistrust no parcel of my fear,
40: And many an old man’s sigh, and many a widow’s
41: And many an orphan’s water-standing eye,
42: Men for their sons, wives for their husbands,
43: Orphans for their parents’ timeless death,
44: Shall rue the hour that ever thou wast born.
45: The owl shrieked at thy birth, an evil sign;
46: The night-crow cried, aboding luckless time;
47: Dogs howled, and hideous tempest shook down trees;
48: The raven rooked her on the chimney’s top;
49: And chatt’ring pies in dismal discords sung;
50: Thy mother felt more than a mother’s pain,
51: And yet brought forth less than a mother’s hope:
52: To wit, an indigested and deformèd lump,
53: Not like the fruit of such a goodly tree.
54: Teeth hadst thou in thy head when thou wast born
55: To signify thou cam’st to bite the world.
56: And if the rest be true which I have heard,
58: I’ll hear no more. Die, prophet, in thy speech;
59: For this amongst the rest was I ordained.
60: Ay, and for much more slaughter after this.
61: O God, forgive my sins, and pardon thee.
62: What, will the aspiring blood of Lancaster
63: Sink in the ground? I thought it would have mounted.
64: See how my sword weeps for the poor king’s death.
65: O, may such purple tears be always shed
66: From those that wish the downfall of our house.
67: If any spark of life be yet remaining,
68: Down, down to hell, and say I sent thee thither—
69: I that have neither pity, love, nor fear.
70: Indeed, ’tis true that Henry told me of,
71: For I have often heard my mother say
72: I came into the world with my legs forward.
73: Had I not reason, think you, to make haste
74: And seek their ruin that usurped our right?
75: The midwife wondered, and the women cried
76: O Jesus bless us, he is born with teeth!
77: And so I was, which plainly signified
78: That I should snarl, and bite, and play the dog.
79: Then, since the heavens have shaped my body so,
80: Let hell make crook’d my mind to answer it.
81: I have no brother, I am like no brother;
82: And this word love, which graybeards call divine,
83: Be resident in men like one another
84: And not in me. I am myself alone.
85: Clarence, beware; thou keep’st me from the light,
86: But I will sort a pitchy day for thee;
87: For I will buzz abroad such prophecies
88: That Edward shall be fearful of his life;
89: And then to purge his fear, I’ll be thy death.
90: King Henry and the Prince his son are gone.
91: Clarence, thy turn is next, and then the rest,
92: Counting myself but bad till I be best.
93: I’ll throw thy body in another room,
94: And triumph, Henry, in thy day of doom.

1: Once more we sit in England’s royal throne,
2: Repurchased with the blood of enemies.
3: What valiant foemen, like to autumn’s corn,
4: Have we mowed down in tops of all their pride!
5: Three dukes of Somerset, threefold renowned
7: Two Cliffords, as the father and the son;
8: And two Northumberlands; two braver men
9: Ne’er spurred their coursers at the trumpet’s sound.
10: With them the two brave bears, Warwick and Montague,
12: That in their chains fettered the kingly lion
13: And made the forest tremble when they roared.
14: Thus have we swept suspicion from our seat
15: And made our footstool of security.—
16: Come hither, Bess, and let me kiss my boy.—
17: Young Ned, for thee, thine uncles and myself
18: Have in our armors watched the winter’s night,
19: Went all afoot in summer’s scalding heat,
20: That thou mightst repossess the crown in peace,
21: And of our labors thou shalt reap the gain.
22: I’ll blast his harvest, if your head were laid;
23: For yet I am not looked on in the world.
24: This shoulder was ordained so thick to heave,
25: And heave it shall some weight or break my back.
26: Work thou the way and that shalt execute.
27: Clarence and Gloucester, love my lovely queen,
28: And kiss your princely nephew, brothers both.
29: The duty that I owe unto your Majesty
30: I seal upon the lips of this sweet babe.
31: Thanks, noble Clarence; worthy brother, thanks.
32: And that I love the tree from whence thou sprang’st,
33: Witness the loving kiss I give the fruit.
34: To say the truth, so Judas kissed his master
35: And cried All hail! whenas he meant all harm.
36: Now am I seated as my soul delights,
37: Having my country’s peace and brothers’ loves.
38: What will your Grace have done with Margaret?
39: Reignier, her father, to the King of France
40: Hath pawned the Sicils and Jerusalem,
41: And hither have they sent it for her ransom.
42: Away with her, and waft her hence to France.
43: And now what rests but that we spend the time
44: With stately triumphs, mirthful comic shows,
45: Such as befits the pleasure of the court?
46: Sound drums and trumpets! Farewell, sour annoy,
47: For here I hope begins our lasting joy.

1: Now is the winter of our discontent
2: Made glorious summer by this son of York,
3: And all the clouds that loured upon our house
4: In the deep bosom of the ocean buried.
5: Now are our brows bound with victorious wreaths,
6: Our bruisèd arms hung up for monuments,
7: Our stern alarums changed to merry meetings,
8: Our dreadful marches to delightful measures.
9: Grim-visaged war hath smoothed his wrinkled front;
10: And now, instead of mounting barbèd steeds
11: To fright the souls of fearful adversaries,
12: He capers nimbly in a lady’s chamber
13: To the lascivious pleasing of a lute.
14: But I, that am not shaped for sportive tricks,
15: Nor made to court an amorous looking glass;
16: I, that am rudely stamped and want love’s majesty
17: To strut before a wanton ambling nymph;
18: I, that am curtailed of this fair proportion,
19: Cheated of feature by dissembling nature,
20: Deformed, unfinished, sent before my time
21: Into this breathing world scarce half made up,
22: And that so lamely and unfashionable
23: That dogs bark at me as I halt by them—
24: Why, I, in this weak piping time of peace,
25: Have no delight to pass away the time,
26: Unless to see my shadow in the sun
27: And descant on mine own deformity.
28: And therefore, since I cannot prove a lover
29: To entertain these fair well-spoken days,
30: I am determinèd to prove a villain
31: And hate the idle pleasures of these days.
32: Plots have I laid, inductions dangerous,
33: By drunken prophecies, libels, and dreams,
34: To set my brother Clarence and the King
35: In deadly hate, the one against the other;
36: And if King Edward be as true and just
37: As I am subtle, false, and treacherous,
38: This day should Clarence closely be mewed up
39: About a prophecy which says that G
40: Of Edward’s heirs the murderer shall be.
41: Dive, thoughts, down to my soul. Here Clarence comes.
43: Brother, good day. What means this armèd guard
46: Tend’ring my person’s safety, hath appointed
47: This conduct to convey me to the Tower.
51: Alack, my lord, that fault is none of yours.
52: He should, for that, commit your godfathers.
53: O, belike his Majesty hath some intent
54: That you should be new christened in the Tower.
55: But what’s the matter, Clarence? May I know?
56: Yea, Richard, when I know, for I protest
57: As yet I do not. But, as I can learn,
58: He hearkens after prophecies and dreams,
59: And from the crossrow plucks the letter G,
60: And says a wizard told him that by G
62: And for my name of George begins with G,
63: It follows in his thought that I am he.
64: These, as I learn, and such like toys as these
65: Hath moved his Highness to commit me now.
66: Why, this it is when men are ruled by women.
67: ’Tis not the King that sends you to the Tower.
68: My Lady Grey his wife, Clarence, ’tis she
69: That tempers him to this extremity.
70: Was it not she and that good man of worship,
72: That made him send Lord Hastings to the Tower,
73: From whence this present day he is delivered?
74: We are not safe, Clarence; we are not safe.
75: By heaven, I think there is no man secure
76: But the Queen’s kindred and night-walking heralds
77: That trudge betwixt the King and Mistress Shore.
78: Heard you not what an humble suppliant
79: Lord Hastings was to her for his delivery?
81: Got my Lord Chamberlain his liberty.
82: I’ll tell you what: I think it is our way,
83: If we will keep in favor with the King,
84: To be her men and wear her livery.
85: The jealous o’erworn widow and herself,
86: Since that our brother dubbed them gentlewomen,

88: I beseech your Graces both to pardon me.

95: Is wise and virtuous, and his noble queen

139: No news so bad abroad as this at home:

1: Set down, set down your honorable load,
2: If honor may be shrouded in a hearse,
4: Th’ untimely fall of virtuous Lancaster.
5: Poor key-cold figure of a holy king,
6: Pale ashes of the house of Lancaster,
7: Thou bloodless remnant of that royal blood,
8: Be it lawful that I invocate thy ghost
9: To hear the lamentations of poor Anne,
10: Wife to thy Edward, to thy slaughtered son,
11: Stabbed by the selfsame hand that made these wounds.
13: Lo, in these windows that let forth thy life
14: I pour the helpless balm of my poor eyes.
15: O, cursèd be the hand that made these holes;
16: Cursèd the heart that had the heart to do it;
17: Cursèd the blood that let this blood from hence.
18: More direful hap betide that hated wretch
19: That makes us wretched by the death of thee
20: Than I can wish to wolves, to spiders, toads,
21: Or any creeping venomed thing that lives.
22: If ever he have child, abortive be it,
23: Prodigious, and untimely brought to light,
25: May fright the hopeful mother at the view,
26: And that be heir to his unhappiness.
27: If ever he have wife, let her be made
28: More miserable by the death of him
29: Than I am made by my young lord and thee.—
30: Come now towards Chertsey with your holy load,
31: Taken from Paul’s to be interrèd there.

33: Rest you, whiles I lament King Henry’s corse.

35: What black magician conjures up this fiend
37: Villains, set down the corse or, by Saint Paul,

39: My lord, stand back and let the coffin pass.
40: Unmannered dog, stand thou when I command!—
41: Advance thy halberd higher than my breast,
