44: What, do you tremble? Are you all afraid?
45: Alas, I blame you not, for you are mortal,
46: And mortal eyes cannot endure the devil.—
47: Avaunt, thou dreadful minister of hell.
48: Thou hadst but power over his mortal body;
49: His soul thou canst not have. Therefore begone.
50: Sweet saint, for charity, be not so curst.
51: Foul devil, for God’s sake, hence, and trouble us not,
53: For thou hast made the happy Earth thy hell,
54: Filled it with cursing cries and deep exclaims.
55: If thou delight to view thy heinous deeds,
56: Behold this pattern of thy butcheries.
57: O, gentlemen, see, see dead Henry’s wounds
58: Open their congealed mouths and bleed afresh!—
59: Blush, blush, thou lump of foul deformity,
60: For ’tis thy presence that exhales this blood
61: From cold and empty veins where no blood dwells.
64: O God, which this blood mad’st, revenge his death!
65: O Earth, which this blood drink’st, revenge his death!
67: Either heaven with lightning strike the murderer dead,
69: Or Earth gape open wide and eat him quick,
70: As thou dost swallow up this good king’s blood,
71: Which his hell-governed arm hath butcherèd.
72: Lady, you know no rules of charity,
73: Which renders good for bad, blessings for curses.
74: Villain, thou know’st nor law of God nor man.
75: No beast so fierce but knows some touch of pity.
76: But I know none, and therefore am no beast.
77: O, wonderful, when devils tell the truth!
78: More wonderful, when angels are so angry.
79: Vouchsafe, divine perfection of a woman,
80: Of these supposèd crimes to give me leave
81: By circumstance but to acquit myself.
82: Vouchsafe, defused infection of a man,
83: Of these known evils but to give me leave
84: By circumstance to curse thy cursèd self.
85: Fairer than tongue can name thee, let me have
86: Some patient leisure to excuse myself.
87: Fouler than heart can think thee, thou canst make
88: No excuse current but to hang thyself.
89: By such despair I should accuse myself.
90: And by despairing shalt thou stand excused
91: For doing worthy vengeance on thyself
92: That didst unworthy slaughter upon others.
93: Say that I slew them not.
94: Then say they were not slain.
95: But dead they are, and, devilish slave, by thee.
96: I did not kill your husband.
98: Nay, he is dead, and slain by Edward’s hands.
99: In thy foul throat thou liest. Queen Margaret saw
100: Thy murd’rous falchion smoking in his blood,
101: The which thou once didst bend against her breast,
102: But that thy brothers beat aside the point.
103: I was provokèd by her sland’rous tongue,
104: That laid their guilt upon my guiltless shoulders.
105: Thou wast provokèd by thy bloody mind,
106: That never dream’st on aught but butcheries.
107: Didst thou not kill this king?
109: Dost grant me, hedgehog? Then, God grant me too
110: Thou mayst be damnèd for that wicked deed.
111: O, he was gentle, mild, and virtuous.
112: The better for the King of heaven that hath him.
113: He is in heaven, where thou shalt never come.
114: Let him thank me, that holp to send him thither,
115: For he was fitter for that place than Earth.
116: And thou unfit for any place but hell.
117: Yes, one place else, if you will hear me name it.
120: Ill rest betide the chamber where thou liest!
121: So will it, madam, till I lie with you.
123: I know so. But, gentle Lady Anne,
124: To leave this keen encounter of our wits
125: And fall something into a slower method:
126: Is not the causer of the timeless deaths
127: Of these Plantagenets, Henry and Edward,
129: Thou wast the cause and most accursed effect.
130: Your beauty was the cause of that effect—
131: Your beauty, that did haunt me in my sleep
132: To undertake the death of all the world,
133: So I might live one hour in your sweet bosom.
134: If I thought that, I tell thee, homicide,
135: These nails should rend that beauty from my cheeks.
137: These eyes could not endure that beauty’s wrack.
138: You should not blemish it, if I stood by.
139: As all the world is cheerèd by the sun,
140: So I by that. It is my day, my life.
141: Black night o’ershade thy day, and death thy life.
142: Curse not thyself, fair creature; thou art both.
143: I would I were, to be revenged on thee.
144: It is a quarrel most unnatural
145: To be revenged on him that loveth thee.
146: It is a quarrel just and reasonable
147: To be revenged on him that killed my husband.
148: He that bereft thee, lady, of thy husband
149: Did it to help thee to a better husband.
150: His better doth not breathe upon the earth.
151: He lives that loves thee better than he could.
155: The selfsame name, but one of better nature.
157: Why dost thou spit at me?
159: Would it were mortal poison for thy sake.
160: Never came poison from so sweet a place.
161: Never hung poison on a fouler toad.
162: Out of my sight! Thou dost infect mine eyes.
163: Thine eyes, sweet lady, have infected mine.
164: Would they were basilisks’ to strike thee dead.
165: I would they were, that I might die at once,
166: For now they kill me with a living death.
167: Those eyes of thine from mine have drawn salt tears,
169: Shamed their aspects with store of childish drops.
170: These eyes, which never shed remorseful tear—
171: No, when my father York and Edward wept
172: To hear the piteous moan that Rutland made
173: When black-faced Clifford shook his sword at him;
174: Nor when thy warlike father, like a child,
175: Told the sad story of my father’s death
176: And twenty times made pause to sob and weep,
177: That all the standers-by had wet their cheeks
178: Like trees bedashed with rain—in that sad time,
179: My manly eyes did scorn an humble tear;
180: And what these sorrows could not thence exhale
181: Thy beauty hath, and made them blind with weeping.
183: I never sued to friend nor enemy;
184: My tongue could never learn sweet smoothing word.
185: But now thy beauty is proposed my fee,
186: My proud heart sues and prompts my tongue to speak.
188: Teach not thy lip such scorn, for it was made
189: For kissing, lady, not for such contempt.
190: If thy revengeful heart cannot forgive,
191: Lo, here I lend thee this sharp-pointed sword,
192: Which if thou please to hide in this true breast
193: And let the soul forth that adoreth thee,
194: I lay it naked to the deadly stroke
195: And humbly beg the death upon my knee.
196: Nay, do not pause, for I did kill King Henry—
197: But ’twas thy beauty that provokèd me.
198: Nay, now dispatch; ’twas I that stabbed young Edward—
200: But ’twas thy heavenly face that set me on.
201: Take up the sword again, or take up me.
202: Arise, dissembler. Though I wish thy death,
203: I will not be thy executioner.
204: Then bid me kill myself, and I will do it.
207: Speak it again and, even with the word,
208: This hand, which for thy love did kill thy love,
209: Shall for thy love kill a far truer love.
210: To both their deaths shalt thou be accessory.
211: I would I knew thy heart.
213: I fear me both are false.
215: Well, well, put up your sword.
216: Say then my peace is made.
218: But shall I live in hope?
219: All men I hope live so.
221: To take is not to give.
222: Look how my ring encompasseth thy finger;
223: Even so thy breast encloseth my poor heart.
224: Wear both of them, for both of them are thine.
225: And if thy poor devoted servant may
226: But beg one favor at thy gracious hand,
227: Thou dost confirm his happiness forever.
229: That it may please you leave these sad designs
230: To him that hath most cause to be a mourner,
231: And presently repair to Crosby House,
232: Where, after I have solemnly interred
233: At Chertsey monast’ry this noble king
234: And wet his grave with my repentant tears,
235: I will with all expedient duty see you.
236: For divers unknown reasons, I beseech you,
238: With all my heart, and much it joys me too
239: To see you are become so penitent.—
240: Tressel and Berkeley, go along with me.
243: But since you teach me how to flatter you,
244: Imagine I have said farewell already.
246: No, to Whitefriars. There attend my coming.
247: Was ever woman in this humor wooed?
248: Was ever woman in this humor won?
249: I’ll have her, but I will not keep her long.
250: What, I that killed her husband and his father,
251: To take her in her heart’s extremest hate,
252: With curses in her mouth, tears in her eyes,
253: The bleeding witness of my hatred by,
254: Having God, her conscience, and these bars against me,
256: And I no friends to back my suit at all
257: But the plain devil and dissembling looks?
258: And yet to win her, all the world to nothing!
260: Hath she forgot already that brave prince,
261: Edward, her lord, whom I some three months since
262: Stabbed in my angry mood at Tewkesbury?
263: A sweeter and a lovelier gentleman,
264: Framed in the prodigality of nature,
265: Young, valiant, wise, and, no doubt, right royal,
266: The spacious world cannot again afford.
267: And will she yet abase her eyes on me,
268: That cropped the golden prime of this sweet prince
269: And made her widow to a woeful bed?
270: On me, whose all not equals Edward’s moiety?
271: On me, that halts and am misshapen thus?
272: My dukedom to a beggarly denier,
273: I do mistake my person all this while!
274: Upon my life, she finds, although I cannot,
275: Myself to be a marv’lous proper man.
276: I’ll be at charges for a looking glass
277: And entertain a score or two of tailors
278: To study fashions to adorn my body.
279: Since I am crept in favor with myself,
280: I will maintain it with some little cost.
281: But first I’ll turn yon fellow in his grave
282: And then return lamenting to my love.
283: Shine out, fair sun, till I have bought a glass,
284: That I may see my shadow as I pass.

18: Here comes the lord of Buckingham, and Derby.

61: Clarence and Edward. O, what cause have I,
62: Thine being but a moiety of my moan,
63: To overgo thy woes and drown thy cries!
64: Ah, aunt, you wept not for our father’s death.
65: How can we aid you with our kindred tears?
66: Our fatherless distress was left unmoaned.
68: Give me no help in lamentation.
69: I am not barren to bring forth complaints.
70: All springs reduce their currents to mine eyes,
71: That I, being governed by the watery moon,
72: May send forth plenteous tears to drown the world.
73: Ah, for my husband, for my dear lord Edward!
74: Ah, for our father, for our dear lord Clarence!
75: Alas for both, both mine, Edward and Clarence!
76: What stay had I but Edward? And he’s gone.
77: What stay had we but Clarence? And he’s gone.
78: What stays had I but they? And they are gone.
79: Was never widow had so dear a loss.
80: Were never orphans had so dear a loss.
81: Was never mother had so dear a loss.
82: Alas, I am the mother of these griefs.
83: Their woes are parceled; mine is general.
84: She for an Edward weeps, and so do I;
85: I for a Clarence weep; so doth not she.
86: These babes for Clarence weep, and so do I;
87: I for an Edward weep; so do not they.
88: Alas, you three, on me, threefold distressed,
89: Pour all your tears. I am your sorrow’s nurse,
90: And I will pamper it with lamentation.
91: Comfort, dear mother. God is much displeased
92: That you take with unthankfulness His doing.
93: In common worldly things, ’tis called ungrateful
94: With dull unwillingness to repay a debt
95: Which with a bounteous hand was kindly lent;
96: Much more to be thus opposite with heaven,
97: For it requires the royal debt it lent you.
98: Madam, bethink you, like a careful mother,
99: Of the young prince your son. Send straight for him.
101: Let him be crowned. In him your comfort lives.
102: Drown desperate sorrow in dead Edward’s grave
103: And plant your joys in living Edward’s throne.
104: Sister, have comfort. All of us have cause
105: To wail the dimming of our shining star,
106: But none can help our harms by wailing them.—
107: Madam my mother, I do cry you mercy;
108: I did not see your Grace. Humbly on my knee
110: God bless thee, and put meekness in thy breast,
111: Love, charity, obedience, and true duty.
112: And make me die a good old man!
113: That is the butt end of a mother’s blessing;
114: I marvel that her Grace did leave it out.
115: You cloudy princes and heart-sorrowing peers
116: That bear this heavy mutual load of moan,
117: Now cheer each other in each other’s love.
118: Though we have spent our harvest of this king,
119: We are to reap the harvest of his son.
120: The broken rancor of your high-swoll’n hates,
121: But lately splintered, knit, and joined together,
122: Must gently be preserved, cherished, and kept.
123: Meseemeth good that with some little train
124: Forthwith from Ludlow the young prince be fet
125: Hither to London, to be crowned our king.
126: Why with some little train, my lord of Buckingham?
128: Marry, my lord, lest by a multitude
129: The new-healed wound of malice should break out,
130: Which would be so much the more dangerous
131: By how much the estate is green and yet ungoverned.
133: Where every horse bears his commanding rein
134: And may direct his course as please himself,
135: As well the fear of harm as harm apparent,
136: In my opinion, ought to be prevented.
137: I hope the King made peace with all of us;
138: And the compact is firm and true in me.
139: And so in me, and so, I think, in all.
140: Yet since it is but green, it should be put
141: To no apparent likelihood of breach,
142: Which haply by much company might be urged.
143: Therefore I say with noble Buckingham
144: That it is meet so few should fetch the Prince.
146: Then be it so, and go we to determine
147: Who they shall be that straight shall post to Ludlow.—
149: Madam, and you, my sister, will you go
150: To give your censures in this business?
151: My lord, whoever journeys to the Prince,
152: For God’s sake let not us two stay at home.
153: For by the way I’ll sort occasion,
154: As index to the story we late talked of,
155: To part the Queen’s proud kindred from the Prince.
156: My other self, my council’s consistory,
157: My oracle, my prophet, my dear cousin,
158: I, as a child, will go by thy direction.
159: Toward Ludlow then, for we’ll not stay behind.

1: Good morrow, neighbor, whither away so fast?
2: I promise you I scarcely know myself.
4: Yes, that the King is dead.
5: Ill news, by ’r Lady. Seldom comes the better.
6: I fear, I fear, ’twill prove a giddy world.

14: In him there is a hope of government,
15: Which, in his nonage, council under him,
16: And, in his full and ripened years, himself,

18: So stood the state when Henry the Sixth
19: Was crowned in Paris but at nine months old.
20: Stood the state so? No, no, good friends, God wot,

22: With politic grave counsel; then the King
23: Had virtuous uncles to protect his Grace.
24: Why, so hath this, both by his father and mother.

30: And the Queen’s sons and brothers haught and proud,

33: This sickly land might solace as before.

37: When great leaves fall, then winter is at hand;
38: When the sun sets, who doth not look for night?
39: Untimely storms makes men expect a dearth.

41: ’Tis more than we deserve or I expect.

44: That looks not heavily and full of dread.

47: Ensuing danger, as by proof we see
48: The water swell before a boist’rous storm.
49: But leave it all to God. Whither away?
50: Marry, we were sent for to the Justices.
51: And so was I. I’ll bear you company.

1: Last night, I hear, they lay at Stony Stratford,
2: And at Northampton they do rest tonight.
3: Tomorrow or next day they will be here.
4: I long with all my heart to see the Prince.
5: I hope he is much grown since last I saw him.
6: But I hear no; they say my son of York
7: Has almost overta’en him in his growth.
8: Ay, mother, but I would not have it so.
9: Why, my good cousin? It is good to grow.
10: Grandam, one night as we did sit at supper,
11: My uncle Rivers talked how I did grow
12: More than my brother. Ay, quoth my uncle Gloucester,
14: Small herbs have grace; great weeds do grow apace.
16: And since, methinks I would not grow so fast
17: Because sweet flowers are slow and weeds make haste.
19: Good faith, good faith, the saying did not hold
20: In him that did object the same to thee!
21: He was the wretched’st thing when he was young,
22: So long a-growing and so leisurely,
23: That if his rule were true, he should be gracious.
24: And so no doubt he is, my gracious madam.
25: I hope he is, but yet let mothers doubt.
26: Now, by my troth, if I had been remembered,
27: I could have given my uncle’s Grace a flout
28: To touch his growth nearer than he touched mine.
29: How, my young York? I prithee let me hear it.

33: Grandam, this would have been a biting jest.

37: If ’twere not she, I cannot tell who told me.

39: Good madam, be not angry with the child.
42: Such news, my lord, as grieves me to report.
46: Lord Rivers and Lord Grey are sent to Pomfret,
47: And, with them, Sir Thomas Vaughan, prisoners.
49: The mighty dukes, Gloucester and Buckingham.
51: The sum of all I can, I have disclosed.
52: Why, or for what, the nobles were committed
53: Is all unknown to me, my gracious lord.
54: Ay me! I see the ruin of my house.
55: The tiger now hath seized the gentle hind.
57: Upon the innocent and aweless throne.
59: I see, as in a map, the end of all.
61: How many of you have mine eyes beheld?
62: My husband lost his life to get the crown,
63: And often up and down my sons were tossed
64: For me to joy, and weep, their gain and loss.
65: And being seated, and domestic broils
67: Make war upon themselves, brother to brother,
68: Blood to blood, self against self. O, preposterous
69: And frantic outrage, end thy damnèd spleen,
70: Or let me die, to look on Earth no more.

73: Stay, I will go with you.
76: And thither bear your treasure and your goods.

78: The seal I keep; and so betide to me
79: As well I tender you and all of yours.

1: Welcome, sweet prince, to London, to your chamber.
2: Welcome, dear cousin, my thoughts’ sovereign.
3: The weary way hath made you melancholy.
4: No, uncle, but our crosses on the way
5: Have made it tedious, wearisome, and heavy.
6: I want more uncles here to welcome me.
7: Sweet prince, the untainted virtue of your years
8: Hath not yet dived into the world’s deceit;
9: Nor more can you distinguish of a man
10: Than of his outward show, which, God He knows,
11: Seldom or never jumpeth with the heart.
12: Those uncles which you want were dangerous.
13: Your Grace attended to their sugared words
14: But looked not on the poison of their hearts.
15: God keep you from them, and from such false friends.
17: God keep me from false friends, but they were none.
18: My lord, the Mayor of London comes to greet you.
19: God bless your Grace with health and happy days.
20: I thank you, good my lord, and thank you all.—
21: I thought my mother and my brother York
22: Would long ere this have met us on the way.
23: Fie, what a slug is Hastings that he comes not
24: To tell us whether they will come or no!
25: And in good time here comes the sweating lord.
26: Welcome, my lord. What, will our mother come?
27: On what occasion God He knows, not I,
28: The Queen your mother and your brother York
29: Have taken sanctuary. The tender prince
30: Would fain have come with me to meet your Grace,
31: But by his mother was perforce withheld.
32: Fie, what an indirect and peevish course
33: Is this of hers!—Lord Cardinal, will your Grace
34: Persuade the Queen to send the Duke of York
36: If she deny, Lord Hastings, go with him,
37: And from her jealous arms pluck him perforce.
38: My lord of Buckingham, if my weak oratory
39: Can from his mother win the Duke of York,
40: Anon expect him here; but if she be obdurate
41: To mild entreaties, God in heaven forbid
42: We should infringe the holy privilege
43: Of blessèd sanctuary! Not for all this land
44: Would I be guilty of so deep a sin.
45: You are too senseless obstinate, my lord,
47: Weigh it but with the grossness of this age,
48: You break not sanctuary in seizing him.
49: The benefit thereof is always granted
50: To those whose dealings have deserved the place
51: And those who have the wit to claim the place.
52: This prince hath neither claimed it nor deserved it
53: And therefore, in mine opinion, cannot have it.
54: Then taking him from thence that is not there,
55: You break no privilege nor charter there.
56: Oft have I heard of sanctuary men,
57: But sanctuary children, never till now.
58: My lord, you shall o’errule my mind for once.—
59: Come on, Lord Hastings, will you go with me?
61: Good lords, make all the speedy haste you may.
62: Say, uncle Gloucester, if our brother come,
63: Where shall we sojourn till our coronation?
64: Where it seems best unto your royal self.
65: If I may counsel you, some day or two
66: Your Highness shall repose you at the Tower;
67: Then where you please and shall be thought most fit
68: For your best health and recreation.
69: I do not like the Tower, of any place.—
70: Did Julius Caesar build that place, my lord?
71: He did, my gracious lord, begin that place,
72: Which, since, succeeding ages have re-edified.
73: Is it upon record, or else reported
74: Successively from age to age, he built it?
76: But say, my lord, it were not registered,
77: Methinks the truth should live from age to age,
79: Even to the general all-ending day.
80: So wise so young, they say, do never live long.
82: I say, without characters fame lives long.
83: Thus, like the formal Vice, Iniquity,
84: I moralize two meanings in one word.
85: That Julius Caesar was a famous man.
86: With what his valor did enrich his wit,
87: His wit set down to make his valor live.
88: Death makes no conquest of this conqueror,
89: For now he lives in fame, though not in life.
90: I’ll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham—
92: An if I live until I be a man,
93: I’ll win our ancient right in France again
94: Or die a soldier, as I lived a king.
95: Short summers lightly have a forward spring.
96: Now in good time here comes the Duke of York.
97: Richard of York, how fares our loving brother?
98: Well, my dread lord—so must I call you now.
99: Ay, brother, to our grief, as it is yours.
100: Too late he died that might have kept that title,
101: Which by his death hath lost much majesty.
102: How fares our cousin, noble lord of York?
103: I thank you, gentle uncle. O my lord,
104: You said that idle weeds are fast in growth.
105: The Prince my brother hath outgrown me far.
108: O my fair cousin, I must not say so.
109: Then he is more beholding to you than I.
110: He may command me as my sovereign,
111: But you have power in me as in a kinsman.
112: I pray you, uncle, give me this dagger.
113: My dagger, little cousin? With all my heart.
115: Of my kind uncle, that I know will give,
116: And being but a toy, which is no grief to give.
117: A greater gift than that I’ll give my cousin.
118: A greater gift? O, that’s the sword to it.
119: Ay, gentle cousin, were it light enough.
120: O, then I see you will part but with light gifts.
121: In weightier things you’ll say a beggar nay.
122: It is too heavy for your Grace to wear.
123: I weigh it lightly, were it heavier.
124: What, would you have my weapon, little lord?
125: I would, that I might thank you as you call me.
128: My lord of York will still be cross in talk.
129: Uncle, your Grace knows how to bear with him.
130: You mean, to bear me, not to bear with me.—
131: Uncle, my brother mocks both you and me.
132: Because that I am little, like an ape,
133: He thinks that you should bear me on your shoulders.
135: With what a sharp-provided wit he reasons!
136: To mitigate the scorn he gives his uncle,
137: He prettily and aptly taunts himself.
138: So cunning and so young is wonderful.
139: My lord, will ’t please you pass along?
140: Myself and my good cousin Buckingham
141: Will to your mother, to entreat of her
142: To meet you at the Tower and welcome you.
143: What, will you go unto the Tower, my lord?
144: My Lord Protector needs will have it so.
145: I shall not sleep in quiet at the Tower.
147: Marry, my uncle Clarence’ angry ghost.
148: My grandam told me he was murdered there.
150: Nor none that live, I hope.
151: An if they live, I hope I need not fear.
152: But come, my lord. With a heavy heart,
153: Thinking on them, go I unto the Tower.
154: Think you, my lord, this little prating York
155: Was not incensèd by his subtle mother
156: To taunt and scorn you thus opprobriously?
157: No doubt, no doubt. O, ’tis a parlous boy,
159: He is all the mother’s, from the top to toe.
160: Well, let them rest.—Come hither, Catesby.
161: Thou art sworn as deeply to effect what we intend
162: As closely to conceal what we impart.
163: Thou knowest our reasons, urged upon the way.
164: What thinkest thou? Is it not an easy matter
165: To make William Lord Hastings of our mind
166: For the installment of this noble duke
167: In the seat royal of this famous isle?
168: He, for his father’s sake, so loves the Prince
169: That he will not be won to aught against him.
170: What think’st thou then of Stanley? Will not he?
171: He will do all in all as Hastings doth.
172: Well then, no more but this: go, gentle Catesby,
173: And, as it were far off, sound thou Lord Hastings
174: How he doth stand affected to our purpose
175: And summon him tomorrow to the Tower
177: If thou dost find him tractable to us,
178: Encourage him and tell him all our reasons.
179: If he be leaden, icy, cold, unwilling,
180: Be thou so too, and so break off the talk,
181: And give us notice of his inclination;
182: For we tomorrow hold divided councils,
183: Wherein thyself shalt highly be employed.
184: Commend me to Lord William. Tell him, Catesby,
185: His ancient knot of dangerous adversaries
186: Tomorrow are let blood at Pomfret Castle,
187: And bid my lord, for joy of this good news,
188: Give Mistress Shore one gentle kiss the more.
189: Good Catesby, go effect this business soundly.
190: My good lords both, with all the heed I can.
191: Shall we hear from you, Catesby, ere we sleep?
193: At Crosby House, there shall you find us both.
194: Now, my lord, what shall we do if we perceive
195: Lord Hastings will not yield to our complots?
196: Chop off his head. Something we will determine.
197: And look when I am king, claim thou of me
198: The earldom of Hereford, and all the movables
199: Whereof the King my brother was possessed.
200: I’ll claim that promise at your Grace’s hand.
201: And look to have it yielded with all kindness.
202: Come, let us sup betimes, that afterwards
203: We may digest our complots in some form.

6: Cannot my Lord Stanley sleep these tedious nights?
7: So it appears by that I have to say.
8: First, he commends him to your noble self.

11: He dreamt the boar had razèd off his helm.

18: And with all speed post with him toward the north

21: Bid him not fear the separated council.

23: And at the other is my good friend Catesby,
24: Where nothing can proceed that toucheth us
25: Whereof I shall not have intelligence.

28: To trust the mock’ry of unquiet slumbers.

30: Were to incense the boar to follow us

33: And we will both together to the Tower,

38: What news, what news in this our tott’ring state?
39: It is a reeling world indeed, my lord,
40: And I believe will never stand upright
41: Till Richard wear the garland of the realm.

45: I’ll have this crown of mine cut from my shoulders
46: Before I’ll see the crown so foul misplaced.

57: God knows I will not do it, to the death.
58: God keep your Lordship in that gracious mind.
59: But I shall laugh at this a twelve-month hence,
60: That they which brought me in my master’s hate,
61: I live to look upon their tragedy.

63: I’ll send some packing that yet think not on ’t.

65: When men are unprepared and look not for it.
66: O monstrous, monstrous! And so falls it out
67: With Rivers, Vaughan, Grey; and so ’twill do
68: With some men else that think themselves as safe
69: As thou and I, who, as thou know’st, are dear
70: To princely Richard and to Buckingham.

72: For they account his head upon the Bridge.

74: Come on, come on. Where is your boar-spear, man?
75: Fear you the boar and go so unprovided?
76: My lord, good morrow.—Good morrow, Catesby.—
77: You may jest on, but, by the Holy Rood,
78: I do not like these several councils, I.

80: And never in my days, I do protest,
81: Was it so precious to me as ’tis now.
82: Think you but that I know our state secure,
83: I would be so triumphant as I am?

85: Were jocund and supposed their states were sure,
86: And they indeed had no cause to mistrust;
87: But yet you see how soon the day o’ercast.
88: This sudden stab of rancor I misdoubt.
89: Pray God, I say, I prove a needless coward!
90: What, shall we toward the Tower? The day is spent.
91: Come, come. Have with you. Wot you what, my lord?
92: Today the lords you talked of are beheaded.
93: They, for their truth, might better wear their heads
94: Than some that have accused them wear their hats.
95: But come, my lord, let’s away.

98: The better that your Lordship please to ask.
99: I tell thee, man, ’tis better with me now
100: Than when thou met’st me last where now we meet.
101: Then was I going prisoner to the Tower
102: By the suggestion of the Queen’s allies.
103: But now, I tell thee—keep it to thyself—
104: This day those enemies are put to death,
105: And I in better state than e’er I was.
106: God hold it, to your Honor’s good content!
107: Gramercy, fellow. There, drink that for me.
109: Well met, my lord. I am glad to see your Honor.
110: I thank thee, good Sir John, with all my heart.

112: Come the next sabbath, and I will content you.

115: Your friends at Pomfret, they do need the priest;
116: Your Honor hath no shriving work in hand.
117: Good faith, and when I met this holy man,
118: The men you talk of came into my mind.

120: I do, my lord, but long I cannot stay there.
121: I shall return before your Lordship thence.
122: Nay, like enough, for I stay dinner there.

1: Sir Richard Ratcliffe, let me tell thee this:
2: Today shalt thou behold a subject die
3: For truth, for duty, and for loyalty.
4: God bless the Prince from all the pack of you!
5: A knot you are of damnèd bloodsuckers.
6: You live that shall cry woe for this hereafter.
7: Dispatch. The limit of your lives is out.
8: O Pomfret, Pomfret! O thou bloody prison,
9: Fatal and ominous to noble peers!
10: Within the guilty closure of thy walls,
11: Richard the Second here was hacked to death,
12: And, for more slander to thy dismal seat,
13: We give to thee our guiltless blood to drink.
14: Now Margaret’s curse is fall’n upon our heads,
15: When she exclaimed on Hastings, you, and I,
16: For standing by when Richard stabbed her son.
17: Then cursed she Richard. Then cursed she Buckingham.
19: Then cursed she Hastings. O, remember, God,
20: To hear her prayer for them as now for us!
21: And for my sister and her princely sons,
22: Be satisfied, dear God, with our true blood,
23: Which, as thou know’st, unjustly must be spilt.
24: Make haste. The hour of death is expiate.
25: Come, Grey. Come, Vaughan. Let us here embrace.
26: Farewell until we meet again in heaven.

1: Now, noble peers, the cause why we are met
2: Is to determine of the coronation.
3: In God’s name, speak. When is the royal day?
4: Is all things ready for the royal time?
5: It is, and wants but nomination.
6: Tomorrow, then, I judge a happy day.
7: Who knows the Lord Protector’s mind herein?
8: Who is most inward with the noble duke?
9: Your Grace, we think, should soonest know his mind.
11: We know each other’s faces; for our hearts,
12: He knows no more of mine than I of yours,
13: Or I of his, my lord, than you of mine.—
14: Lord Hastings, you and he are near in love.
15: I thank his Grace, I know he loves me well.
16: But for his purpose in the coronation,
17: I have not sounded him, nor he delivered
18: His gracious pleasure any way therein.
19: But you, my honorable lords, may name the time,
20: And in the Duke’s behalf I’ll give my voice,
21: Which I presume he’ll take in gentle part.
22: In happy time here comes the Duke himself.

142: When did the tiger’s young ones teach the dam?
143: O, do not learn her wrath; she taught it thee.
144: The milk thou suck’st from her did turn to marble.
145: Even at thy teat thou hadst thy tyranny.
146: Yet every mother breeds not sons alike.
147: Do thou entreat her show a woman’s pity.
148: What, wouldst thou have me prove myself a bastard?
149: ’Tis true; the raven doth not hatch a lark.
150: Yet have I heard—O, could I find it now!—
151: The lion, moved with pity, did endure
152: To have his princely paws pared all away.
153: Some say that ravens foster forlorn children,
154: The whilst their own birds famish in their nests.
155: O, be to me, though thy hard heart say no,
156: Nothing so kind, but something pitiful.
157: I know not what it means.—Away with her.
158: O, let me teach thee! For my father’s sake,
159: That gave thee life when well he might have slain thee,
160: Be not obdurate; open thy deaf ears.
161: Hadst thou in person ne’er offended me,
162: Even for his sake am I pitiless.—
163: Remember, boys, I poured forth tears in vain
164: To save your brother from the sacrifice,
165: But fierce Andronicus would not relent.
166: Therefore away with her, and use her as you will;
167: The worse to her, the better loved of me.
168: O Tamora, be called a gentle queen,
169: And with thine own hands kill me in this place!
170: For ’tis not life that I have begged so long;
171: Poor I was slain when Bassianus died.
172: What begg’st thou, then? Fond woman, let me go!
173: ’Tis present death I beg, and one thing more
174: That womanhood denies my tongue to tell.
175: O, keep me from their worse-than-killing lust,
176: And tumble me into some loathsome pit
177: Where never man’s eye may behold my body.
178: Do this, and be a charitable murderer.
179: So should I rob my sweet sons of their fee.
180: No, let them satisfy their lust on thee.
181: Away, for thou hast stayed us here too long!
182: No grace, no womanhood? Ah, beastly creature,
183: The blot and enemy to our general name,
185: Nay, then, I’ll stop your mouth.—Bring thou her husband.
187: This is the hole where Aaron bid us hide him.
188: Farewell, my sons. See that you make her sure.
189: Ne’er let my heart know merry cheer indeed
190: Till all the Andronici be made away.
191: Now will I hence to seek my lovely Moor,
192: And let my spleenful sons this trull deflower.
193: Come on, my lords, the better foot before.
194: Straight will I bring you to the loathsome pit
195: Where I espied the panther fast asleep.
196: My sight is very dull, whate’er it bodes.
197: And mine, I promise you. Were it not for shame,
198: Well could I leave our sport to sleep awhile.
199: What, art thou fallen? What subtle hole is this,
200: Whose mouth is covered with rude-growing briers
201: Upon whose leaves are drops of new-shed blood
202: As fresh as morning dew distilled on flowers?
203: A very fatal place it seems to me.
204: Speak, brother! Hast thou hurt thee with the fall?
205: O, brother, with the dismal’st object hurt
206: That ever eye with sight made heart lament!
207: Now will I fetch the King to find them here,
208: That he thereby may have a likely guess
209: How these were they that made away his brother.
210: Why dost not comfort me and help me out
211: From this unhallowed and bloodstainèd hole?
212: I am surprisèd with an uncouth fear.
213: A chilling sweat o’erruns my trembling joints.
214: My heart suspects more than mine eye can see.
215: To prove thou hast a true-divining heart,
216: Aaron and thou look down into this den
217: And see a fearful sight of blood and death.
218: Aaron is gone, and my compassionate heart
219: Will not permit mine eyes once to behold
220: The thing whereat it trembles by surmise.
221: O, tell me who it is, for ne’er till now
222: Was I a child to fear I know not what.
223: Lord Bassianus lies berayed in blood,
224: All on a heap, like to a slaughtered lamb,
225: In this detested, dark, blood-drinking pit.
226: If it be dark, how dost thou know ’tis he?
227: Upon his bloody finger he doth wear
228: A precious ring that lightens all this hole,
229: Which like a taper in some monument
230: Doth shine upon the dead man’s earthy cheeks
231: And shows the ragged entrails of this pit.
232: So pale did shine the moon on Pyramus
233: When he by night lay bathed in maiden blood.
234: O, brother, help me with thy fainting hand—
235: If fear hath made thee faint as me it hath—
236: Out of this fell devouring receptacle,
237: As hateful as Cocytus’ misty mouth.
238: Reach me thy hand, that I may help thee out,
239: Or, wanting strength to do thee so much good,
240: I may be plucked into the swallowing womb
241: Of this deep pit, poor Bassianus’ grave.
242: I have no strength to pluck thee to the brink.
243: Nor I no strength to climb without thy help.
244: Thy hand once more. I will not loose again
245: Till thou art here aloft or I below.
246: Thou canst not come to me. I come to thee.
247: Along with me! I’ll see what hole is here
248: And what he is that now is leapt into it.—
249: Say, who art thou that lately didst descend
250: Into this gaping hollow of the earth?
251: The unhappy sons of old Andronicus,
252: Brought hither in a most unlucky hour
253: To find thy brother Bassianus dead.
254: My brother dead! I know thou dost but jest.
255: He and his lady both are at the lodge
256: Upon the north side of this pleasant chase.
257: ’Tis not an hour since I left them there.
258: We know not where you left them all alive,
259: But, out alas, here have we found him dead.
260: Where is my lord the King?
261: Here, Tamora, though grieved with killing grief.
263: Now to the bottom dost thou search my wound.
265: Then all too late I bring this fatal writ,
266: The complot of this timeless tragedy,
267: And wonder greatly that man’s face can fold
268: In pleasing smiles such murderous tyranny.
269: An if we miss to meet him handsomely,
271: Do thou so much as dig the grave for him;
272: Thou know’st our meaning. Look for thy reward
273: Among the nettles at the elder tree
274: Which overshades the mouth of that same pit
275: Where we decreed to bury Bassianus.
276: Do this, and purchase us thy lasting friends.
277: O Tamora, was ever heard the like?
278: This is the pit, and this the elder tree.—
279: Look, sirs, if you can find the huntsman out
280: That should have murdered Bassianus here.
281: My gracious lord, here is the bag of gold.
282: Two of thy whelps, fell curs of bloody kind,
283: Have here bereft my brother of his life.—
284: Sirs, drag them from the pit unto the prison.
285: There let them bide until we have devised
286: Some never-heard-of torturing pain for them.
287: What, are they in this pit? O wondrous thing!
289: High Emperor, upon my feeble knee
290: I beg this boon with tears not lightly shed,
291: That this fell fault of my accursèd sons—
292: Accursèd if the faults be proved in them—
293: If it be proved! You see it is apparent.
294: Who found this letter? Tamora, was it you?
295: Andronicus himself did take it up.
296: I did, my lord, yet let me be their bail,
297: For by my father’s reverend tomb I vow
298: They shall be ready at your Highness’ will
299: To answer their suspicion with their lives.
300: Thou shalt not bail them. See thou follow me.—
301: Some bring the murdered body, some the murderers.
302: Let them not speak a word. The guilt is plain.
303: For, by my soul, were there worse end than death,
304: That end upon them should be executed.
305: Andronicus, I will entreat the King.
306: Fear not thy sons; they shall do well enough.
307: Come, Lucius, come. Stay not to talk with them.

1: So, now go tell, an if thy tongue can speak,
2: Who ’twas that cut thy tongue and ravished thee.
3: Write down thy mind; bewray thy meaning so,
4: An if thy stumps will let thee play the scribe.
5: See how with signs and tokens she can scrowl.
6: Go home. Call for sweet water; wash thy hands.
7: She hath no tongue to call, nor hands to wash;
8: And so let’s leave her to her silent walks.
9: An ’twere my cause, I should go hang myself.
10: If thou hadst hands to help thee knit the cord.
11: Who is this? My niece, that flies away so fast?—
12: Cousin, a word. Where is your husband?
13: If I do dream, would all my wealth would wake me.
14: If I do wake, some planet strike me down
15: That I may slumber an eternal sleep.
16: Speak, gentle niece. What stern ungentle hands
17: Hath lopped and hewed and made thy body bare
18: Of her two branches, those sweet ornaments
19: Whose circling shadows kings have sought to sleep in,
20: And might not gain so great a happiness
21: As half thy love? Why dost not speak to me?
22: Alas, a crimson river of warm blood,
23: Like to a bubbling fountain stirred with wind,
24: Doth rise and fall between thy rosèd lips,
25: Coming and going with thy honey breath.
26: But sure some Tereus hath deflowered thee,
27: And lest thou shouldst detect him cut thy tongue.
28: Ah, now thou turn’st away thy face for shame,
29: And notwithstanding all this loss of blood,
30: As from a conduit with three issuing spouts,
31: Yet do thy cheeks look red as Titan’s face,
32: Blushing to be encountered with a cloud.
33: Shall I speak for thee, shall I say ’tis so?
34: O, that I knew thy heart, and knew the beast,
35: That I might rail at him to ease my mind.
36: Sorrow concealèd, like an oven stopped,
37: Doth burn the heart to cinders where it is.
38: Fair Philomela, why she but lost her tongue,
39: And in a tedious sampler sewed her mind;
40: But, lovely niece, that mean is cut from thee.
41: A craftier Tereus, cousin, hast thou met,
42: And he hath cut those pretty fingers off
43: That could have better sewed than Philomel.
44: O, had the monster seen those lily hands
45: Tremble like aspen leaves upon a lute
46: And make the silken strings delight to kiss them,
47: He would not then have touched them for his life.
48: Or had he heard the heavenly harmony
49: Which that sweet tongue hath made,
50: He would have dropped his knife and fell asleep,
51: As Cerberus at the Thracian poet’s feet.
52: Come, let us go and make thy father blind,
53: For such a sight will blind a father’s eye.
54: One hour’s storm will drown the fragrant meads;
55: What will whole months of tears thy father’s eyes?
56: Do not draw back, for we will mourn with thee.
57: O, could our mourning ease thy misery!

1: Hear me, grave fathers; noble tribunes, stay.
2: For pity of mine age, whose youth was spent
3: In dangerous wars whilst you securely slept;
4: For all my blood in Rome’s great quarrel shed,
5: For all the frosty nights that I have watched,
6: And for these bitter tears which now you see,
7: Filling the agèd wrinkles in my cheeks,
8: Be pitiful to my condemnèd sons,
9: Whose souls is not corrupted as ’tis thought.
10: For two-and-twenty sons I never wept
11: Because they died in honor’s lofty bed.
12: For these, tribunes, in the dust I write
13: My heart’s deep languor and my soul’s sad tears.
14: Let my tears stanch the earth’s dry appetite.
15: My sons’ sweet blood will make it shame and blush.
16: O Earth, I will befriend thee more with rain
17: That shall distil from these two ancient ruins
18: Than youthful April shall with all his showers.
19: In summer’s drought I’ll drop upon thee still;
20: In winter with warm tears I’ll melt the snow
21: And keep eternal springtime on thy face,
22: So thou refuse to drink my dear sons’ blood.
23: O reverend tribunes, O gentle agèd men,
24: Unbind my sons, reverse the doom of death,
25: And let me say, that never wept before,
26: My tears are now prevailing orators.
27: O noble father, you lament in vain.
28: The Tribunes hear you not; no man is by,
29: And you recount your sorrows to a stone.
30: Ah, Lucius, for thy brothers let me plead.—
31: Grave tribunes, once more I entreat of you—
32: My gracious lord, no tribune hears you speak.
33: Why, ’tis no matter, man. If they did hear,
34: They would not mark me; if they did mark,
35: They would not pity me. Yet plead I must,
37: Therefore I tell my sorrows to the stones,
38: Who, though they cannot answer my distress,
39: Yet in some sort they are better than the Tribunes,
40: For that they will not intercept my tale.
41: When I do weep, they humbly at my feet
42: Receive my tears and seem to weep with me,
43: And were they but attirèd in grave weeds,
44: Rome could afford no tribunes like to these.
45: A stone is soft as wax, tribunes more hard than stones;
47: A stone is silent and offendeth not,
48: And tribunes with their tongues doom men to death.
49: But wherefore stand’st thou with thy weapon drawn?
50: To rescue my two brothers from their death,
51: For which attempt the Judges have pronounced
53: O happy man, they have befriended thee!
54: Why, foolish Lucius, dost thou not perceive
55: That Rome is but a wilderness of tigers?
56: Tigers must prey, and Rome affords no prey
57: But me and mine. How happy art thou then
58: From these devourers to be banishèd.
59: But who comes with our brother Marcus here?
60: Titus, prepare thy agèd eyes to weep,
61: Or, if not so, thy noble heart to break.
62: I bring consuming sorrow to thine age.
63: Will it consume me? Let me see it, then.
66: Ay me, this object kills me!
67: Faint-hearted boy, arise and look upon her.—
69: Hath made thee handless in thy father’s sight?
70: What fool hath added water to the sea
71: Or brought a faggot to bright-burning Troy?
72: My grief was at the height before thou cam’st,
73: And now like Nilus it disdaineth bounds.—
74: Give me a sword. I’ll chop off my hands too,
75: For they have fought for Rome and all in vain;
76: And they have nursed this woe in feeding life;
77: In bootless prayer have they been held up,
78: And they have served me to effectless use.
79: Now all the service I require of them
80: Is that the one will help to cut the other.—
81: ’Tis well, Lavinia, that thou hast no hands,
82: For hands to do Rome service is but vain.
83: Speak, gentle sister. Who hath martyred thee?
84: O, that delightful engine of her thoughts,
85: That blabbed them with such pleasing eloquence,
86: Is torn from forth that pretty hollow cage
87: Where, like a sweet melodious bird, it sung
88: Sweet varied notes, enchanting every ear.
89: O, say thou for her who hath done this deed!
90: O, thus I found her straying in the park,
91: Seeking to hide herself as doth the deer
92: That hath received some unrecuring wound.
93: It was my dear, and he that wounded her
94: Hath hurt me more than had he killed me dead.
95: For now I stand as one upon a rock,
96: Environed with a wilderness of sea,
97: Who marks the waxing tide grow wave by wave,
98: Expecting ever when some envious surge
99: Will in his brinish bowels swallow him.
100: This way to death my wretched sons are gone;
101: Here stands my other son a banished man,
102: And here my brother, weeping at my woes.
103: But that which gives my soul the greatest spurn
104: Is dear Lavinia, dearer than my soul.
105: Had I but seen thy picture in this plight
106: It would have madded me. What shall I do,
107: Now I behold thy lively body so?
108: Thou hast no hands to wipe away thy tears,
109: Nor tongue to tell me who hath martyred thee.
110: Thy husband he is dead, and for his death
111: Thy brothers are condemned, and dead by this.—
112: Look, Marcus!—Ah, son Lucius, look on her!
113: When I did name her brothers, then fresh tears
114: Stood on her cheeks as doth the honeydew
115: Upon a gathered lily almost withered.
116: Perchance she weeps because they killed her husband,
117: Perchance because she knows them innocent.
118: If they did kill thy husband, then be joyful,
119: Because the law hath ta’en revenge on them.—
120: No, no, they would not do so foul a deed.
121: Witness the sorrow that their sister makes.—
122: Gentle Lavinia, let me kiss thy lips,
123: Or make some sign how I may do thee ease.
124: Shall thy good uncle and thy brother Lucius
125: And thou and I sit round about some fountain,
126: Looking all downwards to behold our cheeks,
127: How they are stained like meadows yet not dry
128: With miry slime left on them by a flood?
129: And in the fountain shall we gaze so long
130: Till the fresh taste be taken from that clearness
131: And made a brine pit with our bitter tears?
132: Or shall we cut away our hands like thine?
133: Or shall we bite our tongues and in dumb shows
134: Pass the remainder of our hateful days?
135: What shall we do? Let us that have our tongues
136: Plot some device of further misery
137: To make us wondered at in time to come.
138: Sweet father, cease your tears, for at your grief
139: See how my wretched sister sobs and weeps.
140: Patience, dear niece.—Good Titus, dry thine eyes.
141: Ah, Marcus, Marcus! Brother, well I wot
142: Thy napkin cannot drink a tear of mine,
143: For thou, poor man, hast drowned it with thine own.
144: Ah, my Lavinia, I will wipe thy cheeks.
145: Mark, Marcus, mark. I understand her signs.
146: Had she a tongue to speak, now would she say
147: That to her brother which I said to thee.
148: His napkin, with his true tears all bewet,
149: Can do no service on her sorrowful cheeks.
150: O, what a sympathy of woe is this,
151: As far from help as limbo is from bliss.
152: Titus Andronicus, my lord the Emperor
153: Sends thee this word, that if thou love thy sons,
154: Let Marcus, Lucius, or thyself, old Titus,
155: Or any one of you, chop off your hand
156: And send it to the King; he for the same
157: Will send thee hither both thy sons alive,
158: And that shall be the ransom for their fault.
159: O gracious emperor! O gentle Aaron!
160: Did ever raven sing so like a lark,
161: That gives sweet tidings of the sun’s uprise?
162: With all my heart I’ll send the Emperor my hand.
163: Good Aaron, wilt thou help to chop it off?
164: Stay, father, for that noble hand of thine,
165: That hath thrown down so many enemies,
166: Shall not be sent. My hand will serve the turn.
167: My youth can better spare my blood than you,
168: And therefore mine shall save my brothers’ lives.
169: Which of your hands hath not defended Rome
170: And reared aloft the bloody battleax,
171: Writing destruction on the enemy’s castle?
172: O, none of both but are of high desert.
173: My hand hath been but idle; let it serve
174: To ransom my two nephews from their death.
175: Then have I kept it to a worthy end.
176: Nay, come, agree whose hand shall go along,
177: For fear they die before their pardon come.
179: By heaven, it shall not go!
180: Sirs, strive no more. Such withered herbs as these
181: Are meet for plucking up, and therefore mine.
182: Sweet father, if I shall be thought thy son,
183: Let me redeem my brothers both from death.
184: And for our father’s sake and mother’s care,
185: Now let me show a brother’s love to thee.
186: Agree between you. I will spare my hand.
187: Then I’ll go fetch an ax.
188: But I will use the ax.
189: Come hither, Aaron. I’ll deceive them both.
190: Lend me thy hand, and I will give thee mine.
191: If that be called deceit, I will be honest
192: And never whilst I live deceive men so.
193: But I’ll deceive you in another sort,
194: And that you’ll say ere half an hour pass.
195: Now stay your strife. What shall be is dispatched.—
196: Good Aaron, give his Majesty my hand.
197: Tell him it was a hand that warded him
198: From thousand dangers. Bid him bury it.
199: More hath it merited; that let it have.
200: As for my sons, say I account of them
201: As jewels purchased at an easy price,
202: And yet dear, too, because I bought mine own.
203: I go, Andronicus, and for thy hand
204: Look by and by to have thy sons with thee.
205: Their heads, I mean. O, how this villainy
206: Doth fat me with the very thoughts of it!
207: Let fools do good and fair men call for grace;
208: Aaron will have his soul black like his face.
209: O, here I lift this one hand up to heaven,
210: And bow this feeble ruin to the earth.
211: If any power pities wretched tears,
212: What, wouldst thou kneel with me?
214: Do, then, dear heart, for heaven shall hear our prayers,
216: Or with our sighs we’ll breathe the welkin dim
217: And stain the sun with fog, as sometime clouds
218: When they do hug him in their melting bosoms.
220: And do not break into these deep extremes.
221: Is not my sorrow deep, having no bottom?
222: Then be my passions bottomless with them.
223: But yet let reason govern thy lament.
224: If there were reason for these miseries,
225: Then into limits could I bind my woes.
226: When heaven doth weep, doth not the Earth o’erflow?
227: If the winds rage, doth not the sea wax mad,
228: Threat’ning the welkin with his big-swoll’n face?
229: And wilt thou have a reason for this coil?
230: I am the sea. Hark how her sighs doth flow!
231: She is the weeping welkin, I the Earth.
232: Then must my sea be movèd with her sighs;
233: Then must my Earth with her continual tears
234: Become a deluge, overflowed and drowned,
235: Forwhy my bowels cannot hide her woes
236: But like a drunkard must I vomit them.
237: Then give me leave, for losers will have leave
238: To ease their stomachs with their bitter tongues.
239: Worthy Andronicus, ill art thou repaid
240: For that good hand thou sent’st the Emperor.
241: Here are the heads of thy two noble sons,
242: And here’s thy hand in scorn to thee sent back.
243: Thy grief their sports, thy resolution mocked,
244: That woe is me to think upon thy woes
245: More than remembrance of my father’s death.
246: Now let hot Etna cool in Sicily,
247: And be my heart an everburning hell!
248: These miseries are more than may be borne.
249: To weep with them that weep doth ease some deal,
250: But sorrow flouted at is double death.
251: Ah, that this sight should make so deep a wound
252: And yet detested life not shrink thereat!
253: That ever death should let life bear his name,
254: Where life hath no more interest but to breathe.
255: Alas, poor heart, that kiss is comfortless
256: As frozen water to a starvèd snake.
257: When will this fearful slumber have an end?
259: Thou dost not slumber. See thy two sons’ heads,
260: Thy warlike hand, thy mangled daughter here,
261: Thy other banished son with this dear sight
262: Struck pale and bloodless; and thy brother, I,
263: Even like a stony image cold and numb.
264: Ah, now no more will I control thy griefs.
265: Rent off thy silver hair, thy other hand,
266: Gnawing with thy teeth, and be this dismal sight
267: The closing up of our most wretched eyes.
268: Now is a time to storm. Why art thou still?
270: Why dost thou laugh? It fits not with this hour.
271: Why, I have not another tear to shed.
272: Besides, this sorrow is an enemy
273: And would usurp upon my wat’ry eyes
274: And make them blind with tributary tears.
275: Then which way shall I find Revenge’s cave?
276: For these two heads do seem to speak to me
277: And threat me I shall never come to bliss
278: Till all these mischiefs be returned again
279: Even in their throats that hath committed them.
280: Come, let me see what task I have to do.
281: You heavy people, circle me about
282: That I may turn me to each one of you
283: And swear unto my soul to right your wrongs.
284: The vow is made. Come, brother, take a head,
285: And in this hand the other will I bear.—
286: And, Lavinia, thou shalt be employed in these arms.
287: Bear thou my hand, sweet wench, between thy teeth.—
289: As for thee, boy, go get thee from my sight.
290: Thou art an exile, and thou must not stay.
291: Hie to the Goths and raise an army there.
292: And if you love me, as I think you do,
293: Let’s kiss and part, for we have much to do.
295: The woefull’st man that ever lived in Rome.
296: Farewell, proud Rome, till Lucius come again.
297: He loves his pledges dearer than his life.
299: O, would thou wert as thou tofore hast been!
300: But now nor Lucius nor Lavinia lives
301: But in oblivion and hateful griefs.
302: If Lucius live he will requite your wrongs
303: And make proud Saturnine and his empress
304: Beg at the gates like Tarquin and his queen.
305: Now will I to the Goths and raise a power
306: To be revenged on Rome and Saturnine.

1: So, so. Now sit, and look you eat no more
2: Than will preserve just so much strength in us
3: As will revenge these bitter woes of ours.
5: Thy niece and I, poor creatures, want our hands
6: And cannot passionate our tenfold grief
7: With folded arms. This poor right hand of mine
8: Is left to tyrannize upon my breast,
9: Who, when my heart, all mad with misery,
10: Beats in this hollow prison of my flesh,
11: Then thus I thump it down.—
12: Thou map of woe, that thus dost talk in signs,
13: When thy poor heart beats with outrageous beating,
14: Thou canst not strike it thus to make it still.
15: Wound it with sighing, girl, kill it with groans;
16: Or get some little knife between thy teeth
17: And just against thy heart make thou a hole,
18: That all the tears that thy poor eyes let fall
19: May run into that sink and, soaking in,
20: Drown the lamenting fool in sea-salt tears.
21: Fie, brother, fie! Teach her not thus to lay
22: Such violent hands upon her tender life.
23: How now! Has sorrow made thee dote already?
24: Why, Marcus, no man should be mad but I.
25: What violent hands can she lay on her life?
26: Ah, wherefore dost thou urge the name of hands,
27: To bid Aeneas tell the tale twice o’er
28: How Troy was burnt and he made miserable?
29: O, handle not the theme, to talk of hands,
30: Lest we remember still that we have none.—
31: Fie, fie, how franticly I square my talk,
32: As if we should forget we had no hands
33: If Marcus did not name the word of hands!
34: Come, let’s fall to, and, gentle girl, eat this.
35: Here is no drink!—Hark, Marcus, what she says.
36: I can interpret all her martyred signs.
37: She says she drinks no other drink but tears
38: Brewed with her sorrow, mashed upon her cheeks.—
39: Speechless complainer, I will learn thy thought.

1: Help, grandsire, help! My aunt Lavinia
2: Follows me everywhere, I know not why.—

13: Read to her sons than she hath read to thee

18: For I have heard my grandsire say full oft,

32: Which is it, girl, of these?—Open them, boy.—
33: But thou art deeper read and better skilled.
35: Come and take choice of all my library,

37: Reveal the damned contriver of this deed.—
38: Why lifts she up her arms in sequence thus?
39: I think she means that there were more than one
40: Confederate in the fact. Ay, more there was,

42: Lucius, what book is that she tosseth so?
45: For love of her that’s gone,
46: Perhaps, she culled it from among the rest.
47: Soft! So busily she turns the leaves.

49: This is the tragic tale of Philomel,
50: And treats of Tereus’ treason and his rape.

52: See, brother, see! Note how she quotes the leaves.

55: Forced in the ruthless, vast, and gloomy woods?

57: O, had we never, never hunted there!—
58: Patterned by that the poet here describes,
59: By nature made for murders and for rapes.
60: O, why should nature build so foul a den,
61: Unless the gods delight in tragedies?
62: Give signs, sweet girl, for here are none but friends,
63: What Roman lord it was durst do the deed.
64: Or slunk not Saturnine, as Tarquin erst,
65: That left the camp to sin in Lucrece’ bed?

68: Inspire me, that I may this treason find.—
69: My lord, look here.—Look here, Lavinia.
70: This sandy plot is plain; guide, if thou canst,
71: This after me. I have writ my name
72: Without the help of any hand at all.

81: Performers of this heinous, bloody deed?
83: Tam lentus audis scelera, tam lentus vides?

86: To stir a mutiny in the mildest thoughts

21: Non eget Mauri iaculis, nec arcu.

37: What, have you met with her?

52: We will solicit heaven and move the gods
53: To send down Justice for to wreak our wrongs.
54: Come, to this gear. You are a good archer, Marcus.

61: Of my word, I have written to effect;
62: There’s not a god left unsolicited.

103: Nay, truly, sir, I could never say
