94: Than baits to fish or honey-stalks to sheep,
95: Whenas the one is wounded with the bait,
96: The other rotted with delicious feed.
97: But he will not entreat his son for us.
98: If Tamora entreat him, then he will,
99: For I can smooth and fill his agèd ears
100: With golden promises, that were his heart
101: Almost impregnable, his old ears deaf,
102: Yet should both ear and heart obey my tongue.
103: Go thou before to be our ambassador.
104: Say that the Emperor requests a parley
105: Of warlike Lucius, and appoint the meeting
106: Even at his father’s house, the old Andronicus.
108: And if he stand in hostage for his safety,
109: Bid him demand what pledge will please him best.
110: Your bidding shall I do effectually.
111: Now will I to that old Andronicus
112: And temper him with all the art I have
113: To pluck proud Lucius from the warlike Goths.
114: And now, sweet emperor, be blithe again,
115: And bury all thy fear in my devices.
116: Then go successantly, and plead to him.

1: Approvèd warriors and my faithful friends,
2: I have receivèd letters from great Rome
3: Which signifies what hate they bear their emperor
4: And how desirous of our sight they are.
5: Therefore, great lords, be as your titles witness,
6: Imperious, and impatient of your wrongs,
7: And wherein Rome hath done you any scathe,
9: Brave slip sprung from the great Andronicus,
10: Whose name was once our terror, now our comfort,
11: Whose high exploits and honorable deeds
12: Ingrateful Rome requites with foul contempt,
13: Be bold in us. We’ll follow where thou lead’st,
14: Like stinging bees in hottest summer’s day
15: Led by their master to the flowered fields,
16: And be avenged on cursèd Tamora.
17: And as he saith, so say we all with him.
18: I humbly thank him, and I thank you all.
19: But who comes here, led by a lusty Goth?
20: Renownèd Lucius, from our troops I strayed
21: To gaze upon a ruinous monastery,
22: And as I earnestly did fix mine eye
24: I heard a child cry underneath a wall.
25: I made unto the noise, when soon I heard
26: The crying babe controlled with this discourse:
27: Peace, tawny slave, half me and half thy dame!
28: Did not thy hue bewray whose brat thou art,
29: Had nature lent thee but thy mother’s look,
30: Villain, thou mightst have been an emperor.
31: But where the bull and cow are both milk white,
32: They never do beget a coal-black calf.
33: Peace, villain, peace!—even thus he rates the babe—
34: For I must bear thee to a trusty Goth
35: Who, when he knows thou art the Empress’ babe,
36: Will hold thee dearly for thy mother’s sake.
37: With this, my weapon drawn, I rushed upon him,
38: Surprised him suddenly, and brought him hither
39: To use as you think needful of the man.
40: O worthy Goth, this is the incarnate devil
41: That robbed Andronicus of his good hand;
42: This is the pearl that pleased your empress’ eye;
43: And here’s the base fruit of her burning lust.—
44: Say, wall-eyed slave, whither wouldst thou convey
45: This growing image of thy fiendlike face?
46: Why dost not speak? What, deaf? Not a word?—
47: A halter, soldiers! Hang him on this tree,
48: And by his side his fruit of bastardy.
49: Touch not the boy. He is of royal blood.
50: Too like the sire for ever being good.
51: First hang the child, that he may see it sprawl,
52: A sight to vex the father’s soul withal.
55: And bear it from me to the Empress.
56: If thou do this, I’ll show thee wondrous things
57: That highly may advantage thee to hear.
58: If thou wilt not, befall what may befall,
59: I’ll speak no more but Vengeance rot you all!
60: Say on, and if it please me which thou speak’st,
61: Thy child shall live, and I will see it nourished.
62: And if it please thee? Why, assure thee, Lucius,
63: ’Twill vex thy soul to hear what I shall speak;
64: For I must talk of murders, rapes, and massacres,
65: Acts of black night, abominable deeds,
67: Ruthful to hear, yet piteously performed.
68: And this shall all be buried in my death,
69: Unless thou swear to me my child shall live.
70: Tell on thy mind. I say thy child shall live.
71: Swear that he shall, and then I will begin.
72: Who should I swear by? Thou believest no god.
73: That granted, how canst thou believe an oath?
74: What if I do not? As indeed I do not.
75: Yet, for I know thou art religious
76: And hast a thing within thee callèd conscience,
77: With twenty popish tricks and ceremonies
78: Which I have seen thee careful to observe,
79: Therefore I urge thy oath; for that I know
80: An idiot holds his bauble for a god
81: And keeps the oath which by that god he swears,
82: To that I’ll urge him. Therefore thou shalt vow
83: By that same god, what god soe’er it be
84: That thou adorest and hast in reverence,
85: To save my boy, to nourish and bring him up,
86: Or else I will discover naught to thee.
87: Even by my god I swear to thee I will.
88: First know thou, I begot him on the Empress.
89: O, most insatiate and luxurious woman!
90: Tut, Lucius, this was but a deed of charity
91: To that which thou shalt hear of me anon.
92: ’Twas her two sons that murdered Bassianus.
93: They cut thy sister’s tongue, and ravished her,
94: And cut her hands, and trimmed her as thou sawest.
95: O detestable villain, call’st thou that trimming?
96: Why, she was washed, and cut, and trimmed; and ’twas
98: Trim sport for them which had the doing of it.
99: O, barbarous beastly villains, like thyself!
100: Indeed, I was their tutor to instruct them.
101: That codding spirit had they from their mother,
102: As sure a card as ever won the set;
103: That bloody mind I think they learned of me,
104: As true a dog as ever fought at head.
105: Well, let my deeds be witness of my worth.
106: I trained thy brethren to that guileful hole
107: Where the dead corpse of Bassianus lay.
108: I wrote the letter that thy father found,
109: And hid the gold within that letter mentioned,
110: Confederate with the Queen and her two sons.
111: And what not done that thou hast cause to rue,
112: Wherein I had no stroke of mischief in it?
113: I played the cheater for thy father’s hand,
114: And, when I had it, drew myself apart
115: And almost broke my heart with extreme laughter.
116: I pried me through the crevice of a wall
117: When, for his hand, he had his two sons’ heads,
118: Beheld his tears, and laughed so heartily
119: That both mine eyes were rainy like to his.
120: And when I told the Empress of this sport,
121: She sounded almost at my pleasing tale,
122: And for my tidings gave me twenty kisses.
123: What, canst thou say all this and never blush?
124: Ay, like a black dog, as the saying is.
125: Art thou not sorry for these heinous deeds?
126: Ay, that I had not done a thousand more.
127: Even now I curse the day—and yet, I think,
128: Few come within the compass of my curse—
129: Wherein I did not some notorious ill,
130: As kill a man, or else devise his death;
131: Ravish a maid or plot the way to do it;
132: Accuse some innocent and forswear myself;
133: Set deadly enmity between two friends;
134: Make poor men’s cattle break their necks;
135: Set fire on barns and haystalks in the night,
136: And bid the owners quench them with their tears.
137: Oft have I digged up dead men from their graves
138: And set them upright at their dear friends’ door,
139: Even when their sorrows almost was forgot,
140: And on their skins, as on the bark of trees,
141: Have with my knife carvèd in Roman letters
142: Let not your sorrow die, though I am dead.
143: But I have done a thousand dreadful things
144: As willingly as one would kill a fly,
145: And nothing grieves me heartily indeed
146: But that I cannot do ten thousand more.
147: Bring down the devil, for he must not die
148: So sweet a death as hanging presently.
149: If there be devils, would I were a devil,
150: To live and burn in everlasting fire,
151: So I might have your company in hell
152: But to torment you with my bitter tongue.
153: Sirs, stop his mouth, and let him speak no more.
154: My lord, there is a messenger from Rome
155: Desires to be admitted to your presence.
157: Welcome, Aemilius. What’s the news from Rome?
158: Lord Lucius, and you princes of the Goths,
159: The Roman Emperor greets you all by me;
160: And, for he understands you are in arms,
161: He craves a parley at your father’s house,
162: Willing you to demand your hostages,
163: And they shall be immediately delivered.
165: Aemilius, let the Emperor give his pledges
166: Unto my father and my uncle Marcus,
167: And we will come. March away.

1: Thus, in this strange and sad habiliment
3: And say I am Revenge, sent from below
4: To join with him and right his heinous wrongs.
5: Knock at his study, where they say he keeps
6: To ruminate strange plots of dire revenge.
7: Tell him Revenge is come to join with him
8: And work confusion on his enemies.
10: Is it your trick to make me ope the door,
11: That so my sad decrees may fly away
12: And all my study be to no effect?
13: You are deceived, for what I mean to do,
14: See here, in bloody lines I have set down,
15: And what is written shall be executed.
16: Titus, I am come to talk with thee.
17: No, not a word. How can I grace my talk,
18: Wanting a hand to give it action?
19: Thou hast the odds of me; therefore, no more.
20: If thou didst know me, thou wouldst talk with me.
21: I am not mad. I know thee well enough.
22: Witness this wretched stump; witness these crimson lines;
24: Witness these trenches made by grief and care;
25: Witness the tiring day and heavy night;
26: Witness all sorrow that I know thee well
27: For our proud empress, mighty Tamora.
28: Is not thy coming for my other hand?
29: Know, thou sad man, I am not Tamora.
30: She is thy enemy, and I thy friend.
31: I am Revenge, sent from th’ infernal kingdom
32: To ease the gnawing vulture of thy mind
33: By working wreakful vengeance on thy foes.
34: Come down and welcome me to this world’s light.
35: Confer with me of murder and of death.
36: There’s not a hollow cave or lurking-place,
37: No vast obscurity or misty vale
38: Where bloody murder or detested rape
39: Can couch for fear but I will find them out,
40: And in their ears tell them my dreadful name,
41: Revenge, which makes the foul offender quake.
42: Art thou Revenge? And art thou sent to me
43: To be a torment to mine enemies?
44: I am. Therefore come down and welcome me.
45: Do me some service ere I come to thee.
46: Lo, by thy side, where Rape and Murder stands,
47: Now give some surance that thou art Revenge:
48: Stab them, or tear them on thy chariot wheels,
49: And then I’ll come and be thy wagoner,
50: And whirl along with thee about the globe,
51: Provide thee two proper palfreys, black as jet,
52: To hale thy vengeful wagon swift away,
53: And find out murderers in their guilty caves.
54: And when thy car is loaden with their heads,
55: I will dismount and by thy wagon wheel
56: Trot like a servile footman all day long,
57: Even from Hyperion’s rising in the east
58: Until his very downfall in the sea.
59: And day by day I’ll do this heavy task,
60: So thou destroy Rapine and Murder there.
61: These are my ministers and come with me.
62: Are they thy ministers? What are they called?
63: Rape and Murder; therefore callèd so
64: ’Cause they take vengeance of such kind of men.
65: Good Lord, how like the Empress’ sons they are,
66: And you the Empress! But we worldly men
68: O sweet Revenge, now do I come to thee,
69: And if one arm’s embracement will content thee,
70: I will embrace thee in it by and by.
71: This closing with him fits his lunacy.
72: Whate’er I forge to feed his brainsick humors,
73: Do you uphold and maintain in your speeches,
74: For now he firmly takes me for Revenge;
75: And, being credulous in this mad thought,
76: I’ll make him send for Lucius his son;
77: And whilst I at a banquet hold him sure,
78: I’ll find some cunning practice out of hand
79: To scatter and disperse the giddy Goths,
80: Or, at the least, make them his enemies.
81: See, here he comes, and I must ply my theme.
82: Long have I been forlorn, and all for thee.
83: Welcome, dread Fury, to my woeful house.—
84: Rapine and Murder, you are welcome too.
85: How like the Empress and her sons you are!
86: Well are you fitted, had you but a Moor.
87: Could not all hell afford you such a devil?
88: For well I wot the Empress never wags
89: But in her company there is a Moor;
90: And, would you represent our queen aright,
91: It were convenient you had such a devil.
92: But welcome as you are. What shall we do?
93: What wouldst thou have us do, Andronicus?
94: Show me a murderer; I’ll deal with him.
95: Show me a villain that hath done a rape,
96: And I am sent to be revenged on him.
97: Show me a thousand that hath done thee wrong,
98: And I will be revengèd on them all.
99: Look round about the wicked streets of Rome,
100: And when thou findst a man that’s like thyself,
101: Good Murder, stab him; he’s a murderer.
102: Go thou with him, and when it is thy hap
104: To find another that is like to thee,
105: Good Rapine, stab him; he is a ravisher.
106: Go thou with them; and in the Emperor’s court
108: There is a queen attended by a Moor.
109: Well shalt thou know her by thine own proportion,
110: For up and down she doth resemble thee.
111: I pray thee, do on them some violent death.
112: They have been violent to me and mine.
113: Well hast thou lessoned us; this shall we do.
114: But would it please thee, good Andronicus,
115: To send for Lucius, thy thrice-valiant son,
116: Who leads towards Rome a band of warlike Goths,
117: And bid him come and banquet at thy house?
118: When he is here, even at thy solemn feast,
119: I will bring in the Empress and her sons,
120: The Emperor himself, and all thy foes,
121: And at thy mercy shall they stoop and kneel,
122: And on them shalt thou ease thy angry heart.
123: What says Andronicus to this device?
124: Marcus, my brother, ’tis sad Titus calls.
125: Go, gentle Marcus, to thy nephew Lucius.
126: Thou shalt inquire him out among the Goths.
127: Bid him repair to me and bring with him
128: Some of the chiefest princes of the Goths.
129: Bid him encamp his soldiers where they are.
130: Tell him the Emperor and the Empress too
131: Feast at my house, and he shall feast with them.
132: This do thou for my love, and so let him,
133: As he regards his agèd father’s life.
134: This will I do, and soon return again.
135: Now will I hence about thy business
136: And take my ministers along with me.
137: Nay, nay, let Rape and Murder stay with me,
138: Or else I’ll call my brother back again
139: And cleave to no revenge but Lucius.
140: What say you, boys? Will you abide with him
141: Whiles I go tell my lord the Emperor
142: How I have governed our determined jest?
143: Yield to his humor, smooth and speak him fair,
144: And tarry with him till I turn again.
145: I knew them all, though they supposed me mad,
146: And will o’erreach them in their own devices—
147: A pair of cursèd hellhounds and their dam!
148: Madam, depart at pleasure. Leave us here.
150: To lay a complot to betray thy foes.
151: I know thou dost; and, sweet Revenge, farewell.
152: Tell us, old man, how shall we be employed?
153: Tut, I have work enough for you to do.—
154: Publius, come hither; Caius, and Valentine.
157: The Empress’ sons, I take them—Chiron, Demetrius.
158: Fie, Publius, fie, thou art too much deceived.
159: The one is Murder, and Rape is the other’s name;
160: And therefore bind them, gentle Publius.
161: Caius and Valentine, lay hands on them.
162: Oft have you heard me wish for such an hour,
163: And now I find it. Therefore bind them sure,
164: And stop their mouths if they begin to cry.
165: Villains, forbear! We are the Empress’ sons.
166: And therefore do we what we are commanded.—
167: Stop close their mouths; let them not speak a word.
168: Is he sure bound? Look that you bind them fast.
169: Come, come, Lavinia. Look, thy foes are bound.—
170: Sirs, stop their mouths. Let them not speak to me,
171: But let them hear what fearful words I utter.—
173: Here stands the spring whom you have stained with mud,
175: This goodly summer with your winter mixed.
176: You killed her husband, and for that vile fault
177: Two of her brothers were condemned to death,
178: My hand cut off and made a merry jest,
179: Both her sweet hands, her tongue, and that more dear
180: Than hands or tongue, her spotless chastity,
181: Inhuman traitors, you constrained and forced.
182: What would you say if I should let you speak?
183: Villains, for shame you could not beg for grace.
184: Hark, wretches, how I mean to martyr you.
185: This one hand yet is left to cut your throats,
186: Whiles that Lavinia ’tween her stumps doth hold
187: The basin that receives your guilty blood.
188: You know your mother means to feast with me,
189: And calls herself Revenge, and thinks me mad.
190: Hark, villains, I will grind your bones to dust,
191: And with your blood and it I’ll make a paste,
192: And of the paste a coffin I will rear,
193: And make two pasties of your shameful heads,
194: And bid that strumpet, your unhallowed dam,
195: Like to the earth swallow her own increase.
196: This is the feast that I have bid her to,
197: And this the banquet she shall surfeit on;
198: For worse than Philomel you used my daughter,
199: And worse than Procne I will be revenged.
200: And now prepare your throats.—Lavinia, come,
202: And when that they are dead,
203: Let me go grind their bones to powder small,
204: And with this hateful liquor temper it,
205: And in that paste let their vile heads be baked.
207: To make this banquet, which I wish may prove
208: More stern and bloody than the Centaurs’ feast.
209: So. Now bring them in, for I’ll play the cook
210: And see them ready against their mother comes.

1: Uncle Marcus, since ’tis my father’s mind
2: That I repair to Rome, I am content.
3: And ours with thine, befall what fortune will.
4: Good uncle, take you in this barbarous Moor,
5: This ravenous tiger, this accursèd devil.
6: Let him receive no sust’nance. Fetter him
7: Till he be brought unto the Empress’ face
8: For testimony of her foul proceedings.
9: And see the ambush of our friends be strong.
10: I fear the Emperor means no good to us.
11: Some devil whisper curses in my ear
12: And prompt me that my tongue may utter forth
13: The venomous malice of my swelling heart.
15: Sirs, help our uncle to convey him in.
16: The trumpets show the Emperor is at hand.
17: What, hath the firmament more suns than one?
18: What boots it thee to call thyself a sun?
19: Rome’s emperor, and nephew, break the parle.
20: These quarrels must be quietly debated.
21: The feast is ready which the careful Titus
22: Hath ordained to an honorable end,
23: For peace, for love, for league and good to Rome.
24: Please you therefore draw nigh and take your places.
28: And welcome, all. Although the cheer be poor,
29: ’Twill fill your stomachs. Please you eat of it.
30: Why art thou thus attired, Andronicus?
31: Because I would be sure to have all well
32: To entertain your Highness and your empress.
33: We are beholding to you, good Andronicus.
34: An if your Highness knew my heart, you were.—
35: My lord the Emperor, resolve me this:
36: Was it well done of rash Virginius
37: To slay his daughter with his own right hand
38: Because she was enforced, stained, and deflowered?
41: Because the girl should not survive her shame,
42: And by her presence still renew his sorrows.
43: A reason mighty, strong, and effectual;
44: A pattern, precedent, and lively warrant
45: For me, most wretched, to perform the like.
46: Die, die, Lavinia, and thy shame with thee,
47: And with thy shame thy father’s sorrow die.
48: What hast thou done, unnatural and unkind?
49: Killed her for whom my tears have made me blind.
50: I am as woeful as Virginius was,
51: And have a thousand times more cause than he
52: To do this outrage, and it now is done.
53: What, was she ravished? Tell who did the deed.
54: Will ’t please you eat?—Will ’t please your Highness feed?
56: Why hast thou slain thine only daughter thus?
58: They ravished her and cut away her tongue,
59: And they, ’twas they, that did her all this wrong.
60: Go fetch them hither to us presently.
61: Why, there they are, both bakèd in this pie,
62: Whereof their mother daintily hath fed,
63: Eating the flesh that she herself hath bred.
64: ’Tis true, ’tis true! Witness my knife’s sharp point.
65: Die, frantic wretch, for this accursèd deed.
66: Can the son’s eye behold his father bleed?
67: There’s meed for meed, death for a deadly deed.
68: You sad-faced men, people and sons of Rome,
69: By uproars severed as a flight of fowl
70: Scattered by winds and high tempestuous gusts,
71: O, let me teach you how to knit again
72: This scattered corn into one mutual sheaf,
73: These broken limbs again into one body,
74: Lest Rome herself be bane unto herself,
75: And she whom mighty kingdoms curtsy to,
76: Like a forlorn and desperate castaway,
78: But if my frosty signs and chaps of age,
80: Cannot induce you to attend my words,
81: Speak, Rome’s dear friend, as erst our ancestor,
82: When with his solemn tongue he did discourse
84: The story of that baleful burning night
85: When subtle Greeks surprised King Priam’s Troy.
86: Tell us what Sinon hath bewitched our ears,
87: Or who hath brought the fatal engine in
88: That gives our Troy, our Rome, the civil wound.—
89: My heart is not compact of flint nor steel,
90: Nor can I utter all our bitter grief,
91: But floods of tears will drown my oratory
92: And break my utterance even in the time
93: When it should move you to attend me most
95: Here’s Rome’s young captain. Let him tell the tale,
96: While I stand by and weep to hear him speak.
97: Then, gracious auditory, be it known to you
98: That Chiron and the damned Demetrius
99: Were they that murderèd our emperor’s brother,
100: And they it were that ravishèd our sister.
101: For their fell faults our brothers were beheaded,
102: Our father’s tears despised, and basely cozened
103: Of that true hand that fought Rome’s quarrel out
104: And sent her enemies unto the grave;
106: The gates shut on me, and turned weeping out
107: To beg relief among Rome’s enemies,
108: Who drowned their enmity in my true tears
109: And oped their arms to embrace me as a friend.
110: I am the turned-forth, be it known to you,
111: That have preserved her welfare in my blood
112: And from her bosom took the enemy’s point,
113: Sheathing the steel in my advent’rous body.
114: Alas, you know I am no vaunter, I;
115: My scars can witness, dumb although they are,
116: That my report is just and full of truth.
117: But soft, methinks I do digress too much,
118: Citing my worthless praise. O, pardon me,
119: For when no friends are by, men praise themselves.
120: Now is my turn to speak. Behold the child.
122: The issue of an irreligious Moor,
123: Chief architect and plotter of these woes.
124: The villain is alive in Titus’ house,
125: And as he is to witness, this is true.
126: Now judge what cause had Titus to revenge
128: Or more than any living man could bear.
129: Now have you heard the truth. What say you, Romans?
131: Have we done aught amiss? Show us wherein,
132: And from the place where you behold us pleading,
134: Will, hand in hand, all headlong hurl ourselves,
135: And on the ragged stones beat forth our souls,
136: And make a mutual closure of our house.
137: Speak, Romans, speak, and if you say we shall,
138: Lo, hand in hand, Lucius and I will fall.
139: Come, come, thou reverend man of Rome,
140: And bring our emperor gently in thy hand,
141: Lucius our emperor, for well I know
142: The common voice do cry it shall be so.
143: Lucius, all hail, Rome’s royal emperor!
144: Go, go into old Titus’ sorrowful house,
145: And hither hale that misbelieving Moor
146: To be adjudged some direful slaught’ring death
147: As punishment for his most wicked life.
148: Lucius, all hail, Rome’s gracious governor!
149: Thanks, gentle Romans. May I govern so
150: To heal Rome’s harms and wipe away her woe!
151: But, gentle people, give me aim awhile,
152: For nature puts me to a heavy task.
153: Stand all aloof, but, uncle, draw you near
154: To shed obsequious tears upon this trunk.
155: O, take this warm kiss on thy pale cold lips,
156: These sorrowful drops upon thy bloodstained face,
157: The last true duties of thy noble son.
158: Tear for tear, and loving kiss for kiss,
159: Thy brother Marcus tenders on thy lips.
160: O, were the sum of these that I should pay
161: Countless and infinite, yet would I pay them.
162: Come hither, boy. Come, come, and learn of us
163: To melt in showers. Thy grandsire loved thee well.
164: Many a time he danced thee on his knee,
165: Sung thee asleep, his loving breast thy pillow;
166: Many a story hath he told to thee,
167: And bid thee bear his pretty tales in mind
168: And talk of them when he was dead and gone.
169: How many thousand times hath these poor lips,
170: When they were living, warmed themselves on thine!
171: O, now, sweet boy, give them their latest kiss.
172: Bid him farewell; commit him to the grave.
173: Do them that kindness, and take leave of them.
174: O grandsire, grandsire, ev’n with all my heart
175: Would I were dead so you did live again!
176: O Lord, I cannot speak to him for weeping.
177: My tears will choke me if I ope my mouth.
178: You sad Andronici, have done with woes.
179: Give sentence on this execrable wretch
180: That hath been breeder of these dire events.
181: Set him breast-deep in earth and famish him.
182: There let him stand and rave and cry for food.
183: If anyone relieves or pities him,
184: For the offense he dies. This is our doom.
185: Some stay to see him fastened in the earth.
186: Ah, why should wrath be mute and fury dumb?
